Moreover, 10% PEG-based Osmo priming significantly enhanced GP, seedling vigor, seedling growth, chlorophyll a, b, and total chlorophyll content, Fv/Fm, and reduced mean germination time in NILs. Therefore, these findings suggest the effectiveness of PEG-based Osmo priming in significantly enhancing the drought tolerance resilience of IR64-derived NILs. Osmo priming with PEG-6000 resulted in better germination and seedling growth under osmotic stress situations and could be a very simple, inexpensive way of counteracting osmotic stress in rice.

title: Ericoid mycorrhizal fungi recover from nitrogen additions in a dry heathland experiment in southern England
summary: 1. Ericoid mycorrhizal fungi are fundamental for heathlands’ establishment and functioning and contribute to the essential ecosystem services these endangered habitats provide, yet they are overlooked by environmental monitoring policies. A
content: 1. Ericoid mycorrhizal fungi are fundamental for heathlands’ establishment and functioning and contribute to the essential ecosystem services these endangered habitats provide, yet they are overlooked by environmental monitoring policies. As nitrogen pollution declines across Europe, policymakers need measurable indicators of habitat recovery encompassing above- and below-ground parts of the ecosystem. 2. We conducted a manipulation experiment simulating atmospheric nitrogen pollution on pioneer and mature heather (Calluna vulgaris) stands in a dry heathland to determine its impact on the functionality and composition of ericoid mycorrhizal communities, and to assess their viability as short-term recovery indicators in three substrates: heather roots, a common leafy liverwort (Cephaloziella divaricata), and soil. Additionally, we measured aboveground liverwort biomass, rhizoid colonisation and density, soil and heather leaf chemistry. 3. After an initial negative impact of nitrogen fertilisation, ericoid mycorrhizal colonisation in heather roots, ericoid mycorrhizal fungi of the genus Hyaloscypha in roots and soil, and symbiotic Pezoloma in liverworts, all recovered within seven months. Liverwort biomass, density and rhizoid colonisation were negatively affected, and did not recover. 4. The effect of nitrogen fertilisation and recovery trajectories depended on substrate, age of heather stands, and ericoid mycorrhizal morphotype and taxon. Pioneer plants were more sensitive to treatments than mature plants. 5. Policy implications: Our findings open new perspectives on the potential use of mycorrhizal fungi as indicators of recovery from nitrogen pollution in heathlands. The rapid recovery observed in pioneer heather communities suggests that ericoid mycorrhizal fungi can provide short-term measures of belowground recovery, but plant successional stage and fungal identity must be considered. Our results support the development of targeted and stage-specific belowground indicators to complement existing aboveground-focussed indicators, to improve assessment of recovery from nitrogen pollution in heathland conservation and restoration policy.

title: Aerobic methane oxidation by microorganisms exacerbates neurotoxic methylmercury accumulation in rice paddy fields.
summary: Aerobic methane (CH4) oxidation is the dominant biological sink for CH4 in wetland soils and is increasingly linked to diverse biogeochemical processes; however, whether and how aerobic CH4 oxidation influences the production of the neuroto
content: Aerobic methane (CH4) oxidation is the dominant biological sink for CH4 in wetland soils and is increasingly linked to diverse biogeochemical processes; however, whether and how aerobic CH4 oxidation influences the production of the neurotoxin methylmercury (MeHg) through microbial mercury (Hg) methylation remains poorly understood. Here, we combined a ~3300 km field survey across the main rice-producing areas of China with 13CH4-DNA-stable isotope probing (SIP) to investigate the microbial linkage between aerobic CH4 oxidation and Hg methylation in paddy fields. Field observations showed positive relationships between CH4 oxidation activity and the ratio of MeHg at a continental scale, as well as between gene abundances of CH4 oxidation (pmoA) and Hg methylation (hgcA). Microcosm experiments further demonstrated that CH4 addition significantly increased MeHg production by 40.7-177.7% and enhanced hgcA gene expression by 49.5-416.0% across three typical paddy soils. Moreover, 13CH4-DNA-SIP analyses identified 112 hgcA-containing operational taxonomic units (OTUs) that incorporated 13CH4-derived 13C, of which 75.0-85.5% were affiliated with the families Geobacteraceae, Anaerolineaceae, and unclassified Desulfobacterales. Integrated analyses of 13C-metagenome-assembled genomes and metabolomics indicated that this carbon transfer was likely mediated by metabolic handoffs from methanotrophs to Hg-methylating microorganisms through intermediates (e.g., malate and fumarate) released during aerobic CH4 oxidation. Soil incubation and pure-culture experiments further confirmed the functional significance of methanotroph-derived metabolites, as their addition significantly enhanced MeHg production. These findings highlight microbial metabolic handoffs as an important mechanism linking aerobic CH4 oxidation and Hg methylation, with implications for developing synergistic strategies for MeHg pollution mitigation and carbon reduction.

title: Substituting inorganic nitrogen with organic inputs improves yield-scaled greenhouse gas emissions and soil health indicators: evidence from a long-term fertilizer experiment
summary: Introduction Sustainable nitrogen management must maintain cereal productivity while limiting greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and improving soil health. We evaluated whether partial inorganic-N substitution affects cereal productivity and GH
content: Introduction Sustainable nitrogen management must maintain cereal productivity while limiting greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and improving soil health. We evaluated whether partial inorganic-N substitution affects cereal productivity and GHG emissions differently across organic input types in a long-term fertilizer experiment. Methods Eight nutrient-management treatments were evaluated in a fixed-plot experiment established in 2002. Four integrated nutrient-management treatments replaced 25% of Soil Test Crop Response (STCR)-based inorganic N with farmyard manure (FYM), vermicompost (VC), urban compost (UC), or crop residue (CR). Soil CO₂, N₂O, and CH₄ fluxes were monitored during the 2024-2025 wheat season, and post-harvest soil chemical and biological indicators and wheat yield were measured. Results Relative to 100% STCR-based NPK, FYM and UC reduced cumulative N₂O-N emissions by 31% and 26%, respectively, whereas VC and CR increased them by approximately 24% and 21%. Treatment effects on cumulative CO₂-C and CH₄-C fluxes were not significant, and all treatments were small net CH₄ sinks. Organic-containing treatments increased soil organic carbon from 0.49% in the control to 0.55%-0.87%. FYM substitution produced the greatest grain yield (5,388 kg ha⁻¹), 13% above 100% STCR-based NPK. Discussion Long-term nutrient management influenced soil-health indicators and wheat yield, but the reported GHG emissions represent only the 2024-2025 wheat season. Yield-scaled GHG responses depended on organic-input quality and were not uniformly improved by substitution. Locally available, quality-controlled FYM or UC may reduce N₂O intensity, subject to material cost, labor, availability, and competing uses.

title: Foliar biostimulants with nano-chelated Zn-B-Si reduce rind disorders and improve yield and fruit quality in ‘Washington’ Navel orange
summary: Preharvest rind disorders, particularly fruit cracking and creasing, are major causes of yield loss and export downgrading in ‘Washington’ Navel orange. These disorders are associated with impaired peel calcium, boron, and silicon nutrition
content: Preharvest rind disorders, particularly fruit cracking and creasing, are major causes of yield loss and export downgrading in ‘Washington’ Navel orange. These disorders are associated with impaired peel calcium, boron, and silicon nutrition, cell-wall degradation, and rind turgor imbalance. Although biostimulants and nano-nutrients have shown individual benefits in fruit crops, their combined effectiveness against citrus rind disorders has not been systematically evaluated or compared with the industry-standard Ca + GA₃ program. This two-season field study (2024–2025) evaluated melatonin, γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA), and 24-epibrassinolide (EBR), applied individually or combined with a nano-chelated Zn-B-Si formulation, together with a standalone nano-silicon treatment and the conventional Ca + GA₃ program in a randomized complete block design. GABA + nano (Zn-B-Si) (T10) ranked first for most traits, and EBR + nano (Zn-B-Si) (T9) was statistically comparable to it for several traits (e.g., fruit number, fruit set and chlorophyll). Both combinations generally surpassed their individual applications and the conventional Ca + GA₃ standard in vegetative growth, yield and fruit quality across both seasons. T10 reduced fruit cracking by up to 65.5%, creasing by up to 66.8% and fruit drop by up to 53% compared with the untreated control. Biostimulant–nanonutrient co-application, particularly GABA combined with nano-chelated Zn-B-Si, is a promising candidate strategy for reducing rind-disorder incidence and improving yield and fruit quality in ‘Washington’ Navel orange. Costs, total active-ingredient input and packinghouse grading outcomes were not assessed and require further study.

title: Bioconvection flow of Williamson nanofluid due to gyrotactic microorganisms on curved surface with Cattaneo Christov heat and mass fluxes
summary: Characterizing complex fluid dynamics along non-flat boundaries is crucial for developing advanced micro-biofluidic engineering devices, advanced heat exchangers, and target-specific pharmaceutical delivery systems. This study aims to inves
content: Characterizing complex fluid dynamics along non-flat boundaries is crucial for developing advanced micro-biofluidic engineering devices, advanced heat exchangers, and target-specific pharmaceutical delivery systems. This study aims to investigate the bioconvective boundary layer flow of a Williamson nanofluid containing gyrotactic microorganisms over a curved stretching sheet. The physical modelling framework assumes an unsteady-state, two-dimensional, incompressible flow subject to a continuous magnetic field and wave-like transport governed by Cattaneo-Christov heat and mass fluxes. Similarity variables are utilized to reduce the governing partial differential equations into a nonlinear ordinary differential system, which is solved analytically via the Homotopy Analysis Method. The results demonstrate that increasing the geometric surface curvature parameter directly lowers fluid resistance and broadens the velocity boundary layer while, elevating the thermal relaxation time parameter introduces heat transfer delays that systematically shrink the localized thermal boundary thickness. The present work has a close agreement with the published work.

title: Freeze-drying-induced structural enhancement of graphene quantum dot–modified carboxymethyl cellulose beads for highly efficient cypermethrin removal
summary: The influence of drying procedures on the pore structure and adsorption performance of graphene quantum dot-modified carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC/GQD) beads for cypermethrin removal has not been sufficiently elucidated. Therefore, hydrogel
content: The influence of drying procedures on the pore structure and adsorption performance of graphene quantum dot-modified carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC/GQD) beads for cypermethrin removal has not been sufficiently elucidated. Therefore, hydrogel and cryogel forms of CMC/GQD beads were comparatively evaluated to clarify the effect of oven-drying and freeze-drying on cypermethrin adsorption from aqueous media. Freeze-drying preserved the interconnected porous structure and increased the specific surface area from 7.78 m 2 g -1 for the oven-dried hydrogel to 107.86 m 2 g -1 for the cryogel. Taguchi optimization identified an initial cypermethrin concentration of 90 mg L -1 , pH 6, an adsorbent dosage of 1 g L -1 , and a contact time of 120 min as the optimum conditions. Equilibrium analysis showed that the hydrogel and cryogel were better described by the Langmuir (R 2 = 0.9971) and Freundlich (R 2 = 0.9942) models, respectively, indicating predominantly monolayer adsorption on relatively uniform sites for the hydrogel and heterogeneous, multilayer adsorption for the cryogel. The Langmuir model yielded theoretical maximum adsorption capacities of 174.5 and 296.7 mg g -1 for the hydrogel and cryogel, respectively, while the experimentally determined maximum adsorption capacities were 65.4 and 276.12 mg g -1 , respectively. Kinetic analysis indicated that hydrogel adsorption followed the pseudo-second-order model, whereas cryogel adsorption was described by both pseudo-second-order kinetics and liquid-film diffusion. Thermodynamic analysis confirmed spontaneous and exothermic adsorption, with ΔH° = -86.09 kJ mol -1 and ΔS° = -230 J mol -1 K -1 . The cryogel achieved removal efficiencies of 98.7% in deionized water and 98.6% in simulated agricultural runoff. Moreover, using 0.1 M NaOH as the desorption agent, the cryogel maintained a removal efficiency above 75% for six consecutive cycles, although its efficiency decreased from 99.9% in the first cycle to 59.68% after eight cycles. These findings demonstrate that freeze-drying substantially improves the porous structure and adsorption capacity of CMC/GQD beads, providing a reusable adsorbent for cypermethrin-contaminated water.

title: Microbial carbon turnover, particulate organic carbon concentrations, respiration rates from Marine Snow Catcher deployments in the Iceland Basin during RRS Discovery cruise DY180 (May–June 2024)
summary: This dataset contains measurements of microbial respiration, particulate organic carbon concentrations and microbial carbon turnover on suspended, slow sinking and fast-sinking particles collected in the Iceland Basin, North Atlantic Ocean,
content: This dataset contains measurements of microbial respiration, particulate organic carbon concentrations and microbial carbon turnover on suspended, slow sinking and fast-sinking particles collected in the Iceland Basin, North Atlantic Ocean, during RRS Discovery cruise DY180 (May-June 2024). Particles were collected using Marine Snow Catchers deployed at 4 stations (S2-S5) and two depths (55-65 m and 120 m) during repeated occupations spanning different concentrations of chlorophyll. Incubation experiments were conducted to quantify microbial respiration and particulate organic carbon turnover. This work was undertaken by scientists at Imperial College London, National Oceanography Centre, UK, and the University of Liverpool as part of the PARTITRICS (PARTIcle Transformation and Respiration Influence on ocean Carbon Storage) project.

title: Microplastic interactions with terrestrial ecosystems, ecotoxicological risks and innovative degradation strategies
summary: This review examines the environmental fate, transport, and ecotoxicological impacts of Microplastic in terrestrial ecosystems, with emphasis on soil health, nutrient cycling, and plant responses. It also addresses how emerging biotechnolog
content: This review examines the environmental fate, transport, and ecotoxicological impacts of Microplastic in terrestrial ecosystems, with emphasis on soil health, nutrient cycling, and plant responses. It also addresses how emerging biotechnological and thermochemical strategies can enhance degradation efficiency and mitigate long-term ecological risks associated with persistent plastic accumulation. A structured literature review was conducted using peer-reviewed articles from soil science, environmental chemistry, and biotechnology sources. Studies were analyzed to summarize microplastic sources, degradation behavior, and transport pathways in soils, including leaching, bioturbation, wind-driven movement, and pore-scale migration. Microbial degradation mechanisms involving bacteria and fungi and enzyme-mediated breakdown were evaluated. Recent advances in enzyme engineering, protein engineering, gene editing tools, bioinformatics-guided enzyme discovery, and thermochemical methods such as pyrolysis were critically assessed for their potential in microplastic remediation. Microplastic negatively affect soil structure, porosity, and microbial activity, leading to disrupted nutrient cycling and reduced soil fertility. They impair plant growth by altering root architecture, physiological processes, and defense mechanisms, indirectly affecting ecosystem productivity. Although certain microorganisms can degrade plastics, their efficiency is too slow for environmental mitigation. Engineered enzymes and gene-edited microbial systems show improved degradation potential, while pyrolysis offers an alternative waste-to-resource pathway. However, limitations such as scalability, cost, and ecological safety restrict field application. Microplastic contamination poses a persistent threat to soil ecosystems and plant health. Integrated biotechnological and thermochemical approaches offer promising mitigation strategies. Future research should focus on scalable enzymatic systems, engineered microbes, and advanced gene-editing tools to enhance degradation efficiency and support long-term restoration of soil ecological balance. Not applicable.

title: Depth structures metabolic potential and warming responses in marine microbial eukaryotes
summary: Microbial eukaryotes are key drivers of food-web dynamics and nutrient cycling across the ocean's water column. Yet, how their metabolic potential is structured through depth remains largely unknown, limiting our ability to understand how m
content: Microbial eukaryotes are key drivers of food-web dynamics and nutrient cycling across the ocean's water column. Yet, how their metabolic potential is structured through depth remains largely unknown, limiting our ability to understand how microbial communities mediate biogeochemical transformations and how these functions may shift under climate change. Here, we combined a global-scale metagenomic analysis of tropical and subtropical samples spanning the full water column with bathypelagic metatranscriptomics to identify depth-dependent functional patterns across plankton size fractions. At depth, the functional composition of the nanoplankton size fraction was consistent with the export of surface-derived biomass, whereas the picoplankton size fraction showed signatures of resident communities, including depth-specific heterotrophic functions and bathypelagic-restricted fungal assemblages. Metabolic functional diversity was tightly coupled to taxonomic composition along the water column. Heterotrophic lineages contributed to phosphorus and sulfur acquisition at depth, revealing an undercharacterised eukaryotic role in deep-ocean nutrient cycling. Projections under end-of-century warming revealed spatially structured metabolic responses: subtropical intensification of photosynthetic capacity, subpolar stimulation of aerobic metabolism, and a decline of heterotrophic potential consistent with metabolic rebalancing within mixotrophic taxa. Our findings highlight the importance of marine microbial eukaryotes in ocean biogeochemistry, reveal their distinct functional roles across depths, and provide novel projections of how their metabolic potential may change under ocean warming.

title: After Net Zero: Why Holding Atmospheric CO₂ Requires Two Actuators, Bidirectional Emission Rights, and Element-Level Accounting
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: Net zero is defined in the Paris Agreement as a balance of flows, not a target for the atmospheric state. Earth-system simulations show that once anthropogenic CO₂ emissions cease, atmospheric CO₂ declines because sinks continue to absorb c
content: Net zero is defined in the Paris Agreement as a balance of flows, not a target for the atmospheric state. Earth-system simulations show that once anthropogenic CO₂ emissions cease, atmospheric CO₂ declines because sinks continue to absorb carbon. Holding any concentration therefore requires the capacity to move it in both directions, yet policy is designed to eliminate one actuator and build the other. This paper, a conceptual synthesis of Earth-system modelling, project-management science, crop physiology and the NDC record within a control-theoretic framework, treats post-net-zero atmospheric management as a bidirectional control problem. It makes five proposals: incorporate the systematic undershoot of iterative planning into climate target-setting; grow emission and removal flows in balance and control the state through their difference — removal being plannable infrastructure where reduction is fragmented negotiation — so that national gross emissions may rise when matched by verified removal; recognise that the achievable range of flows is bounded by political interests at both edges, fossil and decarbonisation industries above and CO₂-dependent agriculture below; operate emission rights in both directions, extending Article 6 with a removal exchange ratio above 1:1; and resolve inventories to the element level: carbon by pathway, oxygen as a check, methane and by-products.

title: Soil Erosion and Carbon Cycling in Farmland Under Climate Change: A Bibliometric Analysis and Research Progress
summary: Climate change may alter the coupling between farmland soil erosion and soil carbon cycling, yet the evolution of research themes and the net carbon consequences of erosion remain unclear. We combined bibliometric analysis with a critical l
content: Climate change may alter the coupling between farmland soil erosion and soil carbon cycling, yet the evolution of research themes and the net carbon consequences of erosion remain unclear. We combined bibliometric analysis with a critical literature synthesis of 653 publications indexed in the Web of Science Core Collection (1993–2025), using CiteSpace and VOSviewer, with keyword analyses focusing on 2016–2025. Publication output increased after 2010, particularly since 2020. Eight keyword clusters were identified, encompassing land-use change, soil organic carbon, soil erosion, nitrous oxide, remote sensing, climate change mitigation, soil hydrology, and carbon emissions. Keyword bursts for “stabilization” and “productivity” persisted through 2025. The literature synthesis suggests that extreme rainfall, drought–rainfall sequences, and freeze–thaw processes can modify erosion thresholds and sediment connectivity, influencing the selective transport and redistribution of soil organic carbon. Eroded carbon may be buried and stabilized or re-exposed and mineralized; thus, local carbon losses or depositional gains do not necessarily indicate net carbon emissions or sequestration. Divergent findings partly reflect differences in accounting boundaries, observation periods, carbon fractions, and methodological approaches. We propose a conceptual framework linking climate-driven erosion, carbon redistribution, stabilization–mineralization processes, and agricultural management feedbacks. Future research should integrate event-scale observations, source-to-sink carbon budgets, greenhouse gas assessments, and crop productivity to validate these proposed linkages.
