title: Ecosystem responses in Africa under different CO 2 fertilisation futures
source: African Journal of Range and Forage Science
summary: Climate model results and emission scenarios have been used in simulations to project ecosystem changes in Africa in response to warming and changing precipitation patterns. Less explored are plant responses to elevated CO2. The ecosystem m
content: Climate model results and emission scenarios have been used in simulations to project ecosystem changes in Africa in response to warming and changing precipitation patterns. Less explored are plant responses to elevated CO2. The ecosystem model Af-Range was used to address seven hypothesised responses for three climate forecasts and two shared socioeconomic pathways. The application represented Africa and herb, shrub, tree and herbivore dynamics. Remotely sensed surfaces were used to assess simulations. Simulations using the climate forecasts for pathway 3-7.0 and with the nutrient limitation hypothesis showed annual net primary production declining by 32% for the most extreme climate model (i.e. ACCESS-ESM1-5) but small changes under pathway 1-2.6. Tree cover expanded as those C3 plants were favoured by elevated atmospheric CO2, and leaf area indices and total aboveground live biomass increased. Differences in selected outcomes under the elevated CO2 hypotheses were often below 5%, but climate change effects differed greatly across the grasslands, closed and open shrub grasslands, and savanna and wooded savannas summarised. Soil total organic carbon concentration increased in open shrublands across all climate change models, whereas grasslands and savannas showed large changes in primary production, cover estimates and leaf area indices for shared socioeconomic pathway 3-7.0.

title: Comparative screening of organic additives in kerosene-based oil agglomeration of Zonguldak bituminous coal fines
source: Mineral Processing and Extractive Metallurgy Transactions of the Institutions of Mining and Metallurgy
summary: Four organic additives – carbon tetrachloride (CCl 4 ), bromoform (CHBr 3 ), methanol and ethanol – were compared as modifiers in kerosene-based oil agglomeration of Zonguldak bituminous coal fines that had been pre-cleaned by ZnCl 2 float–
content: Four organic additives – carbon tetrachloride (CCl 4 ), bromoform (CHBr 3 ), methanol and ethanol – were compared as modifiers in kerosene-based oil agglomeration of Zonguldak bituminous coal fines that had been pre-cleaned by ZnCl 2 float–sink separation (2.23 wt% ash). A 4 × 4 × 3 matrix of additive type, additive concentration (0.5, 5, 50 and 150 mg/L) and kerosene dosage (5, 10 and 15% of dry coal mass) were tested in three separately prepared runs per condition (48 conditions; 144 observations). Without kerosene, less than 1% of the feed was recovered as an agglomerated product. The recovered-product mass yield depended jointly on the additive type, concentration and kerosene dosage (three-way interaction, F (18, 96) = 5.49, p < 0.001), so no single additive ranking held across kerosene levels. The highest observed mean yield, 83.4%, was obtained with ethanol at 15% kerosene and 150 mg/L, compared with 71.6% for the additive-free control. Ethanol is a priority candidate in mass-yield screening rather than a demonstrated superior modifier. Because product ash and retained kerosene were not determined, the results concern recovered-product mass yield only; ash rejection, combustible recovery and separation selectivity cannot be established, and the low feed ash further limits any assessment of selectivity.

title: A Global Gross Primary Productivity (GPP) dataset derived from ESA’s Sentinel 3 mission data using the Quantum Yield (QY) model
summary: Abstract Gross primary productivity (GPP), the rate at which terrestrial vegetation fixes atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) through photosynthesis, is a fundamental component of the global carbon cycle. Accurate estimation of GPP is theref
content: Abstract Gross primary productivity (GPP), the rate at which terrestrial vegetation fixes atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) through photosynthesis, is a fundamental component of the global carbon cycle. Accurate estimation of GPP is therefore essential for quantifying terrestrial carbon uptake and assessing ecosystem responses to environmental change. This paper introduces a new global GPP dataset, the QY-GPP data, generated using the Quantum Yield (QY) model driven by Sentinel-3 OLCI OTCI and ERA5 climate data at 500-m spatial and 8-day temporal resolution. The QY model builds on the light use efficiency (LUE) concept by incorporating photosynthetic pathway-specific quantum yield terms to quantify the rate at which plants convert absorbed radiation into dry matter. The QY-GPP data shows a strong correlation (R 2 = 0.73, RMSE = 2.17gCm −2 d −1 , and MBE = 0.62gCm −2 d −1 ) with eddy covariance flux tower GPP measurements across diverse International Geosphere-Biosphere Programme (IGBP) biomes. Additionally, the QY-GPP data showed strong spatial consistency with the operational MOD17 GPP product, while exhibiting greater ranges and variability in highly productive biomes such as forests and croplands. The QY-GPP data is produced continuously from 2020 onwards, offering a valuable resource for advancing the understanding of terrestrial carbon dynamics.

title: Push–pull luminescent imidazole derivatives: ICT enables efficient picric acid sensing
summary: and were fully characterized by NMR and mass spectral analyses. The synthesized compounds exhibit strong luminescent properties due to their donor-acceptor (push-pull) electronic structures and possess pronounced excited-state charge transf
content: and were fully characterized by NMR and mass spectral analyses. The synthesized compounds exhibit strong luminescent properties due to their donor-acceptor (push-pull) electronic structures and possess pronounced excited-state charge transfer characteristics, as evidenced by steady-state and time-resolved spectroscopic experiments. Imidazole incorporated with donor groups in the phenyl rings at the 4- and 5-positions (3b) shows a greater extent of charge transfer and emits yellow color in polar solvents like DMSO and acetonitrile. Both the fluorophores were found to act as sensors of picric acid in the solution phase with a very low detection level (nM) by static quenching of the fluorescence emission mechanism. The sensitivity of the detection of picric acid by 3b was found to be almost 1000 fold higher than that by 3a, and the response time of 3b towards picric acid was ∼3 times faster than that of 3a.

title: A Bayesian framework for mapping subtropical montane cloud forest litterfall and its uncertainty from airborne LiDAR canopy structure
summary: Litterfall is a major pathway of forest carbon cycling, but field monitoring is labor-intensive for regional application. We developed a framework to map annual litterfall flux and its pixel-level uncertainty in subtropical montane cloud fo
content: Litterfall is a major pathway of forest carbon cycling, but field monitoring is labor-intensive for regional application. We developed a framework to map annual litterfall flux and its pixel-level uncertainty in subtropical montane cloud forests of northeastern Taiwan. The framework combined 2021–2023 annual litterfall flux and mean monthly leaf area index (LAI) from 16 plots (n = 48, 16 plots × 3 years) with 1-m airborne LiDAR canopy height models (CHMs) acquired in 2019, 2021, and 2024. Annual CHMs were projected across the acquisition gaps using an empirical canopy height growth model, enabling regional LAI upscaling (R 2 = 0.77 for both cross- and external validation). A hierarchical Bayesian model (Gamma likelihood, log link) related litterfall to LAI-derived leaf mass through a leaf-mass coefficient, summarized as an apparent litterfall-to-leaf-mass ratio (1.33 yr -1 ), and propagated uncertainty to every map pixel. Litterfall was mapped as the posterior predictive median (LF P50 ) with pixel-wise 95% credible intervals; regional medians were 4.59, 3.35, and 3.71 Mg ha -1 yr -1 in 2021–2023. Spatial heterogeneity was associated with canopy structure and, in a post hoc analysis, terrain aspect. In an exploratory analysis, replacing the year-level random effect of the leaf-mass coefficient with an annual radiation anomaly from global reanalysis data left the predictions nearly unchanged. The three-year record precludes causal inference, but the hierarchical structure allows this hypothesis to be re-evaluated as data accumulate. This study demonstrates how multi-temporal airborne LiDAR and Bayesian modeling can link plot-scale measurements to regional carbon dynamics in topographically complex forests.

title: Modelling low-trophic aquaculture in the North Sea: From parameter estimation to ecosystem dynamics
summary: The North Sea represents a promising but complex system for expanding sustainable food production through low-trophic aquaculture, particularly using bivalves and seaweed. However, assessing production potential and ecological carrying capa
content: The North Sea represents a promising but complex system for expanding sustainable food production through low-trophic aquaculture, particularly using bivalves and seaweed. However, assessing production potential and ecological carrying capacity in such systems requires mechanistic approaches that account for strong environmental variability and ecosystem interactions. Here, we present the parametrisation, sensitivity analysis, and application of a one-dimensional pelagic ecosystem model for the Dutch North Sea called Aqua-DEB. The model describes three functional groups: phytoplankton, zooplankton, and decomposers, supplemented with blue mussel ( Mytilus edulis ), and sugar kelp ( Saccharina latissima ), within a Dynamic Energy Budget framework. Parameters were estimated using existing empirical datasets, and model behaviour was evaluated under realistic environmental forcing and aquaculture scenarios. The results indicate that seaweed strongly compete with phytoplankton, through higher uptake rates and significant shading effects. In contrast, mussels occupy a niche where they accelerate remineralization, thereby stimulating primary production and their own growth. Sensitivity analysis revealed that the introduction of mussel and seaweed substantially alters the controls on ecosystem dynamics. These findings highlight that low-trophic aquaculture cannot be evaluated in isolation but must be considered within the broader ecosystem context. While the present model is designed to resolve key ecological mechanisms, its parametrisation and process-based structure provide a robust foundation for predictive applications. Coupling Aqua-DEB to three-dimensional hydrodynamic models represents a critical next step towards evaluating aquaculture performance, carrying capacity, and spatial management under future environmental change.

title: Ammonia excretion dynamics of the silverside (Basilichthys microlepidotus) during the juvenile-to-adult grow-out phase, under different body sizes and stocking densities in a recirculating aquaculture system (RAS)
source: Latin American Journal of Aquatic Research
summary: The Chilean silverside (Basilichthys microlepidotus) is an endemic freshwater species with emerging potential for aquaculture and conservation-oriented production. However, key bioengineering parameters required for system design and biomas
content: The Chilean silverside (Basilichthys microlepidotus) is an endemic freshwater species with emerging potential for aquaculture and conservation-oriented production. However, key bioengineering parameters required for system design and biomass management remain poorly defined. This study evaluated how body size and stocking density affect total ammonia nitrogen (TAN) excretion rates in a recirculating aquaculture system (RAS) under controlled conditions. Two stocking densities (1.1 and 1.8 kg m-3) and two size ranges (7.8-77.8 g and 80-297 g), as well as their interaction, were tested using a factorial design with triplicate tanks per treatment. Mean TAN excretion rates ranged from 24.5 to 30.6 mg TAN kg-1 fish h-1. A clear diurnal excretion pattern was observed, with peak TAN release occurring 2-4 h after feeding, followed by a gradual decline. Neither body size nor stocking density significantly affected TAN excretion within the evaluated ranges, indicating that these results provide bioengineering parameters for RAS design and scaling.

title: Evaluating Oxidant Field Representations in Aerosol Modeling: Insights from the ASIA-AQ Campaign and Global Budgets
summary: Abstract. Accurate prediction of secondary inorganic aerosols (e.g., sulfate and nitrate) relies heavily on representing highly variable, nonlinear atmospheric oxidant chemistry. This study systematically evaluates the sensitivity of GOCART
content: Abstract. Accurate prediction of secondary inorganic aerosols (e.g., sulfate and nitrate) relies heavily on representing highly variable, nonlinear atmospheric oxidant chemistry. This study systematically evaluates the sensitivity of GOCART-2G aerosol simulations to the temporal resolution and underlying chemical mechanisms of three oxidant fields: hourly GEOS-Chem (CFH), monthly GEOS-Chem (CFM), and monthly GMI-Chem climatology (GMI). Model performance was assessed using airborne data from the 2024 ASIA-AQ campaign (covering the Philippines, South Korea, and Thailand) and global simulations for 2019. Comparisons show that hourly, time-varying oxidant fields improve simulated oxidant, sulfate, and nitrate correlations over monthly averages. Capturing short-term variability—particularly the strong diurnal cycles of OH and NO3—preserves the temporal covariance and nonlinear coupling that monthly means obscure. Consequently, time-resolved oxidants weaken the overall chemical transformation of dimethyl sulfide (DMS). This results in ~20 % higher global DMS and methanesulfonic acid (MSA) burdens than monthly mean simulations, while exerting substantial regional impacts (>20 %) on sulfur and nitrate budgets over East Asia. Furthermore, variations in monthly mean oxidant magnitude and spatial distribution between GMI-Chem and GEOS-Chem mechanisms impact aerosol burdens. GMI-Chem produces 2 % and 8 % higher column and surface sulfate, respectively, but 148 % and 130 % lower column and surface nitrate. These findings highlight the limitations of decoupled, time-averaged oxidant fields in traditional global models, demonstrating that resolving high-frequency temporal variability and nonlinear feedbacks is critical for Earth System Models.

title: Unraveling SAF Supply Chains: A Global Assessment of CORSIA-Certified Lipid-Based Biomass
summary: Abstract The decarbonization of civil aviation remains one of the most complex challenges in the global energy transition, given the sector’s reliance on high-energy-density liquid fuels and the limited prospects for large-scale electrifica
content: Abstract The decarbonization of civil aviation remains one of the most complex challenges in the global energy transition, given the sector’s reliance on high-energy-density liquid fuels and the limited prospects for large-scale electrification. Within this context, Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) represents the most immediately deployable mitigation option. However, the scalability of SAF is strongly constrained by feedstock availability, sustainability certification, and technological maturity. This review provides a critical and integrated assessment of lipid-based biomass certified under the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA), focusing on their chemical composition, technological conversion routes, greenhouse gas mitigation potential, and global production capacity. Eighteen oleaginous feedstocks, including vegetable oils, animal fats, processing residues, and waste-derived lipids, are systematically evaluated by correlating compositional attributes, impurity levels, seasonality, and logistics with conversion performance and Technology Readiness Levels. Particular emphasis is placed on the dominance of the hydroprocessed esters and fatty acids pathway, which currently represents the most mature and commercially viable route for SAF production. The analysis demonstrates that second-generation feedstocks, especially residual and waste lipids, consistently outperform dedicated crops, achieving life-cycle greenhouse gas reductions of up to 80–90% relative to fossil jet fuel while minimizing land-use change impacts.

title: Study on the nutrient spatiotemporal changes and multi-habitat microbial succession in a decoupled largemouth bass–garlic chive aquaponics system
summary: The decoupled aquaponics system was an important model of circular agriculture and represents a mature circular agricultural framework, yet integrated studies simultaneously tracking nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium and microbial communities
content: The decoupled aquaponics system was an important model of circular agriculture and represents a mature circular agricultural framework, yet integrated studies simultaneously tracking nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium and microbial communities in water, sediment, substrate and fish gut remain scarce. To address this gap, we conducted a three-month continuous monitoring (July to September 2024) of a triplicate indoor decoupled aquaponics system combining largemouth bass ( Micropterus salmoides ) and garlic chives ( Allium tuberosum ) in northern Chinese greenhouses. Nutrient dynamics (total nitrogen, TN; total phosphorus, TP; total potassium, TK) were quantified monthly in aquaculture water, sedimentation tank mud and cultivation substrate, while microbial community structure, succession and putative functions were characterized via 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing, canonical correspondence analysis (CCA), variance partitioning analysis (VPA) and PICRUSt2 functional prediction. The results were as follows: (1) The three modules formed a characteristic “water transport → mud accumulated → substrate consumption” nutrient cascade, with nutrient reserves ordered as mud > substrate > water. (2) TN in water increased by 237.60% over the cultivation period, indicating a latent risk of eutrophication. Microbial communities exhibited strong habitat partitioning, with Proteobacteria as the shared dominant phylum across environmental media, while fish gut harbored a temporally dynamic assemblage shifting from Fusobacteriota (83.11% in July) to Firmicutes (73.31% in September), forming a distinct “environmental versus host” bistable zonation. (3) VPA revealed that TN and TP synergistically regulated mud microbiota (27.70% interaction), whereas TK independently structured substrate communities (19.95% independent contribution), ranking as the strongest single-nutrient driver (K > N > P). (4) PICRUSt2-based functional prediction indicated metabolism as the core function across all habitats, with complementary profiles—sediment for nutrient sensing, substrate for stable transformation, water for temporal adaptation, and gut for host-specific nutrition. These provide species-specific nutrient–microbe linkage data, synchronous four-habitat temporal dynamics, and quantitative partitioning of N/P/K effects, offering actionable baselines for structural optimization, seasonal nutrient regulation and targeted microbial modification in decoupled aquaponics facilities.

title: Excessive flowering induces nutrient competition in albino tea plants: insights from flowering dynamics and flower-shoot resource partitioning across various tea cultivars
summary: Excessive flowering occurs in China’s tea-producing provinces; however, the cultivar-dependent flowering patterns and their role in governing nutrient allocation (N, P, K) between flowers and new shoots remain unclear, hindering targeted st
content: Excessive flowering occurs in China’s tea-producing provinces; however, the cultivar-dependent flowering patterns and their role in governing nutrient allocation (N, P, K) between flowers and new shoots remain unclear, hindering targeted strategies for high-quality and high-efficiency production. We conducted a two-part study (1): a comparative analysis of flowering dynamics and flower biomass across nine tea cultivars, and (2) quantification of resource competition between flowers and new shoots via biomass allocation and N, P, K partitioning in three prolific-flowering albino cultivars (Huangjinya, Baiye 1, Huangjinye) across three regions in Guizhou province. Albino tea cultivars produced significantly more flowers than green-leaf cultivars, with Huangjinya showing the highest flower density and flower biomass. Among albino cultivars, Baiye 1 flowered earliest and Huangjinya latest. The key finding, however, was the extent of resource competition: flowers accumulated 1.3–4.4 times more biomass and up to 3.7 times more K content than new shoots. Despite lower flowers N% (1.77–2.77%) than new shoots (5.21–5.62%), greater flower biomass led to comparable or higher total N content per hectare, with flower-to-shoot N ratios averaging 1.22 (WB/NS) and 1.06 (FB/NS). Excessive flowering in albino cultivars intensifies nutrient competition between flowers and new shoots, particularly for K and N. These findings provide a physiological basis for balancing reproductive and vegetative growth and inform cultivar-specific nutrient management strategies to reduce flower-shoot competition in tea production systems.

title: Mother cells enlarged with starch accumulation produce daughter colonies with increased cell numbers in the colonial green alga Pediastrum duplex ( Chlorophyceae, Chlorophyta )
summary: SUMMARY Spring algal blooms are characterized by the rapid expansion of phytoplankton populations under favorable environmental conditions, yet the intracellular mechanisms that enable this rapid proliferation remain poorly understood. In t
content: SUMMARY Spring algal blooms are characterized by the rapid expansion of phytoplankton populations under favorable environmental conditions, yet the intracellular mechanisms that enable this rapid proliferation remain poorly understood. In this study, using the colonial green alga Pediastrum duplex , we found that mother cells enlarged with starch accumulation under cold conditions in the light promote an increase in the number of cells per daughter colony under subsequent warm conditions. At 11°C under light, the proliferation of P. duplex colonies was arrested. When the arrested cells were transferred to the optimal temperature (25°C), they rapidly resumed growth and preferentially formed new colonies with higher cell numbers. Microscopic analysis revealed that arrested cells cultured at 11°C enlarged and accumulated substantial amounts of starch. When we supplemented the culture medium with glucose at 25°C, we artificially induced starch accumulation and cell enlargement in P. duplex cells without low‐temperature treatment. The presence of enlarged mother cells containing starch led to the formation of daughter colonies with higher cell numbers than those derived from non‐enlarged mother cells lacking starch, suggesting that starch accumulation and/or enlargement of mother cells contribute to the development of daughter colonies. These findings suggest that under low‐temperature conditions in the light (i.e., in winter), P. duplex enters a preparatory state characterized by growth arrest, cell enlargement, and starch accumulation and that upon return to favorable conditions (i.e., in spring), the enlarged mother cells containing starch, together with other physiological changes induced by low temperature and light exposure, support additional rounds of cell division, resulting in daughter colonies with more cells and rapid population expansion. This intracellular mechanism may contribute to the rapid expansion of algal populations during spring algal blooms, highlighting the importance of physiological preconditioning for bloom dynamics.

title: Canopy architecture, solar radiation partitioning, and yield performance of a high-density cactus pear (Opuntia ficus-indica) hedgerow system in a semi-arid region
summary: High-density planting systems are a potential strategy for intensifying cactus pear ( Opuntia ficus-indica ) production in semi-arid regions. However, quantitative assessments of canopy architecture, solar radiation interception, and yield
content: High-density planting systems are a potential strategy for intensifying cactus pear ( Opuntia ficus-indica ) production in semi-arid regions. However, quantitative assessments of canopy architecture, solar radiation interception, and yield dynamics within intensive hedgerows remain limited. This study evaluates the structural and physiological performance of a mature, commercial high-density paired-hedgerow orchard (1,666 trees ha −1 ; 6 × 2 × 0.5 m spacing; north–south orientation) over two consecutive seasons (2024–2025) in Sicily, Italy. Stem area index (SAI), daily photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) distribution across canopy faces, cladode water status, fruit yield, and commercial fruit quality attributes were monitored. In this symmetric hedgerow system, incident solar radiation was evenly partitioned between opposite lateral canopy faces on a daily integrated basis (~50% each), keeping photosynthetically active cladode surfaces well illuminated. Over the two-year period, the orchard sustained average fresh fruit yields exceeding 30 t ha −1 , substantially higher than typical baseline ranges reported in the literature for conventional extensive orchards (12–17 t ha −1 ), while maintaining commercial fruit quality standards (mean fruit weight >120 g; total soluble solids averaging 12.8°Brix). Cladode relative water content (RWC) remained stable (~80%) through flowering and early fruit development, consistent with robust internal water storage buffering. These findings document the structural feasibility and high productivity of intensive cactus pear hedgerows under semi-arid conditions, providing valuable architectural baselines for future comparative trials evaluating multi-density or multi-orientation orchard configurations.

title: From Mineral Projects to Resilient Supply: Value-Chain Bottlenecks in EU Strategic Projects and Ukraine's Mineral Assets
summary: Abstract European raw-material security depends not only on deposits and mine output but also on whether materials can be processed and used by European industry. We assess when a mineral project can strengthen supply resilience by combinin
content: Abstract European raw-material security depends not only on deposits and mine output but also on whether materials can be processed and used by European industry. We assess when a mineral project can strengthen supply resilience by combining investment maturity with six conditions that link a project to a recipient plant: material identity, grade match, validated processing, available capacity, a commercial connection and product qualification. The analysis covers all 13 Strategic Projects selected outside the European Union (EU) in the first round under the Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA) and a purposive set of Ukrainian mineral assets, using dated public evidence to 30 September 2026. Ten of the 13 projects were in preparation; the three in implementation accounted for 5.8–12.0% of the cohort's disclosed investment budgets, and no complete supply route to a qualified EU recipient could be verified. On a selected Ukrainian graphite route to an Italian purification pilot, processing is the binding constraint under stated assumptions: if the pilot accepts Ukrainian feed and an operating mine's nominal capacity is available to the route, a planned 50 kt/y mine raises route throughput only once purification capacity exceeds about 6.1 kt/y, some thirty times the 200 t/y pilot under construction. Issuer-reported unit values for purified graphite and Ukrainian concentrate differ about 4.6-fold. EU accession and recovery of occupied deposits would change institutions and investment options, while supply would still depend on the same project gates. Strategic Project registers should publish stage-compatible evidence, and policy should target the bottlenecks that limit usable supply.

title: National-scale monitoring reveals widespread trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) contamination in UK surface waters
summary: ). Winter and spring were associated with elevated TFA mass loads, driven by higher flow in both seasons and higher concentrations in winter. Golf course exposure and intermediate arable land cover were significantly associated with higher
content: ). Winter and spring were associated with elevated TFA mass loads, driven by higher flow in both seasons and higher concentrations in winter. Golf course exposure and intermediate arable land cover were significantly associated with higher TFA loads, possibly reflecting PFAS pesticide usage. However, our results also highlight the challenges of source attribution for a widespread contaminant with numerous sources, and we propose avenues for future investigation. Overall, this study provides an important baseline of TFA pollution in the UK and suggests prioritising precautionary action to prevent further emissions at source.

title: Warming the World’s Croplands: Coupled Carbon–Nitrogen Cycling, Management Interactions, and the Durability of Soil Carbon Sequestration
summary: Croplands hold about 83 Pg of organic carbon (C) in their topsoil, yet most evidence on how soil C responds to warming comes from nitrogen (N)-limited forests, grasslands, and tundra. Decades of fertilization have given cropland soils a C–N
content: Croplands hold about 83 Pg of organic carbon (C) in their topsoil, yet most evidence on how soil C responds to warming comes from nitrogen (N)-limited forests, grasslands, and tundra. Decades of fertilization have given cropland soils a C–N balance with no close natural equivalent. Drawing on cropland field-warming experiments and quantitative syntheses, we argue that soil C sequestration under warming can only be judged when N is part of the accounting, and that management, not climate alone, decides the outcome. In a global synthesis of mostly East Asian experiments (mean warming about 2 °C), total soil respiration rose by about 15% and nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions by 13%; respiration includes roots, so this is not net C loss. Mineralization depends on the pool exposed, its physical protection, and substrate quality, whereas N losses as N2O or leached nitrate follow soil moisture closely. In N-limited soils, warming drives microbial N mining and C loss. Chronic fertilization may weaken this response in croplands, but no cropland warming experiment has tested this directly. Because the N2O penalty can offset or exceed the C gained, cropland soils are a finite, uneven, and reversible climate sink, best assessed by measuring C and N together.

title: Circular Business Model Innovation: A Systematic Review of Technology and Resource Strategy Choices
summary: ABSTRACT Despite growing scholarly interest in circular business model innovation (CBMI), established frameworks are applied inconsistently: Few empirical studies specify how they conceptualise CBMs or the scope and degree of novelty of the
content: ABSTRACT Despite growing scholarly interest in circular business model innovation (CBMI), established frameworks are applied inconsistently: Few empirical studies specify how they conceptualise CBMs or the scope and degree of novelty of the business model changes reported, raising construct validity concerns that limit comparability across studies. We systematically review 101 empirical papers, following PRISMA, to examine how CBMI is conceptualised and theorised, how digital and material technologies enable it and how resource strategies are realised in practice. Although technology and resource‐strategy choices have typically been studied as independent enablers of circularity, our findings reveal interdependencies between technology and resource‐strategy choices and their association with CBM reconfiguration. We also find the reviewed studies are predominantly atheoretical, with material technologies more prevalent than digital ones, and resource strategies typically deployed in combination rather than in isolation, although these strategies compete for the same material flows, a tension the field has yet to theorise. This paper contributes to the CBMI literature by classifying CBMI's scope and degree of novelty, by proposing an integrative framework that aligns theoretical lenses with CBM conceptualisations and by outlining a future research agenda guiding scholarly and managerial decisions on technology and resource‐strategy choices.

title: Cation Identity and Framework Topology Govern CO2 Adsorption in FAU, MER, and RHO Zeolites
summary: Aluminosilicates are widely investigated for carbon capture and utilization. Understanding the mechanism of CO 2 adsorption in these materials is crucial for designing efficient carbon-capture materials. However, atomistic-level investigati
content: Aluminosilicates are widely investigated for carbon capture and utilization. Understanding the mechanism of CO 2 adsorption in these materials is crucial for designing efficient carbon-capture materials. However, atomistic-level investigation of CO 2 interaction and dynamics within confined pores of zeolites remains challenging due to two main factors: the need for local characterization techniques capable of probing changes in the chemical environment of active sites at the atomic scale, and the predominantly non-covalent nature of CO 2 and adsorbent interactions under confinement. Advanced magic-angle-spinning (MAS) solid-state NMR spectroscopy enables localized characterization of zeolites by probing different nuclei. In this study, all possible nuclei in Na- and Li-exchanged and other ion-exchanged FAU, MER, and RHO zeolites are investigated using advanced multinuclear solid-state NMR experiments, including multiple-quantum magic-angle spinning (MQMAS) and heteronuclear correlation spectroscopy (HETCOR). We are still working on some experiments, such as exchange spectroscopy (EXSY), rotational-echo saturation-pulse double-resonance (RESPDOR), and dipolar heteronuclear multiple-quantum coherence (D-HMQC), to elucidate the influence of CO 2 on their respective environments. We performed all solid-state NMR measurements at two different magnetic fields. We then derived conclusions about how different cations and framework nuclei participate in CO 2 adsorption. A key experimental challenge was performing all solid-state NMR measurements and CO 2 adsorption using the same zeolite sample packed in a solid-state NMR rotor. This challenge was addressed through the engineering development of a custom-built gas adsorption setup for solid-state NMR rotors. In Na- and Li-FAU, CO 2 uptake induced reorganization of the cation sites through migration to the supercage. In contrast, MER and RHO exhibited indications of breathing and trapdoor mechanisms, respectively, upon CO 2 uptake.

title: Changes in nitrous oxide emissions from global permafrost regions during 1901–2013 revealed by CTSM
summary: Nitrous oxide (N 2 O) is a potent greenhouse gas produced mainly through microbial nitrogen transformations in soils.Permafrost regions store large amounts of organic matter under cold, frozen, and often waterlogged conditions, but thawing
content: Nitrous oxide (N 2 O) is a potent greenhouse gas produced mainly through microbial nitrogen transformations in soils.Permafrost regions store large amounts of organic matter under cold, frozen, and often waterlogged conditions, but thawing can make these substrates available for microbial processing and create more favourable conditions for N 2 O production.Despite this potential, the long-term behaviour of N 2 O emissions from northern permafrost regions remains poorly understood.In this study, the Community Terrestrial Systems Model (CTSM) was used to investigate the tem poral, spatial, and seasonal variability of simulated N 2 O emissions across the northern terrestrial region from approximately 25 • N to 90 • N during 1901-2013, with particular attention to the per mafrost domain.The model simulation used the default CTSM/CLM parameterization and standard model input data, without changing or calibrating the model parameters.The simulated northern land domain covered approximately 72.08 million km 2 .N 2 O emissions from nitrification and deni trification were analysed for the full northern region and for the permafrost subset, together with selected soil environmental variables.Simulated fluxes were also compared with field observations from six permafrost sites.Annual simulated N 2 O emissions from the northern region ranged from 4.77 to 5.91 Tg N yr -1 , while simulated emissions from the permafrost region ranged from 1.13 to 1.77 Tg N yr -1 .These values represent the magnitude estimated by the model and are likely higher than the actual re gional emissions.Both regions showed substantial variability throughout the historical period.The permafrost region contributed a smaller but still important part of the total northern N 2 O budget.Spatially, most grid cells showed relatively low emissions, while localized areas had considerably higher fluxes.A clear seasonal pattern was also observed, with low winter emissions and strong increases during spring thaw, followed by a second increase during early autumn.Relationships between N 2 O and soil temperature, soil ice, and mineral NH + 4 were weak, indicating that no single environmental factor alone explained the spatial variability in simulated emissions.Overall, the results show that N 2 O emissions from northern permafrost regions are spatially and temporally variable and are influenced by the combined effects of changing soil and environmental conditions.Although permafrost emissions were lower than those of the full northern region, their contribution should not be ignored, particularly because thawing can increase the availability of previously frozen organic matter and nitrogen for microbial processes that produce N 2 O. title: Distilling an atomistic foundation model is all you need for large-scale molecular dynamics of semiconductor interfaces
summary: State-of-the-art atomistic foundation models provide broadly transferable energy and force predictions, but their direct deployment in large-scale molecular dynamics remains computationally costly. Here we examine whether their knowledge ca
content: State-of-the-art atomistic foundation models provide broadly transferable energy and force predictions, but their direct deployment in large-scale molecular dynamics remains computationally costly. Here we examine whether their knowledge can be distilled into compact potentials while retaining the physical responses of heterogeneous semiconductor interfaces. From 128 pretrained models spanning 22 model families, we select a fixed EquiformerV3 teacher and train atomic cluster expansion (ACE) and neuroevolution potential (NEP) students without target-specific teacher fine-tuning, with both simulation speed and accessible system size improved by several orders of magnitude relative to the teacher model. Matched training configurations and architectures enable direct comparisons with students trained on density-functional-theory (DFT) reference labels. For 79,920-atom BAs/GaN interfaces, direct distillation preserves termination-dependent thermal conductance and dominant spectral features, with conductance differing by at most 6.6% from DFT-trained counterparts. In 29,792-atom Cu/diamond specimens loaded at 500 K, tensile strength and loading work differ by 2.8% and 1.5%, respectively. Exploratory SiC/a-C/SiC simulations retain the principal thermal bottleneck and the direction of the annealing response. Furthermore, a four-model committee retrieves 42-56% of the highest-error teacher configurations with a 10% selection budget and improves high-error force fitting, but does not consistently improve downstream properties. These findings demonstrate that direct distillation can preserve key interfacial thermal and mechanical responses in compact interatomic potentials, opening a path towards large-scale, high-throughput simulations of heterogeneous interfaces.

title: oMEGACat. XI. Kinematic Characterization of Omega Centauri's Subpopulations: A Flattened Primordial Component
summary: Omega Centauri ($ω$ Cen; NGC 5139), the likely stripped nucleus of a dwarf galaxy accreted by the Milky Way, is one of the few galactic nuclei resolvable into individual stars. Because of its long relaxation time, the kinematics of its star
content: Omega Centauri ($ω$ Cen; NGC 5139), the likely stripped nucleus of a dwarf galaxy accreted by the Milky Way, is one of the few galactic nuclei resolvable into individual stars. Because of its long relaxation time, the kinematics of its stars may still retain memory of how this nucleus formed. We combine HST proper motions and MUSE line-of-sight velocities from the oMEGACat survey to compare populations defined by abundance variations (the chromosome map), metallicity, and age within the half-light radius. The chromosome-map division separates two dynamically distinct components. The primordial stars have a flattened dispersion field, with kinematic ellipticity $ε\approx 0.7$ ($σ_{\rm minor} / σ_{\rm major} \approx 0.8$), which we recover independently in the line-of-sight velocities and the proper motions. The enriched stars are consistent with $ε=0$ in the line-of-sight velocities and are no more flattened than the full sample in the proper motions, and the two components show no strong difference in rotation. Metallicity bins show no comparable structure, because each bin mixes stars from both components, and the age-metallicity sample covers only the cluster core, where it cannot test for the flattening. The present-day central concentration of the most enriched (P2) stars suggests that they formed more centrally concentrated than the primordial stars, independent of assembly scenario. These results favor a picture in which the primordial stars retain the flattened orbital structure of the progenitor, while the enriched stars fell inward as dense clumps or formed in compact, centrally concentrated starbursts.

title: PathwayDesigner: an interactive SBML/KEGG/Reactome/Escher compatible editor for biochemical network diagrams
summary: PathwayDesigner is an interactive editor for biochemical network diagrams. A network can be drawn directly on the screen, or described as an Antimony model, which PathwayDesigner then lays out and draws. PathwayDesigner reads and writes SBM
content: PathwayDesigner is an interactive editor for biochemical network diagrams. A network can be drawn directly on the screen, or described as an Antimony model, which PathwayDesigner then lays out and draws. PathwayDesigner reads and writes SBML using the Layout and Render packages, writing Render in a form that other tools can interpret correctly. PathwayDesigner can read and write a diagram's layout and appearance using either Antimony's own layout statements or in a new, more concise format that we propose. PathwayDesigner can also open Escher maps, KEGG maps and Reactome's SBML-based maps. Other components of the model, such as events, rules, functions, and units, are kept and can be edited within the application. Species and reactions can be annotated with references to any database, and PathwayDesigner can find and add annotation references automatically by searching the BiGG, ChEBI, PubChem, and Rhea databases with a component's Id or Display Name, or contextually with a reaction's reactants and products. The network's stoichiometry matrix, conservation laws, and flux null space are computed and visualized on the diagram. The visual style of a diagram can be set with named styles or themes, saved and reused across models. One built-in theme follows the Escher style. The software is written in pure Rust as one code base for Windows, macOS, Linux, and the web browser, where it runs as WebAssembly. The web version is hosted on a GitHub page so that a user doesn't need to manually install code. All 1,062 curated BioModels models and the 1,823 semantic cases of the SBML Test Suite were read and written back without change. Diagrams were exchanged in both directions with COPASI and SBMLNetwork. PathwayDesigner is released as open source with MIT licence, at https://github.com/sys-bio/PathwayDesigner-rs, and runs in the browser at https://sys-bio.github.io/PathwayDesigner-rs/.

title: A heavy molybdenum reservoir in Neoarchean seawater tracks extensive iron oxidation
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
summary: The lead-up to the Great Oxidation Event (GOE; between 2.5 and 2.2 Ga) was arguably as consequential as the event itself, yet substantial uncertainties remain regarding the timing and magnitude of oxygen rise in early Earth’s oceans. Heavy
content: The lead-up to the Great Oxidation Event (GOE; between 2.5 and 2.2 Ga) was arguably as consequential as the event itself, yet substantial uncertainties remain regarding the timing and magnitude of oxygen rise in early Earth’s oceans. Heavy molybdenum isotope compositions (δ 98 Mo) in Neoarchean marine sediments have traditionally been interpreted as evidence for adsorption of dissolved Mo onto iron oxyhydroxides [e.g., ferrihydrite; Fe(OH) 3 ] and manganese oxides (MnO 2 ) formed in oxygenated marine environments, implying at least regional surface oxygen accumulation immediately prior to the GOE. Here, we propose an alternate explanation in which these isotopic signatures arose in a largely anoxic ocean. Analyses of Neoarchean banded iron formations (BIFs) deposited at 2.57 to 2.51 Ga reveal a broad range of δ 98 Mo values, which are best explained by the combined effects of Mo adsorption onto primary ferrihydrite, followed by its diagenetic incorporation into Fe(II)-Mo(IV)-sulfides. After accounting for isotopic fractionation during adsorption, we estimate that Neoarchean seawater δ 98 Mo maintained a relatively stable composition between 1.5‰ and 1.6‰. A newly developed Mo isotope mass balance model further indicates that only a minor MnO 2 sink was required to generate these heavy δ 98 Mo values. Instead, the dominant control was likely removal of isotopically light Mo via adsorption to settling ferrihydrite particles in ferruginous seawater. Given the lack of oxygen indicators for cyanobacterial photosynthesis, we posit that anoxygenic photosynthetic bacteria (photoferrotrophs) were the primary drivers of ferrihydrite precipitation during BIF deposition. Together, these findings imply that the Neoarchean Mo isotope record reflects anaerobic biological oxidation of Fe(II) rather than pervasive surface seawater oxygenation preceding the GOE.

title: Forces at the scale of the cell
summary: The importance of molecular-scale forces in sculpting biological form and function has been acknowledged for more than a century. Accounting for forces in biology is a problem that lies at the intersection of soft condensed matter physics,
content: The importance of molecular-scale forces in sculpting biological form and function has been acknowledged for more than a century. Accounting for forces in biology is a problem that lies at the intersection of soft condensed matter physics, statistical mechanics, and experimental methods, all adapted to a cellular context. This review surveys how forces arise within the cell. We provide a summary of the relevant background in cell biophysics, of soft-matter systems in and out of thermodynamic equilibrium, and of various force measurement methods. These ideas are then deployed to describe how forces are generated, transmitted, and sensed in specific cell-scale processes. We emphasize active matter descriptions, methodological tools that provide ways of incorporating non-equilibrium effects in a systematic manner into conceptual as well as quantitative descriptions. Our examples include polymerization forces, the motion of molecular motors, the properties of the actomyosin cortex, the mechanics of cell division, and shape changes in tissues. We suggest that a deeper understanding of cell function will necessarily require integrating the action of cell-scale physical forces with the assimilation and processing of information.

title: Plant-soil interactions drive GHG dynamics in organic soil under variable water tables: a case study with poplar
summary: Organic soils provide a substantial capacity for carbon storage both in below- and above-ground biomass, but they are also a significant contributor to natural terrestrial greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. Management of soils with high organi
content: Organic soils provide a substantial capacity for carbon storage both in below- and above-ground biomass, but they are also a significant contributor to natural terrestrial greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. Management of soils with high organic matter content, particularly through drainage and productivity enhancement, often leads to increased CO 2 emissions. By monitoring in a controlled environment, it is possible to determine how groundwater level and environmental conditions influence the carbon cycle, including plant vitality and productivity, and consequently shape future carbon sequestration potential. The aim of this study was to develop a system under semi-controlled conditions to assess the impact of different groundwater levels on GHG emissions, accumulated biomass, and tree vitality. We determined the effects of different groundwater levels: −2; −15; −25; and −35 cm. We monitored CH 4 and CO 2 autotrophic and heterotrophic emission, soil chemical analyses, and plant morphological (biomass, root and leaf area, shoot length) and physiological (leaf chlorophyll a and b content indices) parameters. Temporal variation strongly impacted GHG fluxes, while diurnal variation in CO 2 emissions depended on groundwater level, with a distinct day–night response at −35 cm, whereas no groundwater-dependent diurnal response was detected for CH 4 . During soil temperature extremes, extremely high CH 4 emissions occurred at a −2 cm groundwater level. Higher plant productivity had a greater influence on GHG fluxes: it decreased both CH 4 and CO 2 emissions during the day compared to bare soil. Therefore, the autotrophic respiration rate increased with increased productivity, but the primary determinant was heterotrophic respiration. The study demonstrates that groundwater level, together with plant productivity and environmental conditions, jointly regulates GHG emissions in organic soil.

title: A national baseline for methane sink habitats and methanotroph diversity
summary: Methane emissions account for nearly a third of the Earth’s effective radiative forcing, with methanotrophs playing a critical role in mitigating emissions by oxidising methane in diverse environments. Despite their ecological importance, m
content: Methane emissions account for nearly a third of the Earth’s effective radiative forcing, with methanotrophs playing a critical role in mitigating emissions by oxidising methane in diverse environments. Despite their ecological importance, methanotrophic diversity and environmental distribution remain incompletely characterised due to cultivation challenges, incomplete or low-quality metagenome-assembled genomes, and limited taxonomic resolution in marker gene surveys. Here, we present a national study of the biogeography of novel and known methanotrophs across Denmark’s major natural, urban and agricultural habitats, using genome-resolved classification of 10,683 metagenomes and 102 new methanotrophic species. By linking metabolic potential to habitat-specific distributions, we reveal uncharacterised methanotrophs as dominant in natural ecosystems. These findings provide a comprehensive baseline of methanotroph diversity, reveal clear contrasts between natural and disturbed habitats, and highlight candidate species and habitats for future methane-mitigation strategies. In this study, the authors use metagenomics to map the diverse and previously unknown bacteria responsible for taking up methane across Denmark’s varied environments and highlight the natural habitats and methanotroph species with the potential for methane mitigation.

title: Open LHC Monte Carlo event generation
summary: The LHC physics programme involves a vast amount of Monte Carlo event simulation. This paper reviews current efforts towards sharing the generated events as Open Data. Open Event Generation helps reduce duplication of effort and resource co
content: The LHC physics programme involves a vast amount of Monte Carlo event simulation. This paper reviews current efforts towards sharing the generated events as Open Data. Open Event Generation helps reduce duplication of effort and resource consumption, and benefits the whole High Energy Physics community. We give examples of use cases and user experiences, discuss financial and environmental savings, and suggest future directions.

title: TopoToolbox 3, a laboratory for quantitative geomorphology
summary: TopoToolbox has been widely used to analyze and model landscapes across geomorphology and other geospatial disciplines for the past 15 years. Its documentation and accessible interfaces have made it a valuable resource for teaching and lear
content: TopoToolbox has been widely used to analyze and model landscapes across geomorphology and other geospatial disciplines for the past 15 years. Its documentation and accessible interfaces have made it a valuable resource for teaching and learning quantitative geomorphology while its customizability and efficiency have allowed researchers to use it as a platform for experimentation and implementation of their own analyses and models. Its third version, TopoToolbox 3, builds on these developments by improving access to the software, integrating with a larger ecosystem of geomorphology software, and establishing sustainable research software engineering practices. TopoToolbox, previously available only in MATLAB, is now also available to users of Python, and an R interface is under development. The redesigned architecture of TopoToolbox 3 is based on a shared library of core computational routines that makes these and other integrations possible while maintaining the MATLAB interface for existing users of the software. We illustrate the power of this design with examples of how users can integrate TopoToolbox into their workflows. First, we compare the implementation of a basic application, χ maps, in MATLAB and Python. Second, we show how property-based testing can successfully identify bugs in the absence of known solutions to test cases. We then use the GraphFlood hydraulic model, now available in TopoToolbox, to showcase the potential of integrating simulation tools and analyzing their output in one computational environment. Finally, we demonstrate a two-way coupling between TopoToolbox and the Python-based Landlab landscape evolution modeling framework. We conclude by discussing how improved quality assurance and community-driven development practices ensure that TopoToolbox continues to serve the evolving needs of the geomorphology community.

title: Valley-bottom wetland agricultural conversion and recovery shape greenhouse gas dynamics and soil organic carbon stocks in an African tropical highland system
summary: Tropical wetlands significantly impact global greenhouse gas (GHG) budgets and carbon storage; however, data from sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) remain limited. Highland valley-bottom wetland (HVBW) agriculture supports millions, yet its effects
content: Tropical wetlands significantly impact global greenhouse gas (GHG) budgets and carbon storage; however, data from sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) remain limited. Highland valley-bottom wetland (HVBW) agriculture supports millions, yet its effects on GHG emissions and carbon storage remain undocumented. This study quantified soil emissions of nitrous oxide (N 2 O), carbon dioxide (CO 2 ), and methane (CH 4 ) in the Taita Hills, Kenya, from 12 converted, 10 recovering, and one reference (intact) HVBW. Agricultural conversion shifted wetland emissions from CH 4 to N 2 O dominance. Converted HVBWs were N 2 O sources (1.6 kgN2O-Nha-1yr-1), driven by elevated soil nitrate, whereas the intact HVBW was an N 2 O sink (−0.3 kgN2O-Nha-1yr-1), with high soil moisture and a high soil C/NO3--N ratio suggesting complete denitrification. Recovering HVBWs showed intermediate N 2 O emissions (0.5 kgN2O-Nha-1yr-1). CO 2 emissions were similar between converted and recovering HVBWs (9534 vs. 9610 kgCO2-Cha-1yr-1) but lower in the intact (2923 kgCO2-Cha-1yr-1). CH 4 emissions were highest in the intact HVBW (2757 kgCH4-Cha-1yr-1), intermediate in recovering sites (781 kgCH4-Cha-1yr-1), and lowest in converted sites (38 kgCH4-Cha-1yr-1). The intact HVBW had an SOC stock of 224 Mg C ha −1 , indicating carbon loss rates of 2.7 MgCha-1yr-1 over 45 years for converted HVBWs. Comparing recovering with converted HVBWs suggests an SOC recovery of about 1.1 MgCha-1yr-1 after abandonment, offsetting ∼0.0005 % of Kenya's annual agricultural GHG emissions, or 9.8 % when scaled nationally. However, recovering HVBWs also emitted considerably more CH 4 , so their net climate effect cannot be derived from SOC stocks alone. These findings highlight trade-offs between GHG emissions and carbon storage in HVBWs, with wetland recovery promoting partial functional restoration and SOC recovery in SSA, but at the cost of increased CH 4 emissions.

title: Evaluating maternal pod variability and early growth dynamics in Moringa oleifera progenies
summary: Moringa oleifera is an important crop globally, but there is limited characterisation of maternal pod traits and progeny seedling performance. In this study, growth patterns of 10 accessions (MO-11 to MO-20) and their half-sib progeny (P-11
content: Moringa oleifera is an important crop globally, but there is limited characterisation of maternal pod traits and progeny seedling performance. In this study, growth patterns of 10 accessions (MO-11 to MO-20) and their half-sib progeny (P-11 to P-20) were evaluated to select the best germplasm. Maternally, MO-11 exhibited largest pod dimensions and weight, and MO-16 had the highest 100-seed weight (19.14 g). Seed prolificacy was relatively high in genotype MO-20 while the individual seed mass was relatively low, which is in agreement with the negative phenotypic correlation that occurred between the accessions. Reduced subsequent germination vigour was also observed to be related to lower seed mass. A difference between establishment and late-stage structural vigour was observed during the 90 day progeny evaluation after sowing (DAS). P-15 had the highest germination rate at sowing while P-16 was the best line for structural growth, with the highest total seedling length at 90 DAS. Biomass analysis showed that P-19 was better than other progenies in dry matter accumulation. Independent traits were used to cluster and PCA to isolate the most extreme phenotypes, and P-16 and P-19 emerged as two outlier phenotypes, characterized by vertical elongation and dry mass. Correlation analysis confirmed a positive correlation was established between shoot and root extension, working separately from initial germination percentage. The coefficient of variation in the 100-seed weight and 90-day growth were low, indicating uniformity of these properties in this nursery. MO-11 had relatively strong pod characteristics while MO-16 and its progeny P-16 had variations in seed and biomass-related characteristics. The observed variability between accessions, especially for the traits of pod, seed and early biomass, may be used as selection criteria for further studies. The results are therefore preliminary and only reflect the early stage of the nursery establishment and should not be used to make a final commercial recommendation until further multi-environment tests have been conducted.

title: Ecophysiological responses and adaptation strategies of Suaeda salsa (L.) Pall. to combined flooding and litter addition
summary: Hydrological changes and litter accumulation are critical factors affecting the ecological restoration of coastal saline-alkali wetlands. To elucidate the physiological adaptation mechanisms of the dominant species Suaeda salsa (L.) Pall. t
content: Hydrological changes and litter accumulation are critical factors affecting the ecological restoration of coastal saline-alkali wetlands. To elucidate the physiological adaptation mechanisms of the dominant species Suaeda salsa (L.) Pall. to the combined effects of flooding and litter addition, this study established three waterlogging regimes (non-waterlogged, intermittently waterlogged, and continuously waterlogged) and four litter addition treatments (no litter addition, aboveground litter addition only, belowground litter addition only, and a combination of both addition), and systematically examined the response patterns of its growth performance, photosynthetic capacity, and physiological and biochemical traits. The results showed that: (1) Waterlogging significantly suppressed the growth of S. salsa , and the alleviating effects of litter addition strongly depended on the waterlogging regime. Full and belowground litter additions were most effective under continuous waterlogging; belowground addition yielded the greatest benefits under non-waterlogged and intermittent waterlogging; and compensatory growth was observed under intermittent waterlogging without litter. (2) Litter addition mitigated waterlogging-induced damage to the photosynthetic apparatus, driving a shift from passive defense to active optimization, Notably, belowground litter more strongly promoted carboxylation efficiency and light use efficiency. (3) Belowground litter alone enhanced antioxidant enzyme activities and reduced lipid peroxidation, whereas full litter addition maintained cellular homeostasis through osmotic adjustment. (4) Correlation and PCA indicated that flooding condition was the dominant factor, whereas litter component was associated with resource allocation patterns, suggesting coordinated responses among photosynthetic efficiency, biomass accumulation, and antioxidant defense in S. salsa . In summary, flooding conditions primarily determined the physiological responses of S. salsa . Belowground litter addition was associated with higher resource use efficiency and greater antioxidant enzyme activities, and with a larger contribution of non-stomatal limitations to the decline in P n . These patterns suggest that belowground litter may help maintain growth under flooding, but the mechanisms proposed here remain speculative and require further experimental validation. Unlike previous studies that have largely focused on the individual effects of flooding or litter decomposition, this study reveals the interactive regulation of S. salsa ecophysiological processes by flooding regime and litter component, demonstrating that belowground litter plays an essential role in alleviating flooding stress and maintaining plant growth and resource use efficiency. These findings provide a theoretical basis for promoting the conservation and restoration of S. salsa populations through litter management in coastal saline wetlands, and also offer a reference for the reha

title: Use of Chronosequences to Determine Carbon Payback Times in Tree Planting Schemes: A Proof-of-Concept Study
summary: Corporate carbon offsetting schemes heavily rely on tree planting for carbon sequestration, and in Scotland, the government presents tree planting as a key carbon sink in the face of climate change. However, carbon offsetting schemes rarely
content: Corporate carbon offsetting schemes heavily rely on tree planting for carbon sequestration, and in Scotland, the government presents tree planting as a key carbon sink in the face of climate change. However, carbon offsetting schemes rarely consider associated fluxes in soil organic carbon (SOC) driven by afforestation. Soils in woodlands store approximately 75% of the total ecosystem carbon, yet planting trees on existing carbon-rich soils or grassland may result in changes in soil carbon that take decades for tree biomass to recover. This study provides a methodological framework using the chronosequence approach (space-for-time substitution) to measure whole-ecosystem carbon storage for existing commercial carbon sequestration schemes. A proof-of-concept pilot study was carried out at the University of Edinburgh’s Rullion Green site, gathering 35 soil samples across unplanted baselines, a recent 2025 planting scheme, and a mature mixed woodland. The findings of this proof-of-concept study show that soil carbon in the newly planted area (5.06% SOC) was lower than in the mature woodland (7.64% SOC) and was significantly lower (p = 0.026) than the unplanted baseline (7.11–8.65% SOC depending on slope). The carbon in the recently planted trees (5.00 t C/ha) did not offset the carbon losses from soil, with a drop in ecosystem carbon of 155.51 t C/ha compared to all baseline samples, 97.98 t C/ha when compared to baseline samples at the same topographic elevation, and 418.23 t C/ha compared to the mature woodland. Previous studies have found that deep soil carbon losses may be deeper than topsoil losses, so this may be an underestimate of carbon losses following planting, requiring further study. The methodology and trial study suggest that initial tree planting may not guarantee an immediate net increase in ecosystem carbon until trees become mature. The methodology therefore provides a tool to help mitigate greenwashing in the offsetting industry. The methodology will now be applied in further research to other sites across northern England to determine what the impact of tree planting for carbon sequestration is on soil in the UK.

title: Metastable dimeric intermediate drives native-like spidroin fibrillogenesis, while dehydration promotes cross-β transition
summary: Abstract The exceptional mechanical properties of spider dragline silk originate from hierarchical spidroin self-assembly, yet mimicking this process to generate native-like structures remains challenging. Here, we report a metastable dimer
content: Abstract The exceptional mechanical properties of spider dragline silk originate from hierarchical spidroin self-assembly, yet mimicking this process to generate native-like structures remains challenging. Here, we report a metastable dimeric intermediate as an essential molecular factor for fibrillogenesis. Small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) and atomic force microscopy (AFM) revealed a compact core surrounded by extended random coil regions. We propose that the core is stabilized by solvent-excluded “dry interfaces”: a subset of the polyalanine blocks is held by side-chain packing rather than by main-chain hydrogen bonding; the majority remain exposed in the surrounding coil regions. Upon lowering the denaturant concentration, these exposed polyalanine segments pair with their counterparts at a fibril end, forming intermolecular β-sheets that act as linkers and drive the stepwise end-to-end polymerization of the dimeric particles. In solution, the resulting fibrils exhibit an ordered β-structure in which the polypeptide chains run parallel to the fibril axis, in contrast to amyloid-like cross-β, in which the strands lie perpendicular to it; this matches key features of native silk nanofibril architecture. However, X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis demonstrates that these native-like nanofibrils undergo an effectively irreversible transition toward amyloid-like cross-β structures upon drying. Native-like fibrils are thus achievable by self-assembly, but structural control is lost during the final dehydration step. Accordingly, we propose a general principle for decoupling self-assembly from dehydration: native-like nanofibrils are formed first, then dried under conditions that restrict molecular-chain mobility—for example, mechanical constraint or immobilization on a surface—which we expect to suppress thermodynamic relaxation into cross-β structures.

title: Reflective, water-permeable diatomite masks enhancing output voltage of water-floating single-walled carbon nanotube thermoelectric generators
summary: Abstract Water-floating single-walled carbon nanotube (SWCNT) thermoelectric generators (TEGs) raise their own temperature gradient by evaporative cooling and therefore run without a heat source or a heat sink. Earlier work enlarged this sm
content: Abstract Water-floating single-walled carbon nanotube (SWCNT) thermoelectric generators (TEGs) raise their own temperature gradient by evaporative cooling and therefore run without a heat source or a heat sink. Earlier work enlarged this small gradient by feeding more water to the cooling regions, where the water evaporates. Sunlight also warms the cooling regions, so reflecting it away opens a second route to a larger gradient. We compared four devices covering combinations of reflectivity and water permeability on the cooling regions: an unmasked reference, a white acrylic resin mask, a two-layer acrylic + diatomite mask, and a diatomite mask. Under artificial sunlight of 1000 W/m 2 , the diatomite-masked device gave an output voltage of 0.50 mV, against 0.25 mV for the unmasked device. Two thickness-matched device pairs locate the origin of this gain. Covering the bare film with a thin reflective mask raised the output voltage by 0.09 mV, net of the evaporation it costs. A water-permeable diatomite mask raised it by a further 0.16 mV over a sealed one. Junction thermocouples on replicate devices agree with the derived temperature differences. A cooling-side layer that reflects sunlight and conducts water thus offers a route to larger gradients in devices that raise their own.

title: Evaluation of heat-activated and unactivated persulfate oxidation coupled with biodegradation for naphthenic acid removal and acute toxicity reduction in oil sands process-affected water
summary: ABSTRACT Oil sands process-affected water (OSPW) contains complex mixtures of naphthenic acid fraction compounds (NAFCs) that contribute to acute toxicity. This study evaluated whether residual persulfate remaining after heat-activated oxid
content: ABSTRACT Oil sands process-affected water (OSPW) contains complex mixtures of naphthenic acid fraction compounds (NAFCs) that contribute to acute toxicity. This study evaluated whether residual persulfate remaining after heat-activated oxidation (60ºC, 8 h) could be coupled with biodegradation by Pseudomonas fluorescens during a subsequent unactivated stage at room temperature (20ºC, 150 d). Commercial Merichem naphthenic acids (NAs) and aged OSPW were compared to assess the influence of water matrix complexity on oxidation efficiency and microbial viability. Heat-activated persulfate reduced OSPW-NAFCs by 45–89% at 250–1000 mg/L persulfate, increasing to 70–95% with continued reaction at room temperature, mostly within 30 d. Oxidation preferentially removed higher molecular weight, more unsaturated, O 2 -NAFCs, shifting the distribution toward more oxidized species. In OSPW, acute toxicity to Aliivibrio fischeri initially increased following activated oxidation, then declined to near background with continued reaction, consistent with progressive transformation of toxic intermediates. The addition of P. fluorescens did not improve NAFC removal and often hindered toxicity reduction, particularly in OSPW. Coupled treatments exhibited reduced persulfate reactivity, increased chemical oxygen demand, and elevated toxicity, which we hypothesize reflect oxidative stress, limited bioavailable carbon, and release of soluble microbial products that may scavenge oxidants. Only the 250 mg/L persulfate coupled treatment improved toxicity reduction relative to oxidation alone for Merichem NAs and coincided with higher viable cell counts. Overall, persulfate oxidation was effective for NAFC removal; however, simultaneous coupling with biodegradation was not effective for the OSPW tested and may be constrained by water chemistry, oxidative stress, and microbial viability.

title: The Plastic Ceiling - Opportunities and Limitations of Microbial Carbon Recovery in Crewed Spaceflight
summary: Abstract The International Space Station operates on an open resource model: consumables are delivered from Earth, used once, and disposed of by atmospheric re-entry or venting. While the water cycle is substantially closed and oxygen parti
content: Abstract The International Space Station operates on an open resource model: consumables are delivered from Earth, used once, and disposed of by atmospheric re-entry or venting. While the water cycle is substantially closed and oxygen partially so, virtually all elemental carbon in food, clothing, and packaging is lost, a paradigm incompatible with the autonomy and planetary-protection demands of deep-space operations. Microbial biotechnology has repeatedly been proclaimed a route to carbon-loop closure, yet the recovery capacity of resupply-derived waste has never been quantified. Here, we deliver an empirical carbon-accounting record covering 25 years of stable ISS operations, over which logistics resupply carried approximately 87 metric tons of carbon to low Earth orbit. An accompanying Bio-Process Sizing Framework converts user-defined operational inputs into projected carbon-recovery capacities and required reactor volumes under the physical constraints of aqueous bioprocess design, cross-checking what physics permits against what extant biology delivers. Across every scenario the framework resolves, the ceiling is set by the composition of the waste stream: packaging polymers bound what biology can recover.

title: Global Carbon Budget 2026
summary: Abstract. Accurate assessment of anthropogenic carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions and their partitioning among the atmosphere, ocean, and terrestrial biosphere in a changing climate is critical to better understand the global carbon cycle, supp
content: Abstract. Accurate assessment of anthropogenic carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions and their partitioning among the atmosphere, ocean, and terrestrial biosphere in a changing climate is critical to better understand the global carbon cycle, supporting the development of climate policies, and project future climate change. Here we describe and synthesise datasets and methodologies to quantify the five major components of the global carbon budget and their uncertainties. Fossil CO2 emissions (EFOS) are based on energy and cement production data. Emissions from land-use change (ELUC) are estimated by bookkeeping models based on land-use data. The global atmospheric CO2 growth rate (GATM) is computed from changes in concentration measured at surface stations. The global net uptake of CO2 by the ocean (SOCEAN) is estimated with global ocean biogeochemistry models and observation-based fCO2-products. The global net uptake of CO2 by the land (SLAND) is estimated with dynamic global vegetation models. Additional lines of evidence are provided by atmospheric inversions, atmospheric oxygen measurements, ocean interior observation-based estimates, and Earth System Models. The sum of all sources and sinks results in the carbon budget imbalance (BIM), a measure of imperfect data and incomplete understanding of the contemporary carbon cycle. All uncertainties are reported as ±1σ. For the year 2025, EFOS increased by 1.2% relative to 2024, with fossil emissions at 10.5 ± 0.5 GtC yr-1 (including the cement carbonation sink, 0.2 GtC yr-1), ELUC was 1.2 ± 0.7 GtC yr-1, for total anthropogenic CO2 emissions of 11.7 ± 0.9 GtC yr-1 (42.8 ± 3.2 GtCO2 yr-1). Also, for 2025, GATM was 4.4 ± 0.2 GtC yr-1 (2.06 ± 0.1 ppm yr-1), 3.6 GtC lower than the record high 2024 growth rate. SOCEAN was 3.2 ± 0.7 GtC yr-1 and SLAND was 3.6 ± 0.9 GtC yr-1, with a small BIM (0.5 GtC yr-1). The global atmospheric CO2 concentration averaged over 2025 reached 425.6 ± 0.1 ppm. Preliminary data for 2026 suggest a decrease in EFOS relative to 2025 of 0.40% (–1.5% to +0.6%) globally, and atmospheric CO2 concentration increasing by 2.2 ppm reaching 427.7 ppm, 54% above the pre-industrial level (around 278 ppm in 1750). Overall, the mean and trend in the components of the global carbon budget are consistently estimated over the period 1959–2025, with a small positive overall budget imbalance, (0.6 GtC yr-1 averaged over the period 1959–2025), although discrepancies of up to around 1 GtC yr-1 persist for the representation of annual to decadal variability in CO2 fluxes. Comparison of estimates from multiple approaches and observations shows: (1) a persistent large uncertainty in the estimate of land-use change emissions, (2) a low agreement between the different estimates on the magnitude of the land CO2 flux, particularly in the northern extra-tropics, and (3) a discrepancy between the different estimates on the mean ocean sink and its trend. This living data update documents changes in methods and da

title: Sea ice, wind and mixed layer depth: a sea ice-ocean model study of drivers of mixing in the Antarctic Peninsula region
summary: Around Antarctica, complex interactions between the cryosphere, ocean and atmosphere create an environment with large geographical, seasonal and interannual variability which is highly vulnerable to climate change. Upper-ocean mixing plays
content: Around Antarctica, complex interactions between the cryosphere, ocean and atmosphere create an environment with large geographical, seasonal and interannual variability which is highly vulnerable to climate change. Upper-ocean mixing plays an important role in structuring this environment through its role in primary productivity and biogeochemistry, and by moderating exchanges between the atmosphere and interior ocean. Mixed layer depth (MLD) varies throughout the seasons, with a distinct seasonal cycle of deep winter mixing and shallow spring shoaling. Wind mixing and the sea ice seasonal cycle of brine rejection and meltwater input have long been recognised as key drivers of MLD. However, there is considerable uncertainty surrounding the relative importance of these processes, with a range of studies attesting to the primary importance of each. To further complicate an assessment of the importance of MLD drivers, wind and sea ice also interact, for example through wind-driven sea ice transport separating areas predominantly characterised by sea ice freezing and melting, and through the effect of sea ice cover on the magnitude of wind stress at the ocean surface. This thesis makes use of MIT General Circulation Model (MITgcm) three-dimensional as well as one-dimensional modelling to examine the role that wind and sea ice play in setting the seasonal MLD in two regions on the western and eastern side of the Antarctic Peninsula: the Bellingshausen Sea and Weddell Sea. Beginning with the question of how sea ice impacts MLD, the first research chapter presents regional correlations between winter sea ice concentration (SIC) and spring MLD. This specific focus on spring MLD is due to its importance for primary producers. Regional differences in the sign of the correlation point towards a difference in the relationship between sea ice and MLD on and off the West Antarctic Peninsula (WAP) continental shelf.
