This study evaluates both pathways for a representative 24-h photovoltaic generation and demand profile in Nusantara Capital City, Indonesia. A year-specific representative-day dispatch model for 2024–2046 includes photovoltaic degradation, battery state of charge and replacement, electrolysis, hydrogen compression and storage, fuel-cell reconversion, and lifecycle costs. Delivered electricity, curtailment, and levelized cost of storage (LCOS) were assessed under mixed-vintage, monetary-normalised, and provenance-locked economic scenarios, followed by break-even analysis. In 2024, battery storage delivered 206.08 kWh/day, compared with 174.08 kWh/day from hydrogen, while curtailment was 437.82 and 151.45 kWh/day, respectively. Mixed-vintage LCOS favoured batteries (IDR 4,581.41/kWh versus IDR 8,105.05/kWh). Under provenance-locked assumptions, the ranking reversed (IDR 10,498.69/kWh for batteries versus IDR 8,947.97/kWh for hydrogen), with battery-capital-cost parity near USD 292.97/kWh at the baseline electrolyser CAPEX. The findings establish that technology rankings depend on storage service and documented economic inputs rather than being universal. These conditional thresholds provide decision evidence relevant to Sustainable Development Goal 7 on clean-energy systems and Goal 9 on sustainable infrastructure, without measuring progress towards either goal or seasonal storage performance.

title: Heat transfer of an experimentally characterized hybrid nanofluid over a curved surface for nuclear reactor cooling
summary: Abstract The current study investigates the nonlinear convection flow of an experimentally characterized ternary nanofluid over a permeable curved heat exchanger tube by incorporating temperature-dependent viscosity and thermal conductivity
content: Abstract The current study investigates the nonlinear convection flow of an experimentally characterized ternary nanofluid over a permeable curved heat exchanger tube by incorporating temperature-dependent viscosity and thermal conductivity. The formulated boundary layer equations are presented in a curvilinear coordinate system, accounting for nonlinear thermal radiation, spatially varying volumetric heat generation, convective heating at wall tubes, and viscous dissipation. Experimentally derived equations for viscosity and thermal conductivity for temperatures $$25^\circ $$ to $$50^\circ $$ and 1.4 to 3% nanoparticle concentrations are incorporated. The nonlinear Boussinesq approximation is employed to capture the large temperature gradient within the boundary layer. The Chebyshev collocation method is employed to solve the compacted equations, and an accord with the literature is established. The study reveals that key parameters such as curvature intensify the fluid’s temperature and entropy generation by about 18% and 22%, respectively, while the skin friction and Nusselt number drop by about 15% and 12%, respectively. The volume heat generation increased the fluid’s temperature by up to 19% but decreased the skin friction Nusselt number and entropy by about 6%, 4%, and 11%, respectively. Thermal radiation elevates the temperature by 14% and the Nusselt number by 8% and drops the skin friction and entropy by about 10% and 7%, respectively. The performance evaluation criterion (PEC) values are obtained as 1.1083, 1.4966, and 1.9179 for the mono, hybrid, and ternary nanofluids, respectively. The ternary fluid exhibits the highest PEC, indicating its superior heat transfer performance over mono- and hybrid mixtures with about 73% and 28%, respectively. These outcomes depict that the ternary nanofluid, with its experimentally validated temperature-dependent properties, provides significant potential for advanced thermal management applications, especially in nuclear energy systems, compact heat exchangers, and high-temperature thermal devices where efficient heat removal and thermodynamic optimization are significant.

title: Geometric Design Optimization of an Energy-efficient Propeller Retrofit for Small-scale Shallow-water Maritime Transport
summary: The small-scale shallow-water maritime transport in Southeast Asia heavily relies on traditional two-blade propellers, which frequently suffer from severe hydrodynamic degradation, ventilation, aeration and sheet cavitation under shallow im
content: The small-scale shallow-water maritime transport in Southeast Asia heavily relies on traditional two-blade propellers, which frequently suffer from severe hydrodynamic degradation, ventilation, aeration and sheet cavitation under shallow immersion. To address these constraints, this study introduces an engineering design framework to develop an energy-efficient, three-blade retrofit propeller, designated as model B3-55. The blade geometry was optimized using a multi-subprogram algorithm incorporating regression analysis and response surface methodology to maximize open-water efficiency while minimizing cavitation risks. Hydrodynamic validations were executed utilizing Lattice Boltzmann method (LBM)-based CFD simulations via XFlow, coupled with water tunnel and field testing at 650-750 rpm. under a 50-cm immersion depth. Numerical and empirical results revealed that the optimized wide-chord tip geometry of model B3-55 achieved a remarkable open-water efficiency (η_o) of 0.830 at an advance coefficient (η_o) of 0.701. Crucially, the wide-chord configuration significantly suppressed tip vortex bursting and delayed destructive ventilation compared to the local baseline. This propulsion framework offers a scalable, socio-economically resilient solution that reduces fuel consumption and operational expenditures for rural fishing communities.

title: High-Temperature Resistant Sealing Materials from Chitosan-Modified Alkali-Activated Coal Gangue for Mine Fire Prevention
summary: Abstract Coal spontaneous combustion remains a persistent hazard in underground mining, demanding sealing materials that retain structural integrity and low gas permeability under sustained thermal loading. Therefore, this study prepared a
content: Abstract Coal spontaneous combustion remains a persistent hazard in underground mining, demanding sealing materials that retain structural integrity and low gas permeability under sustained thermal loading. Therefore, this study prepared a cementitious firefighting material by alkali activation of coal gangue and modified with low-dosage chitosan for goaf sealing applications. The formulation for the base aluminosilicate matrix was optimized to a 4:6 mass ratio of coal gangue to ground granulated blast furnace slag, a water-to-precursor ratio of 0.40, an activator modulus of 1.0, and a 6% alkali dosage. To overcome the inherent thermal vulnerability of the conventional alkali-activated materials, chitosan was introduced to coordinate with Ca2+ ions released during activation. FTIR, XRD, and SEM characterizations reveal that this coordination forms an interpenetrating organic–inorganic dual-network that bridges the aluminosilicate matrix. Results indicate that at a low chitosan dosage of 0.5%, the material exhibits an optimal 3-day compressive strength of 11.05 MPa. Following thermal exposure, the coordination cross-links effectively dissipate thermal stress and suppress crack propagation, reducing thermally shrinkage by approximately 40% relative to the unmodified matrix at 600 °C. Although this differential narrows at 800 °C, the modification critically preserves macroscopic integrity throughout the 200–600 °C range where crack suppression is most consequential for sealing performance. Permeability and porosity analyses demonstrate that chitosan modification preserves the sealing capacity primarily by disrupting the connectivity of the thermally damaged pore network, yielding an SDR-estimated permeability as low as 0.03 mD. The material utilizes coal gangue as the dominant precursor and achieves marked thermal-resistance enhancement at low chitosan dosage, offering a scalable and resource-efficient strategy for preventing coal spontaneous combustion in underground coal mines.

title: Application of nitric oxide donor improves the response of Khaya grandifoliola C. DC seedlings to water deficit
summary: Abstract The cultivation of Khaya grandifoliola has expanded in tropical regions, as a promising option for high-quality timber production. However, water deficit caused by prolonged drought can lead to seedling mortality and reduced biomas
content: Abstract The cultivation of Khaya grandifoliola has expanded in tropical regions, as a promising option for high-quality timber production. However, water deficit caused by prolonged drought can lead to seedling mortality and reduced biomass accumulation. Nitric oxide (NO) has been reported to play a role in plant responses to abiotic stress, including drought. This study aimed to evaluate the potential of NO to mitigate the effects of water deficit on the physiological performance of K. grandifoliola seedlings. Plants were treated with NO donor S-nitroso-mercaptosuccinic acid (MSNO) applied to the substrate at concentrations of 0, 0.1, 0.2, and 0.4 mM. Water deficit was imposed by interrupting irrigation for 22 days. Each treatment consisted of 15 replicates. The application of 0.2 mM MSNO improved leaf gas exchange, resulting in higher net photosynthesis, transpiration, stomatal conductance, and water use efficiency compared to plants under water deficit. In addition, MSNO-treated plants showed higher relative water content, lower proline accumulation, and reduced mortality. These results suggest that MSNO application enhances drought tolerance in K. grandifoliola seedlings, representing a potential strategy for improving seedling establishment under water-limited conditions.

title: Implementing the (3ms) Framework to Achieve Sustainable Facade Design and Architectural Resilience in Developing Countries
summary: Rapid urbanization, increasing electricity demand, and developing environmental challenges have created a pressing need for sustainable and climate-responsive architectural solutions in Bangladesh. Despite the growing adoption of sustainabl
content: Rapid urbanization, increasing electricity demand, and developing environmental challenges have created a pressing need for sustainable and climate-responsive architectural solutions in Bangladesh. Despite the growing adoption of sustainable façade techniques, there remains a lack of an integrated design framework that systematically connects sustainability goals with practical architectural implementation in developing-country contexts. This study aims to propose and apply the 3Ms framework—Missions, Milestones, and Methods—as a structured approach for achieving sustainable façade design and enhancing architectural resilience. The study adopts a qualitative design methodology combining an in-depth literature review, architectural case-study analysis, on-site field research, and design development using AutoCAD, SketchUp, ArchiCAD, and Lumion for drafting, modelling, documentation, and visualization. The gathered evidence from literature, case studies, and field observations is synthesized to develop the 3Ms framework, where Missions outline sustainability and resilience targets, Milestones establish progressive design goals, and Methods identify appropriate architectural strategies for implementation. The framework is finally applied to a proposed building design incorporating passive façade interventions, locally available materials, green design techniques, natural ventilation principles, and photovoltaic façade integration. The study presents the architectural application of the proposed framework and evaluates its potential contribution to sustainable façade design through comparative design considerations and photovoltaic integration. The findings highlight the relevance of a structured decision-making framework for guiding architects and planners in developing context-responsive and environmentally conscious building envelopes. However, the study is limited by its design-based and case-study-oriented approach, and further research involving validated building-performance simulation and long-term post-occupancy evaluation is recommended. The major contribution of this research is the development of the 3Ms framework as a practical architectural approach that links sustainability goals with implementable façade design strategies for Bangladesh and other developing countries.

title: Phosphogypsum as a soil amendment: mechanisms, applications, and environmental risks
summary: Phosphogypsum (PG) is a calcium sulfate-rich by-product of phosphoric acid production. Agricultural reuse can recover calcium and sulfur and improve soils constrained by sodicity, subsoil acidity, or nutrient deficiency. This review examine
content: Phosphogypsum (PG) is a calcium sulfate-rich by-product of phosphoric acid production. Agricultural reuse can recover calcium and sulfur and improve soils constrained by sodicity, subsoil acidity, or nutrient deficiency. This review examines PG characteristics, soil interactions, agronomic responses, and environmental risks. Structured literature screening, evidence classification, bibliometric analysis, and critical narrative synthesis were combined. Phosphogypsum supplies Ca 2+ for sodium displacement and clay flocculation in saline-sodic soils and can improve subsoil calcium availability and reduce aluminum toxicity in acid soils. Responses depend on material composition, soil properties, application rate, water management, climate, and crop requirements. Evidence for greenhouse gas mitigation is concentrated in flooded rice systems, with limited validation in upland agriculture. Residual acidity, soluble salts, fluorine, potentially toxic elements, and naturally occurring radionuclides require assessment through contaminant speciation, leachability, cumulative loading, crop uptake, and exposure pathways. Inconsistent material characterization, short experimental durations, and limited long-term field, regulatory, and economic assessments constrain the transfer of published results to practice. Agricultural use requires source-specific quality control, rates matched to soil requirements and environmental limits, long-term monitoring, and economic comparison with conventional amendments and other PG management options.

title: Assessing future eco-hydrological behaviour of a typical Sahelian agro-ecosystem under climate change for the 21st century
summary: Study Region The Sahel is dominated by a monsoon climate, where most of the population relies on subsistence agriculture. This study focuses on a typical agro-pastoral area in southwestern Niger. Study Focus Significant gaps remain in clima
content: Study Region The Sahel is dominated by a monsoon climate, where most of the population relies on subsistence agriculture. This study focuses on a typical agro-pastoral area in southwestern Niger. Study Focus Significant gaps remain in climate change impact projections in the Sahel. Indeed, capturing the impact of rapid hydrological processes necessitates high temporal resolution scenarios and adapted ecohydrological models, which has rarely been done in Sahel. This study addresses this gap by building climate scenarios at a 30-minute time step, by combining an observational dataset with CMIP6 projections for five models, two emission pathways (SSP245 and SSP585), and two horizons (2050 and 2100). These scenarios are used in a land surface model, SiSPAT, to assess future changes in water and energy cycles. Vegetation response to climate evolution is also considered. New Hydrological Insights for the Region All scenarios project a temperature increase for 2100 (+3.8°C for SSP245, +6.3°C for SSP585), with up to 10 days over 45°C during the growing season. Projected rainfall intensification is more uncertain (+27 to +56% by 2100). It leads to an increase in runoff (+168 mm/yr) and drainage (+132 mm/yr) for SSP585–2100, raising concern over flooding and soil erosion. Considering vegetation response to climate evolution strongly affects evapotranspiration seasonality (+/- 1 mm/day during some months). This study highlights the impact of climate scenarios on water and energy cycles with current agricultural practices.

title: Performance, Combustion, and Emission Analysis of a Ternary Hybrid Ethyl Ester Blend and Its Impact in a Single-Cylinder Compression Ignition Engine
summary: Heavy-duty diesel engines significantly contribute to environmental degradation, motivating the search for sustainable alternatives like plant-derived biodiesel. This study investigates the performance and emissions of a novel ternary hybri
content: Heavy-duty diesel engines significantly contribute to environmental degradation, motivating the search for sustainable alternatives like plant-derived biodiesel. This study investigates the performance and emissions of a novel ternary hybrid biodiesel blend made from shea butter, neem oil, and waste kitchen oils (40.41:19.73:39.86 w/w) in a direct-injection, four-stroke, single-cylinder diesel engine. Various fuel blends (B0, B10, B20, B30, B40, B100) were evaluated against conventional diesel. The experimental results show that all tested biodiesel blends exhibit consistently shorter ignition delays than diesel due to higher cetane numbers (57 for B100 versus 52 for B0). At full load, biodiesel blends reduced carbon monoxide and hydrocarbon emissions by up to 26.79% and 41.06%, respectively. B30 blend demonstrated the most favorable balance between emission reductions and overall engine performance, despite a moderate increase in brake-specific fuel consumption (0.42 kg/kWh versus 0.35 kg/kWh for B0). Conversely, nitrogen oxide emissions increased by 15.8% for B100 because of higher in-cylinder peak temperatures. Crucially, this hybridization showed no significant synergistic improvement in performance: a scientifically valuable negative finding proving multi-feedstock blending does not automatically enhance fuel quality, likely due to counteracting effects from distinct saturated, monounsaturated, and mixed fatty acid profiles. For real-world applications, recommendations include fuel preheating (60–80 °C) and injection timing retardation (2–3 °CA) for B30–B40, alongside a 10–15% injection pressure increase for B100. Despite achieving an impressive 78% carbon dioxide reduction, several research gaps remain regarding long-term engine impact and comprehensive lifecycle analyses, which are vital for scaling this ternary biodiesel adoption.

title: Gratification vs. gravity: A dual-factor model of socio-psychological and structural drivers in Vietnam’s green mobility transition
summary: As Vietnam grapples with the escalating challenges of urban air pollution and systemic traffic congestion, the transition to green mobility has shifted from a policy preference to a sustainable development imperative. This study proposes a
content: As Vietnam grapples with the escalating challenges of urban air pollution and systemic traffic congestion, the transition to green mobility has shifted from a policy preference to a sustainable development imperative. This study proposes a dual-factor framework, "Gratification vs. Gravity", grounded in Uses and Gratifications Theory, to investigate the interplay between socio-psychological gratifications and structural constraints in shaping adoption intention among Vietnamese urban consumers. Data from 328 respondents in four major cities were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM), complemented by an artificial neural network (ANN). The empirical results reveal that pro-Environmental Attitudes emerged as the strongest predictor, followed by Level of Safety, Convenience, Eco-Hedonic Motivation, and Eco-Innovativeness, whereas Perceived Affordability and Eco-warrior Social Media Influencers showed no significant direct effects. The ANN results confirm Pro-Environmental Attitudes and Level of Safety as the most important predictors. These findings suggest that Vietnamese consumers, particularly the younger demographic, perceive green vehicles not merely as tools for conservation, but as symbols of a modern, flexible, and emotionally rewarding lifestyle. On the structural side, safety appears to be a key condition for bridging the value–action gap, as psychological motivation is less likely to translate into usage without it. This study provides empirical support for a dual-factor conceptual framework that balances socio-psychological gratification against structural gravity. For policymakers and stakeholders, the strategic focus should shift from basic price subsidies toward rigorous safety standards and integrated smart infrastructure that enhances the experiential value of the green transition.

title: Overview of Bioinput Commercialization for Staple Food Crops in Central-Southern Brazil (2019–2023)
summary: Abstract The transition toward the use of bioinputs represents a strategic pillar for the sustainability and resilience of global food systems; however, patterns of their practical adoption in staple food crops across the Global South remai
content: Abstract The transition toward the use of bioinputs represents a strategic pillar for the sustainability and resilience of global food systems; however, patterns of their practical adoption in staple food crops across the Global South remain poorly quantified. This study investigated the commercialization of bioinputs in Central-Southern Brazil from 2019 to 2023 for crops included in the Brazilian Basic Food Basket, using official data from agricultural defense agencies in the states of Mato Grosso, Paraná, Rio Grande do Sul, and Santa Catarina. Active ingredients and commercialized volumes were quantified for rice, coffee, sugarcane, common bean, soybean, and wheat. The relative volume of biological products compared with synthetic products was highest for wheat (0.29%), followed by soybean (0.06%). Regarding bioinput diversity, soybean accounted for the highest relative proportion (7.29%), followed by rice (6.15%). A total of 32 individual biological active ingredients were identified, with soybean showing the greatest diversity (n = 30). Microbial agents dominated the market (78.12%; n = 25), comprising fungi (34.37%; n = 11), bacteria (28.12%; n = 9), and viruses (15.62%; n = 5), with viral agents restricted to baculoviruses used in soybean. Botanical products accounted for 21.87% (n = 7). The bioinsecticide Bacillus thuringiensis showed the broadest commercialization across all evaluated crops, followed by a common pattern of commercialization of Bacillus subtilis , Beauveria bassiana , Metarhizium anisopliae , Purpureocillium lilacinum , and Trichoderma harzianum across sugarcane, common bean, soybean, and wheat. Among botanical products, Azadirachta indica and Sophora flavescens were prominent in rice, coffee, common bean, and soybean. The findings demonstrate the heterogeneous expansion of bioinputs across the region and provide an empirical basis for public policies and scientific strategies aimed at strengthening food security and ecosystem integrity. Future studies should maintain longitudinal monitoring of bioinput commercialization to inform regional guidelines and support the consolidation of sustainable agricultural systems.

title: Overcoming Financial and Capacity Barriers to Empower Small-Scale Enterprises in South Africa: Focus on Renewable, Reliable, Secure and Affordable Energy in Mpumalanga and the Western Cape
summary: South Africa’s efforts to build a renewable, secure, reliable and affordable energy system are creating new opportunities to mobilise finance and investment, especially in renewable energy. This requires unlocking finance, particularly in c
content: South Africa’s efforts to build a renewable, secure, reliable and affordable energy system are creating new opportunities to mobilise finance and investment, especially in renewable energy. This requires unlocking finance, particularly in coal-dependent regions such as Mpumalanga, where the need for economic diversification and job creation is greatest.Improving access to finance for micro, small and medium-sized enterprises in support of renewable energy can support economic competitiveness, job creation and access to secure, reliable and affordable energy. However, many small enterprises continue to face barriers to accessing financing, especially in renewable energy. South Africa is home to an estimated 2.6 million small-scale enterprises, around two-thirds of which operate informally, underscoring the need for broader access to emerging economic opportunities.This report identifies actions to unlock access to financing for small‑scale enterprises in renewable energy and related value chains. It also explores financing approaches for community-centric renewable energy microgrids.Drawing on extensive consultations with government, financial institutions, business support organisations, small-scale enterprises and local communities, the report provides practical recommendations to unlock finance and support local development, economic opportunity and investment in a renewable, secure, reliable and affordable energy system.

title: Composting performance, nitrogen retention, and microbial succession differ among urea-only and organic co-substrate-amended Camellia oleifera shell formulations
summary: Camellia oleifera shell is a lignocellulosic by-product, and its inefficient decomposition limits waste reduction and nutrient recovery. To identify practical amendment strategies, we compared urea alone (CK) with urea combined with goat du
content: Camellia oleifera shell is a lignocellulosic by-product, and its inefficient decomposition limits waste reduction and nutrient recovery. To identify practical amendment strategies, we compared urea alone (CK) with urea combined with goat dung (GD), C. oleifera seed meal (CM), or rice bran (RB) in terms of nitrogen retention, compost maturation, and microbial succession during C. oleifera shell composting over 77 days. Organic co-amendments improved compost heating and prolonged thermophilic conditions relative to urea alone. RB achieved the highest nitrogen retention (91.64 ± 0.96%), whereas CK had the lowest measured inorganic nitrogen concentration. Co-amendments increased bacterial diversity and were associated with succession of fungal communities toward saprotrophy. Bacterial community patterns were related to the carbon/nitrogen (C/N) ratio, electrical conductivity (EC), and the extract optical index (E4/E6), while fungal succession was more strongly associated with composting time. Overall, supplementing urea with organic co-substrate was associated with nitrogen retention and several maturity indices relative to urea alone, although no single amendment performed best on every compost quality criterion. Although RB's final total nutrient content was below the cited 4.0% criterion and final-product safety was not established, these findings provide a practical basis for converting C. oleifera shell into a more stable, nutrient-retaining compost and support the resource-efficient utilization of this agricultural by-product.

title: Triple Bottom Line-Based Dynamic System Modeling for Sustainable Rice Food Security in East Java
source: Journal of Engineering Management and Systems Engineering
summary: This study addresses the strategic engineering management challenge of balancing short-term farm economic profitability with long-term soil carrying capacity restoration in staple crop systems.It aims to evaluate policy trade-offs and inter
content: This study addresses the strategic engineering management challenge of balancing short-term farm economic profitability with long-term soil carrying capacity restoration in staple crop systems.It aims to evaluate policy trade-offs and inter-agency coordination mechanisms across the Triple Bottom Line (TBL) dimensions-People, Planet, and Profit-to enhance regional rice food security in East Java, Indonesia.A system dynamics (SD) simulation model was engineered using STELLA software, integrating demographic demand, biophysical soil degradation/regeneration loops, farmer financial investment flows, and policy execution dynamics.Model parameters were calibrated using empirical historical data (2021-2025) and stakeholder interviews (N = 45).Structural validity was evaluated through dimensional consistency, extreme-condition tests, and mean relative error (E1), defined as the average percentage deviation between simulated and historical behavior (E1 ≤ 4.73%).Four policy intervention scenarios were simulated over a 2026-2030 horizon: Baseline, Economic Intervention, Environmental Intervention, and a Combined Policy Intervention.The Baseline scenario experiences saturation after 2028, with the Sustainable Rice Food Security Index (SFSI) declining to 70.41 by 2030 due to unmitigated soil health degradation.The Economic Intervention scenario enhances immediate farmer profitability (SFSI = 75.43),but performance levels off over time due to ongoing biophysical soil depletion.The Environmental Interventio scenario restricting subsidized chemical fertilizer to 1,034,209 tons/year and transitioning to organic inputs exhibits steady ecological resilience (SFSI = 77.61).The Combined Policy Intervention scenario achieves the highest projected performance (SFSI = 81.12),buffering short-term financial transition shocks while supporting soil carrying capacity restoration.Overall, the simulation results suggest that biophysical soil health restoration constitutes a primary structural leverage point preventing limits-to-growth system degradation.Successful policy execution requires an integrated inter-agency roadmap: the National Food Agency must align price floors, the Ministry of Agriculture must reallocate chemical subsidies toward bio-organic supply chains and extension training, and the Ministry of Environment and Forestry must enforce regional soil organic monitoring.

title: PROPOSTA DE CRITÉRIOS PARA AVALIAR TERMELÉTRICAS FLUTUANTES A GNL NO BRASIL: O CASO DA BAÍA DE SEPETIBA
summary: As termelétricas flutuantes a gás natural liquefeito (GNL), ou powerships, são navios que geram eletricidade e a entregam a uma subestação em terra. Como dependem de combustível importado e ocupam áreas costeiras, sua contribuição à seguran
content: As termelétricas flutuantes a gás natural liquefeito (GNL), ou powerships, são navios que geram eletricidade e a entregam a uma subestação em terra. Como dependem de combustível importado e ocupam áreas costeiras, sua contribuição à segurança energética deve ser avaliada com seus efeitos ambientais. Este artigo acompanha a trajetória das quatro powerships instaladas na Baía de Sepetiba (RJ), que somam 560 MW de potência contratada em 2021, para propor critérios de avaliação dessa tecnologia. O trabalho combina revisão narrativa e análise documental de publicações de 2022 a 2026: artigos científicos, balanços oficiais, documentos do Tribunal de Contas da União e reportagens especializadas. A contratação foi uma resposta à crise hídrica de 2021. A primeira usina, porém, só operou comercialmente após o prazo-limite, com os reservatórios já recuperados, e o caso gerou disputas judiciais, regulatórias e ambientais até um acordo que reduziu a geração obrigatória e a remuneração fixa. A literatura indica que as emissões da cadeia do GNL e as da queima devem ser separadas, e que riscos possíveis ao ambiente costeiro não se confundem com danos comprovados. O principal resultado é uma matriz com sete dimensões (serviço elétrico, prontidão, custo, combustível, clima e ar, ambiente costeiro e saúde, governança), proposta para orientar futuras contratações. No caso examinado, a mobilidade da usina não garantiu o cumprimento dos prazos; custo comparativo e adequação ambiental dependem de avaliações específicas.

title: Model-Informed Kinetic Synchronization for Intensified Methane-to-Poly(3-hydroxybutyrate) Bioconversion
summary: Abstract Biological conversion of methane into poly(3-hydroxybutyrate) (PHB) offers a promising route for greenhouse gas mitigation, yet its industrial deployment remains constrained by inherently low volumetric productivity. To overcome th
content: Abstract Biological conversion of methane into poly(3-hydroxybutyrate) (PHB) offers a promising route for greenhouse gas mitigation, yet its industrial deployment remains constrained by inherently low volumetric productivity. To overcome this limitation, a multistage, repeated-batch strategy was developed to physically decouple biomass growth from PHB accumulation and synchronize their disparate kinetics using parallel reactors. Single-batch cultivation of Methylocystis sp. MJC1 revealed three phases: exponential growth, gas-transfer-limited growth, and PHB synthesis. Repeated-batch experiments using a dedicated cell generator and PHB producer demonstrated stable, reproducible biomass production without physiological deterioration. Based on the kinetic characteristics derived from these single- and repeated-batch cultivations, a simplified process model was constructed. Model-informed simulations identified a three-reactor configuration comprising a single cell generator supplying two parallel PHB producers as a critical step change, delivering substantial productivity gains while maintaining operational feasibility. Experimental validation of this configuration, using a transfer biomass concentration of 12 g/L, a transfer fraction of 79%, and a cell generator cultivation time of 20 h, yielded a volumetric productivity of 0.218 g-PHB/L/h, a 1.32-fold improvement over single-batch cultivation. Overall, this work establishes a robust and scalable framework for intensifying the production of methane-derived biodegradable polymers through synchronized multistage cultivation.

title: The Effects of Climate Change in Africa: Replicating the GCA Model for Economic Development
source: American Journal of Theoretical and Applied Business
summary: Climate change represents one of the most significant challenges confronting economic development in Africa during the twenty-first century. Although the continent contributes less than four percent of global greenhouse gas emissions, Afric
content: Climate change represents one of the most significant challenges confronting economic development in Africa during the twenty-first century. Although the continent contributes less than four percent of global greenhouse gas emissions, African countries remain among the most vulnerable to climate-induced shocks, including rising temperatures, prolonged droughts, flooding, desertification, biodiversity loss, and disruptions to agricultural productivity. This study replicates and extends the analytical framework developed by the Global Center on Adaptation (GCA) to evaluate the economic consequences of climate change and the effectiveness of adaptation investments across African economies. Using a panel dataset covering 48 African countries from 2000-2023, the study employs fixed-effects estimation, System Generalized Method of Moments (GMM), and instrumental variable techniques to examine the relationship between climate exposure, adaptation finance, vulnerability, and economic growth. The findings indicate that climate-related shocks significantly reduce GDP per capita growth, particularly in agriculture-dependent economies. However, adaptation investments substantially mitigate economic losses and improve resilience outcomes. Counterfactual simulations suggest that scaling adaptation financing in line with the Africa Adaptation Acceleration Program (AAAP) could reduce cumulative GDP losses by between 12 and 30 percent over a decade. The study concludes that adaptation investments constitute not only a climate policy response but also a critical development strategy for Africa.

title: Investigating power transfer technologies for electric vehicles towards the development of electric road system in e-highway networks
summary: Electric Vehicles (EV) adoption has become a potential contributor for promoting the sustainability of road transportation, due to lower environmental impacts as compared to traditional fossil fuel vehicles. However, the widespread adoption
content: Electric Vehicles (EV) adoption has become a potential contributor for promoting the sustainability of road transportation, due to lower environmental impacts as compared to traditional fossil fuel vehicles. However, the widespread adoption of EV is still limited due to several challenges such as the availability and accessibility of static or dynamic charging infrastructures. Additionally, the deployment of Electric Road Systems (ERS) is gaining acceptance as a technological solution for charging road transport vehicles, few studies have addressed the drivers that influences adoption from a holistic perspective. Therefore, this article addresses this gap by examining the implementation of ERS as a plausible solution that enables dynamic charging of EVs by supplying electrical power from the electrified road to the EV in-motion, either via a conductive or inductive approach. In this study a qualitative review is carried grounded on empirical data from the literature to empirically analyses the potential benefit of implementing ERS, dynamic on-road conductive power transfer and inductive power transfer wireless charging approach are further examined in detail. Findings from this study discusses the drivers based on the lifecycle approach that need to be considered for successful implementation of ERS technologies within electric Highway (e-Highway) road networks. Key findings from this study highlights the current state-of-the-art of ERS infrastructure providing implications towards the electrification of e-highway networks.

title: Integrating Income-Stratified Dietary Transitions into the AFOLU_India Model: Implications for Fertiliser Use and N₂O Emissions in India
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: Rapid income growth and structural transformation in India are reshaping dietary patterns, with important implications for nutrition, agricultural systems, and climate mitigation. Targeting developed-nation status by 2047 under the Viksit B
content: Rapid income growth and structural transformation in India are reshaping dietary patterns, with important implications for nutrition, agricultural systems, and climate mitigation. Targeting developed-nation status by 2047 under the Viksit Bharat vision, the country faces acute trade-offs between meeting growing nutritional needs and containing agricultural greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, particularly from nitrogen fertilizer use. Existing integrated assessment models (IAMs) have limited capacity to capture income-disaggregated, nutrition-sensitive demand dynamics particularly for rapidly developing economies like India. This study addresses that gap using HCES data across five income groups, projecting food demand under two GDP growth trajectories: a BAU Scenario and a Sustainable Diet Scenario aligned with the Viksit Bharat 2047 target (per capita GDP ~$18,000) and national nutrition policies including Mission LiFE and POSHAN Abhiyaan. Results show divergent dietary pathways. The BAU Scenario sees continued cereal-heavy demand with limited diversification, while the Sustainable Diet Scenario stabilises cereal consumption and significantly expands nutrient-dense foods pulses, vegetables, fruits, and milk. Total food demand rises from 476 MT (2024) to 661 MT (BAU) and 853 MT (Sustainable Diet Scenario) by 2050. Production requirements are linked to nitrogen fertilizer use and N₂O emissions via the AFOLU-B model. Despite higher output under the Sustainable Diet Scenario, fertilizer efficiency gains and manure substitution partially decouple emissions from production growth (145 vs. 160 MtCO₂e by 2050, a ~10% difference). The findings demonstrate that sustainable dietary transitions can deliver substantial nutritional gains with manageable emission trade-offs, underscoring the need to integrate income-heterogeneous, demand-side dynamics into IAM frameworks and climate policy.

title: Interprofessional Pedagogy for the Anthropocene: Faculty Perspectives on the imperative for Climate Change and SDG-Aligned Planetary Health Education in Medicine, Veterinary Medicine, and Conservation and Marine Ecology programs
summary: Abstract Background: Climate change is one of the planetary boundaries that has been transgressed and is increasingly affecting human, animal, and ecosystem health. Its impacts include the expansion of vector-borne diseases, food and water
content: Abstract Background: Climate change is one of the planetary boundaries that has been transgressed and is increasingly affecting human, animal, and ecosystem health. Its impacts include the expansion of vector-borne diseases, food and water insecurity, extreme weather events, poor air quality, and adverse mental health outcomes. Despite growing recognition of these threats, climate change and planetary health education remain inconsistently integrated across health professions curricula. Faculty perspectives on embedding planetary health education through interprofessional education (IPE) remain underexplored, particularly in Small Island Developing States (SIDS) where climate vulnerability is acute. Methods: This qualitative study explored faculty perceptions of planetary health education and the role of IPE in its delivery. Heterogeneous focus groups and one individual interview were conducted with 49 faculty members representing Medicine, Veterinary Medicine, Public Health, Biology/Ecology, Marine Conservation, and pre-medical/pre-veterinary programmes across 18 geographical regions. The focus group/interview questions are provided in Appendix 1. Data were analysed using thematic analysis guided by two research questions addressing the importance of planetary health education and strategies for interprofessional curricular integration. Results: Three themes emerged. First, faculty expressed strong consensus on the need to align planetary health competencies with the Sustainable Development Goals and identified key curricular topics, including vector-borne and zoonotic diseases, food and water security, heat stress, marine health, mental health, and social determinants of health. Second, participants proposed strategies for curricular integration, including curriculum mapping, vertical integration of competencies, simulation- and case-based learning, shared electives, and experiential learning through institutional partnerships. Third, faculty identified barriers to implementation, including limited accreditation requirements, insufficient faculty development, curriculum overcrowding, and a hidden curriculum in which relevant content exists across programmes but remains poorly coordinated and largely siloed. Conclusions: Faculty across disciplines view planetary health education as an urgent professional responsibility and support its delivery through interprofessional approaches. However, institutional barriers continue to impede implementation. Existing climate- and One Health-related content across programmes provides a foundation for developing integrated, competency-based planetary health curricula, particularly in climate-vulnerable regions seeking to strengthen health system resilience.

title: Sustainable Food Systems in Sub-Saharan Africa: Plant Derived Nutritious Foods
source: Journal of Central and Eastern European African Studies
summary: Joy West and Rattan Lal, representing leading institutions in Norway, Malawi, and the United States.The publication forms part of a broader initiative aimed at advancing sustainable food systems and improving food and nutrition security in
content: Joy West and Rattan Lal, representing leading institutions in Norway, Malawi, and the United States.The publication forms part of a broader initiative aimed at advancing sustainable food systems and improving food and nutrition security in Sub-Saharan Africa.The volume contains 574 pages and 28 chapters organized into five major thematic sections, bringing together the work of more than 110 scientists from Africa, Europe, Asia, and North America.

title: The Climate–Pollution Feedback Loop
summary: Climate change and pollution are often treated as separate challenges, yet they are connected through a climate-pollution feedback loop in which each reinforces the other. This report examines the mechanisms linking warming, air pollution,
content: Climate change and pollution are often treated as separate challenges, yet they are connected through a climate-pollution feedback loop in which each reinforces the other. This report examines the mechanisms linking warming, air pollution, ecosystem stress, and additional greenhouse gas emissions, demonstrating how climate change can worsen ozone formation, wildfire smoke, dust, water pollution, and energy demand, while pollutants such as carbon dioxide, methane, ozone, and black carbon contribute to further warming. Drawing on atmospheric records, IPCC datasets, public environmental data, and original analyses of 81 major cities between 2023 and 2025, the report evaluates the strength, speed, and confidence of fourteen interconnected pathways.The findings indicate that the climate-pollution relationship functions as an amplifier rather than a runaway system. Ozone concentrations increased with temperature in most cities studied, wildfire smoke impacts intensified despite declining global burned area, and natural feedbacks involving permafrost, wetlands, freshwater systems, and wildfires may add 20–30% to human-caused warming by 2100. The report highlights methane as the most effective near-term mitigation lever due to its dual climate and air-quality benefits, while also examining the implications of declining aerosol pollution and the resulting reduction of atmospheric cooling. Human health, food systems, ecosystems, and vulnerable regions face overlapping risks as heat and pollution interact.The report concludes that the most effective interventions target shared sources of climate change and pollution simultaneously. Priorities include methane abatement, clean cooking, clean power deployment, improved land and fire management, efficient cooling systems, and integrated governance frameworks. By addressing the common drivers of both climate and pollution impacts, policymakers can reduce health burdens, strengthen resilience, and slow the reinforcing dynamics of the climate-pollution feedback loop.

title: Artificial pollination and ecosystem services in cocoa systems of Bahia: an economic and environmental viability analysis
summary: Abstract In southern Bahia, Brazil, the predominant cocoa production system is cabruca, an agroforestry model in which cocoa trees are cultivated under the native forest canopy, reconciling agricultural production with environmental conserv
content: Abstract In southern Bahia, Brazil, the predominant cocoa production system is cabruca, an agroforestry model in which cocoa trees are cultivated under the native forest canopy, reconciling agricultural production with environmental conservation. Due to shading, productivity in this system is lower than that observed in full-sun systems. This has encouraged producers to adopt management practices, such as artificial pollination, to increase productivity. In this context, this exploratory multiple-case study evaluates the effects of artificial pollination on cocoa production and productivity. Eight farms located in the municipalities of Canavieiras, Itacaré, Ilhéus, Una, and Jequié were evaluated. Data were collected between November 2023 and April 2024 and included the implementation costs of artificial pollination, as well as direct and indirect production costs. The analysis compared areas in which cocoa trees were subjected to artificial pollination, either manually (using tweezers) or mechanically (using an air blower), with areas managed without this practice. Economic viability was assessed using the benefit–cost ratio (BCR), break-even analysis, return on investment (ROI), sensitivity analysis, regression analysis, technical efficiency assessment, and projected returns over time. In addition, an integrated index combining economic (ROI) and environmental indicators is proposed to support the assessment of artificial pollination adoption. From an economic perspective, manual artificial pollination had an estimated implementation cost of US$ 1281.22, whereas mechanized artificial pollination had an estimated cost of US$ 36,865.61. Manual pollination in cabruca systems showed the best economic performance among the farms evaluated. The cost–benefit analysis indicated that manual pollination in cabruca systems generated a mean return of more than eight times for each monetary unit invested, whereas mechanized pollination in full-sun systems generated a return of approximately four times the amount invested. The results suggest that the additional costs associated with artificial pollination, when not offset by productivity gains, may favor the adoption of less sustainable agricultural practices, such as intensified use of chemical inputs, the replacement of agroforestry systems with full-sun monocultures, and reduced investment in agroecological management practices, with potential indirect environmental impacts. In this context, the adoption of manual artificial pollination, combined with the conservation of the cabruca system, may contribute to the socioeconomic and environmental sustainability of cocoa production in Bahia.

title: Deliverable 2.3 Occupant behaviour web tool for buildings
summary: This deliverable presents the development and functionalities of the Sharing Spaces Web Tool, a digital platform designed to assess the potential of shared space usage as a climate mitigation strategy within the construction sector. Develop
content: This deliverable presents the development and functionalities of the Sharing Spaces Web Tool, a digital platform designed to assess the potential of shared space usage as a climate mitigation strategy within the construction sector. Developed under the Co2nstruct project, the tool supports evidence-based decision-making by quantifying the effects of shared spaces on building stock, operational energy consumption, and CO₂ emissions across European countries.The tool evaluates four scenarios of space-sharing willingness, ranging from none to strong, based on survey data from nine EU countries. These scenarios are applied to both residential and office buildings using detailed national data on building stock, energy use (JRC IDEES database), and occupancy standards. The analysis integrates regional construction trends and minimum habitable space regulations, a robust framework for modelling future adoption of shared-space living.

title: Engineering Soils to Improve the Performance and Sustainability of Phytoremediation
summary: Abstract. Phytoremediation uses plants and plant-associated processes to manage contaminated soils while supporting ecosystem restoration. However, its effectiveness is often constrained by degraded soil quality, limited rooting depth and c
content: Abstract. Phytoremediation uses plants and plant-associated processes to manage contaminated soils while supporting ecosystem restoration. However, its effectiveness is often constrained by degraded soil quality, limited rooting depth and contaminant access, and long-term management requirements. While constructed soils have increasingly been used to rehabilitate degraded land and support vegetation establishment, their potential role in enhancing phytoremediation performance has not been comprehensively reviewed. This review examines how constructed soils can be integrated with phytoremediation approaches to overcome soil-related limitations and improve contaminant management at contaminated sites. We focus on contamination characteristics, soil design and amendments, engineering practices, biotic and abiotic site conditions, and plant selection strategies. The reviewed literature demonstrates that appropriate soil engineering, including the use of constructed soils, can improve plant establishment, modify contaminant bioavailability and mobility, and enhance the performance of phytoremediation strategies. Overall, integrating soil engineering and constructed soils with phytoremediation represents a promising framework for contaminated-site management. By improving rooting conditions, enhancing contaminant accessibility or immobilization as required, and facilitating vegetation establishment, constructed soils can increase phytoremediation effectiveness and long-term sustainability. This integrated approach can also support ecosystem-service restoration, climate-change adaptation and mitigation, and the circular reuse of locally available surplus materials, although evidence on cost and long-term field performance remains limited.

title: Decomposing Health Co-benefits and Climate Penalties of Net-Zero Mitigation: PM2.5 and O3 Evidence from Taiwan
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: Net-zero mitigation is expected to improve human health through air-quality co-benefits, but these benefits may be constrained by climate-driven warming, particularly in small greenhouse gas-emitting economies. Using Taiwan as a case study,
content: Net-zero mitigation is expected to improve human health through air-quality co-benefits, but these benefits may be constrained by climate-driven warming, particularly in small greenhouse gas-emitting economies. Using Taiwan as a case study, this study applied an integrated LEAP-CMAQ-CRF framework to link net-zero energy pathways, air-quality responses, and mortality impact assessment. A 2×2 scenario design was used to separate mitigation co-benefits from climate penalties under present-day and +2°C warming conditions. Under present-day meteorology, net-zero mitigation reduced population-weighted PM2.5 (-35.7%) but increased MDA8 O3 (+18.8%). Under the combined warming and net-zero scenario relative to the baseline, PM2.5 remained substantially reduced (-35.0%), while O3 increased (+21.6%). Mortality decomposition further showed that +2°C warming added 97 PM2.5-related deaths (+0.3%) and 220 O3-related deaths (+0.6%), whereas net-zero mitigation reduced PM2.5-related deaths by 2,626 (-7.0%) but added 2,062 O3-related deaths (+5.5%). The final combined scenario reached 37,047 premature deaths, equivalent to 99.3% of the baseline level. Spatially, PM2.5 reductions were widespread, while O3 increases were concentrated mainly along western Taiwan and overlapped with several medium-high and high-SVI counties. These findings indicate that net-zero mitigation can reduce aggregate mortality risks, but its benefits are not pollutant-neutral or spatially uniform. Health-oriented integrated assessment should therefore evaluate both total risk reduction and residual burden redistribution across pollutants, climate conditions, and vulnerable regions.

title: Unraveling the hydraulic regulation mechanisms in iron-carbon materials enhanced anaerobic digestion of kitchen waste: Insights from carbon and nitrogen metabolismlllk
summary: Abstract This study investigated the effects of different rotation speeds on the performance, microbial communities, and carbon and nitrogen metabolism functions of an iron-carbon material-enhanced semi-continuous anaerobic digestion system
content: Abstract This study investigated the effects of different rotation speeds on the performance, microbial communities, and carbon and nitrogen metabolism functions of an iron-carbon material-enhanced semi-continuous anaerobic digestion system for kitchen waste. The reactors were operated at 36 ± 1 °C, an organic loading rate of 2.51 g VS/L/d, and a sludge retention time of 45 d, with four stirring conditions of 20, 60, 80, and 120 rpm. The results showed that the 60 rpm group achieved the highest average methane production rate of 492.0 mL/g VS, which was 5%–7% higher than that of the other groups. Moderate stirring helped maintain stable concentration levels of volatile fatty acids and ammonia nitrogen. Community analysis showed that Chloroflexi, Bacteroidetes, Proteobacteria, and Firmicutes were the dominant bacterial phyla, while Methanothrix was the dominant methanogen. Functional analysis indicated that stirring at 60 rpm enhanced the potential for glycolysis, pyruvate metabolism, and volatile fatty acid metabolism, while promoting ammonia assimilation. Excessive stirring may enhance denitrification and intensify competition for carbon sources between denitrifying bacteria and methanogens.

title: Transnational Law at the Intersection of Technology and Sustainability: UNIDROIT’S Work on Digital Assets, Verified Carbon Credits, and Private Law
summary: In this article, Giulia Stella Previti examines UNIDROIT’s initiatives at the intersection of technology, private law, and sustainable development. The author provides an overview of the UNIDROIT Principles on Digital Assets and Private Law
content: In this article, Giulia Stella Previti examines UNIDROIT’s initiatives at the intersection of technology, private law, and sustainable development. The author provides an overview of the UNIDROIT Principles on Digital Assets and Private Law (published in 2023) and the draft UNIDROIT Principles on the Legal Nature of Verified Carbon Credits. Both soft law instruments offer jurisdiction-, tech-, and organizationally-neutral legislative guidance designed to clarify how emerging asset classes fit within existing domestic proprietary legal frameworks. By establishing core private law rules—such as defining control, protecting innocent acquirers, and setting priority rules for secured transactions—these initiatives aim to reduce legal uncertainty and lower transaction costs in cross-border markets. Ultimately, the article demonstrates how transnational private law can harmonize international standards, promoting financial inclusion and unlocking climate finance without unnecessarily overhauling established national legal systems.

title: Green nudges for sustainable e-commerce: a bibliometric analysis
summary: In view of the rising online consumption and growing environmental concerns, e-commerce platforms face a critical dilemma. They need to influence consumer choices toward sustainability without compromising user autonomy or crossing ethical
content: In view of the rising online consumption and growing environmental concerns, e-commerce platforms face a critical dilemma. They need to influence consumer choices toward sustainability without compromising user autonomy or crossing ethical boundaries. Incorporating green nudges—subtle design prompts intended to steer users toward more eco-friendly decisions—has emerged as a promising yet controversial strategy. This study conducts a systematic literature review, following PRISMA guidelines, to examine how green nudges are used in digital commerce and how effective they are in promoting sustainable purchasing patterns. A comprehensive Scopus search of studies on green nudging in e-commerce reveals a 28.21% annual publication growth rate and an average of 25.68 citations across 33 countries. Bibliometric and content analysis reveals emerging themes and identifies the contextual factors that shape the success of these interventions. The findings highlight the potential of green nudges but also reveal key challenges, including inconsistent implementation, culturally variable outcomes, and ethical concerns about manipulation. The review underscores the need for a more nuanced, context-sensitive approach to green nudge design, accounting for user demographics, digital architecture, and behavioral science. This work both synthesizes current knowledge and proposes a research agenda to guide ethical and effective use of green nudges in sustainable e-commerce.

title: Explainable Physics-Guided Machine Learning for Modeling and Prediction of Facies-Supported Unconfined Compressive Strength: Implication for CO 2 Storage
summary: Abstract The geomechanical stability of CO₂ storage reservoirs, particularly the Unconfined Compressive Strength (UCS) of caprocks and reservoir formations, is critical for ensuring long-term containment security. Traditional UCS estimation
content: Abstract The geomechanical stability of CO₂ storage reservoirs, particularly the Unconfined Compressive Strength (UCS) of caprocks and reservoir formations, is critical for ensuring long-term containment security. Traditional UCS estimation methods, laboratory testing and empirical correlations, are often cost-prohibitive, time-intensive, or insufficiently accurate for heterogeneous subsurface systems. This study introduces a novel Explainable Physics-Guided Machine Learning (PGML) framework that, for the first time, combines facies-specific empirical equations with five advanced machine learning algorithms, AdaBoost, Gradient Boosting (GBT), Random Forest (RF), CatBoost, and Radial Basis Function Neural Network (RBFNN), in a discrepancy learning mode. Rather than predicting UCS directly, the models learn the residual between empirical predictions and laboratory-measured values using conventional well logs (porosity, density, gamma ray, resistivity, slowness, and ultrasonic velocity) from 45 core samples across seven wells in the Zubair Oil Field, Iraq. This physics-anchored approach preserves physical interpretability while capturing complex data-driven patterns. Results demonstrate substantial improvements across all algorithms: PGML increased the coefficient of determination (R²) from 0.10–0.84 (conventional ML) to 0.82–0.98, with the AdaBoost-PGML model achieving the highest accuracy (R² = 0.975, RMSE = 5.9 MPa), a 72% reduction in prediction error compared to conventional AdaBoost (R² = 0.68, RMSE = 21 MPa). SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis reveals that depth, porosity, bulk density, and gamma ray are the primary controls on the empirical-model discrepancy, indicating that compaction trends, pore structure, and clay content, absent from simple velocity-based equations, critically influence UCS. Applied to CO₂ storage assessment in the Zubair Field, the framework identifies a thick sandstone reservoir (φ = 16.9%, k = 428 mD) with high-integrity caprock (UCS = 156 MPa) as highly suitable for secure sequestration, while flagging a deeper interval where moderate caprock strength (UCS < 100 MPa) poses leakage risks. This hybrid PGML-XAI approach provides a robust, interpretable, and practically implementable tool for geomechanical characterization, directly supporting risk-informed decision-making in carbon storage projects.

title: Latitude modulates climate-driven maize yield gains across the central U.S. “warming hole”
summary: Abstract Maize yield responses to climate change differ seasonally and regionally, with both positive and negative impacts shaped by local climate trends and management decisions. Here, using a phenology-aligned moving crop-season framework
content: Abstract Maize yield responses to climate change differ seasonally and regionally, with both positive and negative impacts shaped by local climate trends and management decisions. Here, using a phenology-aligned moving crop-season framework and the Hybrid-Maize model (1991–2024) across five U.S. Corn Belt states, we quantify climate-driven yield contributions and show that they transition from southern declines to northern gains, reflecting the persistent influence of the central U.S. summer warming hole characterized by cooling maximum temperatures and increasing rainfall. A systematic thermal mismatch between environmental heat availability and hybrid growing degree day requirements is observed, particularly south of 42°N, where thermal matching declined despite favorable thermal conditions. Contrasting trends in thermal matching and reproductive duration help explain the latitude-dependent structure of climate-driven yield contributions. Our findings highlight how hybrid selection modulates the impacts of temperature, precipitation, vapor pressure deficit, and radiation trends on maize yield gains across the U.S. Corn Belt.

title: Investigating ESG’s influence on European listed real estate market performance
source: International Journal of Strategic Property Management
summary: This study employs Bloomberg data from six European listed markets to investigate the extent to which the performance of real estate companies can be explained by the Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) attributes at the corporate le
content: This study employs Bloomberg data from six European listed markets to investigate the extent to which the performance of real estate companies can be explained by the Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) attributes at the corporate level. By accounting for firm-level characteristics, we utilise Pedroni’s Cointegration and Granger Causality methods to examine long-term cointegration and causal relationships. Additionally, we construct panel regression models to explore the role of ESG attributes in determining firm- level performance. Key findings reveal no statistical evidence that ESG attributes depress the performance of listed real estate companies, as indicated by raw return, Sharpe ratio, and Tobin’s q. Notably, the causality analysis uncovers that certain ESG attributes indeed Granger-cause the performance indicators. For instance, higher environmental, social, and governance performance scores, as measured by the three aggregate Bloomberg ESG scores, lead to superior returns on both raw and risk-adjusted bases in the long run.

title: Costs Versus Benefits From an Environmental, Service User, Unpaid Carer and Staff Perspective, of a Hybrid Community/Regional Collaboration to Provide Functional Electrical Stimulation Rehabilitation to a Rural Population
source: Journal of Evaluation in Clinical Practice
summary: RATIONALE: Service users and unpaid carers living in rural mid-west Wales travel long distances to attend a Functional Electrical Stimulation (FES) gait clinic in South Wales, United Kingdom (UK). It negatively affects their symptoms, and i
content: RATIONALE: Service users and unpaid carers living in rural mid-west Wales travel long distances to attend a Functional Electrical Stimulation (FES) gait clinic in South Wales, United Kingdom (UK). It negatively affects their symptoms, and is financially and environmentally costly. An alternative rural/hybrid clinic was set up representing a community/regional service collaboration. AIMS AND OBJECTIVES: To compare a hybrid community-based rural FES clinic led remotely by specialists in a regional, urban hospital in South Wales, with business as usual. METHOD: Qualitative and quantitative measures were collected from multiple perspectives. Services users and unpaid carers were interviewed, and staff from both services gave feedback. Costs and savings were estimated for travel mileage and time, fuel costs, CO2 emissions, loss of earnings for service users and unpaid carers, hotel costs and staff costs. RESULTS: Service users and unpaid carers saved an estimated average £121.42 per appointment when attending the local hybrid clinic compared with travelling to the South Wales clinic. An estimated 123 travel miles were saved per appointment and 417.2 CO2 total emissions saved. An average of 3 h 31 min travel time were saved per appointment; 11 lost working days total were saved for service users and unpaid carers. Costs remained the same for the South Wales service, with an estimated £554.19 additional staff costs for the rural community service, for the hybrid clinic. CONCLUSION: Financial costs for service users and unpaid carers, and the environmental impact of travel to healthcare appointments, should be considered as part of holistic clinical decision-making and healthcare service design. Rural community healthcare services require different delivery models compared with urban hospital-based services, and this needs to be reflected in funding allocation.

title: Improving data quality in German office construction: a template-based framework for an SME-driven market
summary: Germany’s construction industry lags behind other European countries in terms of digital transformation, particularly in building information modelling (BIM). This is attributed to several factors, including a large proportion of small and
content: Germany’s construction industry lags behind other European countries in terms of digital transformation, particularly in building information modelling (BIM). This is attributed to several factors, including a large proportion of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and limited investment resulting from insufficient data quality (DQ) in 3D deliverables. Against this backdrop, this study investigates barriers to DQ during information production, the affected DQ dimensions, and potential solutions. The aim is to contribute to the ongoing discussion on improving DQ in construction by offering practical solutions tailored to the constraints of SMEs. Specifically, this study focuses on the planning phase of office building projects in Germany. Data were collected through focus groups and individual interviews. Data analysis revealed several critical barriers that compromise DQ in the examined environment: incomplete information requirements, unresolved interfaces, limited participation in Closed BIM environments, inadequate implementation of the Exchange Information Requirements, inconsistent 3D deliverables, insufficient data validation expertise, and non-compliance with schedules and model structures. The most affected DQ dimensions are completeness, reliability, and usability. Among the potential solutions identified, object templates emerged as a practical approach to improving these critical dimensions. Preliminary stakeholder feedback was collected to explore the suitability of object templates for improving DQ in 3D deliverables. The proposed approach centres on four key principles: purpose-driven design, regional adaptability, type-level modularity, and integration with proprietary formats. This study makes four distinct contributions to the field of DQ improvement in the examined context. First, it empirically identifies SME-relevant DQ barriers, complementing existing research with insights into their underlying mechanisms and interdependencies. Second, it conceptually reframes DQ improvement as a preventive, process-based challenge, shifting the focus from tools to workflows and collaboration. Third, it delivers a methodological and practical contribution through an ISO 19650-2-integrated workflow for object template implementation, embedding preventive DQ measures into standardised processes to ensure feasibility for SMEs. Finally, it develops four key principles for template development, which collectively enable immediate adoption without requiring full BIM maturity. Together, these contributions bridge the gap between high-level BIM standards and the practical realities of SMEs, offering actionable, resource-efficient solutions.

title: Reserva Natural Montaña Sagrada: un exitoso caso de conservación impulsado por la sociedad civil y el sector privado en el norte de Costa Rica
summary: The Montaña Sagrada Nature Reserve, located within Juan Castro Blanco National Water Park, is a conservation initiative led by Coopelesca, a multi-service cooperative serving the country’s Northern Region. The reserve emerged as an innovati
content: The Montaña Sagrada Nature Reserve, located within Juan Castro Blanco National Water Park, is a conservation initiative led by Coopelesca, a multi-service cooperative serving the country’s Northern Region. The reserve emerged as an innovative response to the challenge of protecting strategic ecosystems in a landscape where a significant proportion of the land designated as national park remains under private ownership. Through a solidarity-based financing mechanism supported by contributions from its members, Coopelesca has secured and protected land dedicated to safeguarding water sources, restoring forest ecosystems, and conserving biodiversity. Today, Montaña Sagrada integrates conservation, environmental education, scientific research, and sustainable tourism. These efforts generate benefits for local communities by strengthening water security, protecting biodiversity, mitigating climate change, and creating nature-based opportunities for local development. The reserve demonstrates how collective action and collaboration among different sectors can complement conventional conservation strategies and contribute to the long-term protection of natural heritage.

title: A Separations Perspective on Low-Temperature CO2 Electrolysis
summary: Abstract Electrochemical reduction of CO2 to valuable chemicals is a fast-developing power-to-X concept for decarbonizing hard-to-abate sectors. While intensive research in the past two decades has enabled production of several value-added
content: Abstract Electrochemical reduction of CO2 to valuable chemicals is a fast-developing power-to-X concept for decarbonizing hard-to-abate sectors. While intensive research in the past two decades has enabled production of several value-added chemicals at high current densities and selectivities with low cell voltages, separations required to deliver these products at market purity have received far less attention. In this perspective, we present a list of parameters that capture the separations problem, characterize the drivers of separations difficulty in CO2R systems, and outline best practices for conducting techno-economic analysis, integrating upstream and downstream separations, such that separations are codesigned with the reactor rather than treated as an afterthought.

title: Community-Based Approaches to Climate Change: Pathways for Sustainable Development—A Review of Academic and Grey Literature
summary: This review explores how community-based approaches can offer effective, context-specific strategies that both adapt to and mitigate climate change, while simultaneously advancing the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).It interrogates how
content: This review explores how community-based approaches can offer effective, context-specific strategies that both adapt to and mitigate climate change, while simultaneously advancing the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).It interrogates how bottom-up activities have helped strengthen vulnerable populations, especially in climate-affected regions, to be more resilient and achieve a meaningful transition.A structured review of peerreviewed and grey literature published between 2015 to 2025 was undertaken.The search identified 153 records; after duplicates were removed and titles, abstracts and full texts were screened, 21 publications met the inclusion criteria and were included in the final synthesis.The included sources comprised peer-reviewed journal articles together with 4 grey literature sources from the United Nations SDGs, the Paris Agreement and the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).The results reveal that community-based approaches are context-specific, foster social inclusion, and enhance the adaptive capacity.They align with the SDGs 1, 2, 5, 6, 7, 10, 11, 13, 14, 15, 16 and 17.Such initiatives can be scaled up, with policy enabling and partnership, as evidenced in Indonesia's Climate Village Program (Proklim).This review highlights the benefits of using indigenous knowledge in climate practices and the production of co-created knowledge integration, and multi-stakeholder governance.However, gaps in funding, poor financial monitoring, and restrictive legal systems often make it harder for local communities to adapt.This paper integrates new information related to the ability of community-based approaches to bridge the global-local divide in climate governance and offers a new approach to resilience-building based on climate justice in a participatory framework.

title: Forage dry matter yield, nutritive value, and botanical composition of diverse perennial forage species mixtures
summary: This field study examined the forage dry matter (DM) yields, nutritive values, and botanical compositions of 29 perennial forage mixtures and monoculture grasses over 3 consecutive production years in Fairview, Alberta, Canada. Treatments c
content: This field study examined the forage dry matter (DM) yields, nutritive values, and botanical compositions of 29 perennial forage mixtures and monoculture grasses over 3 consecutive production years in Fairview, Alberta, Canada. Treatments consisted of 6 simple binary mixtures (grass-legume), 18 diversified mixtures (each with 3 or more species, comprising grass-legume, grass-only, and legume-only mixtures), and 5 monoculture grasses (single species) as references. The forage DM yields of grass–legume and legume-only mixtures were the highest during the first (2.4 Mg ha−1) and third (4.9 Mg ha−1) production years, with monoculture meadow bromegrass [Bromopsis biebersteinii (Roem. & Schult.) Holub] producing the highest DM yield (4.8 Mg ha−1) in the second year of production. Averaged across the 3-year period, grass–legume and legume-only mixtures had greater DM yields compared to monoculture grasses or grass-only mixtures. Legume mixtures had the highest crude protein (CP) followed by grass–legume mixtures. The grass–legume mixtures had the lowest neutral detergent fiber (NDF) and acid detergent fiber (ADF). Total digestible nutrients (TDN) were highest in a five‑species blend of a grass-only mixture, whereas NDF digestibility over 48 h was highest in monoculture grasses and grass-only mixtures. Among legumes, alfalfa (Medicago sativa L.) dominated the botanical composition relative to sainfoin (Onobrychis viciifolia Scop.), cicer milkvetch (Astragulus cicer L.), and birdsfoot trefoil (Lotus corniculatus L.), whereas the AC Success hybrid bromegrass (Bromus spp.) was the dominant grass cultivar within the forage mixtures. Highly diversified mixtures, including six- and eight‑species blends , suppressed weeds better than simpler forage combinations.

title: Introducing final- and useful-stage energy and exergy extensions for the EXIOBASE Multi-Regional Input-Output Model
summary: Abstract Environmentally Extended Multi-Regional Input-Output (EE-MRIO) models are increasingly used to account for the upstream (supply chain) requirements and implications of any level of final demand. Energy use is recognised to be a key
content: Abstract Environmentally Extended Multi-Regional Input-Output (EE-MRIO) models are increasingly used to account for the upstream (supply chain) requirements and implications of any level of final demand. Energy use is recognised to be a key driver of anthropogenic climate change and reducing energy use (at least in higher-income regions) is considered to be a key lever to meet climate targets. However, the availability of energy extensions for EE-MRIO models is very limited, preventing the quantification of energy use embodied in supply chains. Here, we introduce and document a novel set of energy extensions for the EXIOBASE EE-MRIO model. The extensions we introduce cover energy use at both the final and useful stage of the energy conversion chain. Further, we isolate extensions capturing the energy industry own energy use, energy used for non-energy purposes, as well as final-to-useful conversion losses.
