This method allows us to capture heterogeneous effects across the distribution of FDI inflows. Results show that governance quality significantly influenced FDI in the pre‑COVID era, with voice and accountability, political stability, regulatory quality, rule of law, and control of corruption showing positive effects across multiple quantiles. Whereby, government effectiveness was negative at lower quantiles. Post‑COVID findings reveal a narrower impact. Specifically, governance quality matters only at the median (50th quantile), with political stability, government effectiveness, and regulatory quality emerging as the only relevant dimensions. Through pre- and postCOVID-19 comparison, the study highlights that governance quality not only depends on distribution patterns but is also sensitive to crises. The study also points to the need for overall governance improvements in stable periods. Specifically, a more targeted reform in areas like political stabilit

title: A qualitative framework analysis of treatment burden, psychological resilience and exercise self-efficacy among adults aged 18–45 years living with inflammatory bowel disease
summary: Background Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a chronic, relapsing condition that predominantly affects adults aged 18–45 years, a life stage characterized by important career development and family responsibilities. As a lifelong conditio
content: Background Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a chronic, relapsing condition that predominantly affects adults aged 18–45 years, a life stage characterized by important career development and family responsibilities. As a lifelong condition, IBD can significantly impair patients’ physical, psychological, and social functioning. Although the health benefits of exercise for individuals with IBD are well established, existing qualitative studies have rarely captured patients’ lived experiences of the disease and have not adequately elucidated the experiential interrelationships among treatment burden (TB), psychological resilience (PR), exercise self-efficacy (ESE), and the multilayered social environment. Aim This study explores the interrelationships among TB, PR, and ESE and identifies their multilevel influencing factors to provide evidence for individualized chronic disease nursing interventions. Methods Using maximum variation sampling, 19 adult patients with a confirmed diagnosis of IBD were recruited from Jinhua Central Hospital between October 2025 and January 2026. Participants underwent in-person semi-structured interviews, which were audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim. Data were analyzed using framework analysis, with Bronfenbrenner’s social-ecological system theory serving as the analytical framework and deductive and inductive analytical processes being integrated. Results Based on participants’ accounts, four core themes were identified: (1) micro-, meso-, and macro-ecosystems, through cross-level interactions, created a multidimensional, cumulative TB; (2) PR followed a nonlinear trajectory across three disease-related stages: acute crisis, gradual adaptation, and stable remission; (3) multilevel ecological determinants constrained the development and sustained maintenance of ESE; and (4) perceived bidirectional experiential interactions generated both positive reinforcing cycles and negative vicious cycles linking TB, PR, and ESE. The trajectories and cycles described above are based on subjective accounts from cross-sectional interviews; their exact chronology and causal relationships cannot be determined. Conclusion This study provides explanatory evidence that the interaction among TB, PR, and ESE in adult IBD patients aged 18–45 years is influenced by socioecological factors across multiple levels. The findings suggest that clinical care for IBD should move beyond a narrow biomedical perspective toward a multilevel, context-sensitive, patient-centered care model.

title: Modeling and solving workflow scheduling problems on shared computing units with makespan and energy cost objectives
source: Central European Journal of Operations Research
summary: Abstract This research addresses the workflow scheduling problem on shared computing units. A set of interdependent tasks, originating from a workflow or project, requires processing by computing units such as virtual machines, while respec
content: Abstract This research addresses the workflow scheduling problem on shared computing units. A set of interdependent tasks, originating from a workflow or project, requires processing by computing units such as virtual machines, while respecting precedence constraints and capacity restrictions, for example, in terms of virtual central processing units. The computing units may be heterogeneous or homogeneous in their capacities and cost rates. This problem arises in cloud environments that allow multiple tasks to share resources to improve utilization and reduce energy consumption in accordance with a race-to-idle strategy. We present different mathematical model formulations for this integrated model of workflow scheduling and vector bin packing: a mixed-integer program based on the pulse disaggregated discrete-time formulation, a mixed-integer quadratically constrained program, and a constraint programming satisfiability model, which can be further extended to related scheduling settings. The formulations are evaluated under a makespan objective and under a weighted-sum objective combining makespan and active-unit energy cost. Computational experiments with the Gurobi Optimizer and the CP-SAT solver show that the pulse-based formulation provides the strongest bounds and proves optimality most often, whereas the constraint programming formulation quickly finds high-quality incumbent solutions for the combined objective.

title: Towards verifiable accountability for autonomous AI agents via cryptographic decision anchoring
summary: As robots increasingly operate under the control of autonomous AI agents in safety-critical and socially sensitive environments, the ability to audit and verify past decisions becomes essential for trust, liability, and post-incident analys
content: As robots increasingly operate under the control of autonomous AI agents in safety-critical and socially sensitive environments, the ability to audit and verify past decisions becomes essential for trust, liability, and post-incident analysis. However, conventional logging mechanisms do not provide guarantees against post hoc manipulation of recorded agent behavior. This paper proposes a lightweight, reproducible framework for tamper-evident logging of autonomous multi-agent decisions, based on cryptographic commitments and blockchain anchoring, as an integrity building block for AI accountability. In the proposed approach, agents record selected decision events off-chain, aggregate them using Merkle trees, and periodically anchor resulting root hashes to an immutable ledger. This design enables efficient storage while ensuring that any modification of committed decision logs after anchoring becomes cryptographically detectable. We implement the framework in an open-source multi-agent robotic simulation and evaluate it under honest and adversarial logging scenarios. Across twelve attack types with 1,000 trials each, every modification of committed decision records was detected against the on-chain commitment, with no false positives in 1,000 honest runs, whereas a local check without the anchor missed every attack once the attacker also rewrote the local commitments. Verification took about 7 µs per recorded decision, a single decision could be verified in about 20 µs with a proof below 1 kB, and each run required one anchoring transaction of 188 virtual bytes, regardless of the number of agents and decisions. The framework guarantees the integrity of what has been committed while keeping the underlying decision records off-chain until an audit requires them. The main contribution is a practical architecture for verifiable decision records of AI agents. It combines selective logging, efficient cryptographic verification, and reproducible experimentation, and lays a foundation for post hoc auditing of autonomous robotic systems.

title: CO-SUSTAIN: Cross-case comparative analysis of the CO-SUSTAIN case studies and deliberation processes
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: This document is one of the final deliverables of the CO-SUSTAIN project. It compares the implementation and results of the six deliberation processes run in the six case studies of civic and political participation between November 2025 an
content: This document is one of the final deliverables of the CO-SUSTAIN project. It compares the implementation and results of the six deliberation processes run in the six case studies of civic and political participation between November 2025 and June 2026: the regeneration of public space in Annelinn (Tartu, Estonia), resident participation in large-scale energy projects, starting from small modular reactors (Espoo, Finland), the activist campaign for the Westbahnareal (Vienna, Austria), the food solidarity system of Turin (Italy), an inclusive shared-energy network in El Raval (Barcelona, Spain) and an energy community in the Alpujarra (Órgiva, Spain). In doing so, it returns to the question formulated at the start of the project: under which conditions, and through which factors and dynamics, does participation produce which effects on democratic pathways to transition? In simpler terms: what happens, where, why, and with what results? The comparison builds on the CO-SUSTAIN theoretical triangle: sustainability transition theory (the multi-level perspective, MLP, read together with social movement theory following Törnberg), political and civic participation (Ekman and Amnå’s typology of latent and manifest participation and Tilly’s theory of collective action) and participatory, deliberative and prefigurative democracy. It adopts a generalising approach, complementary to the case-specific Impact Assessment Framework of Task 4.1, and a context–mechanism–outcome (CMO) logic inspired by realist evaluation. The comparison is organised in three stages. Stage 1 compares the contexts in two steps: an MLP reading of the causal loop diagrams (CLDs) produced in the panels, which identifies the loops that stabilise the regime, those that challenge it, the dynamics within the niches and the connections across levels; and the partners’ answers on collective action mobilisation, windows of opportunity, niche–regimeinteraction and transition pathways. Stage 2 compares the deliberation processes on six dimensions of implementation, coded from D3.1 and validated by all partners. Stage 3 compares outcomes on five dimensions, combining the Theories of Change (ToCs) with the evidence of D4.1 and of a workshop with all partners (7 October 2026). The comparison of the contexts (Stage 1) shows that the stability of the regime rests less on open opposition to the initiatives than on political inertia, administrative constraints, organisational fatigue and forms of participation that do not redistribute power, and that bridging actors are present in every case. The six cases fall into three distinct patterns of interaction between niche initiatives and established regimes. In Turin and Barcelona (embedded niches), initiatives led by organisations and by the third sector work with a regime that acts as a partner or incorporates them, through dense networks of intermediary actors; their main risk is co-optation. In Vienna and Órgiva (contested niches), citizen-led initiativ

title: Passivity-aware reactive diffusion policy for stable contact-rich manipulation
summary: Contact-rich manipulation demands stable, low-impact interaction with uncertain environments. Reactive diffusion policies (RDP) achieve strong task success, yet their high-frequency corrective actions can inject energy into the contact, pro
content: Contact-rich manipulation demands stable, low-impact interaction with uncertain environments. Reactive diffusion policies (RDP) achieve strong task success, yet their high-frequency corrective actions can inject energy into the contact, producing large contact forces and instability under disturbance. We propose PaRDP (Passivity-Aware Reactive Diffusion Policy), which augments a slow-fast visual-tactile diffusion base with three lightweight, provably passivity-bounded modules: (i) a Passivity-aware Interaction Frame & Hybrid Force-Position (PIF-HFP) module that selects free-motion degrees of freedom in an estimated interaction frame; (ii) a Passivity-Bounded Fast Force Correction (PB-FFC) shell that projects out energy-increasing corrections through an energy tank with a bounded injection allowance; and (iii) Stability-Conditioned Training (SCT), a training-time regularizer that penalizes net energy injection. We prove that the closed-loop system remains stable whenever the environment is passive. On RDP/TactAR, our primary benchmark, PaRDP improves the All score by $$+0.02$$ to $$+0.05$$ over RDP(Force) and reduces peak contact force by up to $$34\%$$ while adding under $$7\%$$ inference overhead; we additionally list published ForceVLA-Data and RH20T baselines as external reference context for force-aware and cross-dataset settings. Ablation and sensitivity studies confirm the contribution of each module.

title: Pathways to impact: Lessons from water and energy experiments.
summary: Australia’s water and energy sectors are transforming — a shift from large, centralised infrastructure toward resilient, localised systems that can better withstand climate extremes. With nearly $200 billion in infrastructure investments pl
content: Australia’s water and energy sectors are transforming — a shift from large, centralised infrastructure toward resilient, localised systems that can better withstand climate extremes. With nearly $200 billion in infrastructure investments planned over the next decade, there is a growing need to ensure these funds foster climate-resilient services and contribute to achieving net-zero targets. As urban areas face the intensifying pressures of climate change, the choices we make now in scaling these innovations will set the trajectory for sustainable urban transformation across Australia for decades to come. This report presents key policy takeaways for industry leaders and policymakers on how to effectively support experimentation and urban sustainability transitions.

title: Personal and professional key experiences influencing pre-service teachers’ identity development
summary: Pre-service teachers’ identity development has been investigated from the viewpoint of professional key learning experiences, but not so often from the perspective of personal experiences. This study aims to include personal experiences as
content: Pre-service teachers’ identity development has been investigated from the viewpoint of professional key learning experiences, but not so often from the perspective of personal experiences. This study aims to include personal experiences as part of the pre-service teachers’ (PST) teacher identity development, and to illustrate how personal and professional key experiences have positive and negative influences on PSTs’ teacher identity development. The data of this study includes storylines and interviews from 19 pre-service teachers from Finland (n = 12) and Austria (n = 7). The main findings indicate that the professional key learning experiences, although very much following the structure of the teacher education program, were found to be more various than what we expected. Furthermore, the data of this study implies that personal key experiences have influence on PSTs’ teacher identity development. Those experiences are various and can have strengthening or weakening effects. Thirdly, the connections between professional and personal experiences are evident and fresh findings in this research genre. This study contributes to teacher education research by demonstrating how teacher identity development is shaped by key personal experiences and how these experiences are intertwined with professional key learning experiences.

title: Biofuel Mandate Changes, Renewable Energy Share, and Fertilizer Intensity: Panel Evidence from Ten Economies
summary: Biofuel blending mandates may support renewable energy transitions, while feedstock production may increase agricultural pressures. This study examines the short-run associations between changes in mandate intensity and two outcomes, the ag
content: Biofuel blending mandates may support renewable energy transitions, while feedstock production may increase agricultural pressures. This study examines the short-run associations between changes in mandate intensity and two outcomes, the aggregate renewable energy share and fertilizer intensity. The analysis uses a balanced panel of ten developed and developing economies from 2005 to 2022, yielding 170 country-year observations after differencing. The models include country fixed effects, and the preferred specifications also include year fixed effects. Robustness is assessed using two-way clustered standard errors. In developing economies, mandate increases are positively associated with annual percentage point changes in the renewable energy share. Both the estimate for developed economies and the estimated difference between the two groups are statistically insignificant. In the preferred fertilizer intensity model, mandate increases are associated with lower annual growth in fertilizer use per hectare of arable land when trade openness is unchanged. The negative and statistically significant interaction indicates that this estimated association becomes more negative as annual log changes in trade openness increase. The estimated mandate association at unchanged trade openness is statistically insignificant under two-way clustered inference. The estimates describe conditional short-run associations. By examining the aggregate renewable energy share and fertilizer use per hectare in the same cross-country panel, the study provides complementary evidence on the energy and agricultural dimensions of biofuel mandates. The findings support tracking both indicators when evaluating blending policies and accounting for the sensitivity of the fertilizer estimates to the choice of standard errors.

title: China’s energy transition strategy favoring both coal and renewables: Economic risks and global implications
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
summary: China’s energy strategy is navigating a complex policy landscape: While leading the world in renewable energy manufacturing and deployment, it is simultaneously pursuing a continued expansion of its coal-fired power fleet. This paper examin
content: China’s energy strategy is navigating a complex policy landscape: While leading the world in renewable energy manufacturing and deployment, it is simultaneously pursuing a continued expansion of its coal-fired power fleet. This paper examines this dual trajectory by building an integrated analytical framework that combines domestic and international perspectives to analyze the social, economic, climate, and geopolitical impacts of China’s new coal-power plant investments. Combining historical trends, government planning, and projections from influential policy teams, we find that a tripling of renewable capacity by 2030, a pace China is on track to meet, is sufficient to satisfy all projected electricity demand scenarios when considered alongside the evolving generation mix and planned storage deployment. We further show that additional coal capacity is not required to ensure adequate electricity supply under these scenarios. The coal pathway could expose up to $223.6 billion of stranded assets from new projects and add an additional 327,000 workers in a declining industry. Furthermore, this trajectory may weaken the alignment between China’s domestic energy investment and its international clean energy leadership. We conclude that a clean-energy-led pathway that halts new coal construction is lower-cost, better for job growth, and more consistent with China’s role as a leader in the global clean energy transition.

title: Displacement, COVID-19, and Food Security: A Photovoice Study with Resettled Syrian Women in Kitchener-Waterloo, Canada
summary: This chapter examines the multiple ways forced migration and the COVID-19 pandemic shaped the food security experiences and food-focused activities of resettled Syrian women in Kitchener-Waterloo, Canada. Based on a participatory Photovoice
content: This chapter examines the multiple ways forced migration and the COVID-19 pandemic shaped the food security experiences and food-focused activities of resettled Syrian women in Kitchener-Waterloo, Canada. Based on a participatory Photovoice study with 11 Syrian women, it explores how displacement undermines food security, including cultural food security, and why recovery remains difficult even after resettlement in a high-income country like Canada. Participants reported that forced migration from Syria disrupted their regular food practices and food consumption due to financial constraints and limited access to familiar ingredients, creating a persistent gap between food memories, rituals, and available diets. While resettlement in Canada increased food availability, many families still faced challenges in accessing healthy and culturally appropriate foods. The COVID-19 pandemic worsened these gaps through food inflation, mobility restrictions, social distancing requirements, increased financial pressures, chronic illness, and gendered care-based duties. It also disrupted food-centred social and religious rituals, such as communal meals during Ramadan and Eid. As primary caregivers in their households, women faced greater domestic pressures even as they developed new food-related coping strategies.

title: Leadership and organizational sustainability among NGOs working with displaced populations in Greece
summary: Abstract Non-governmental organizations (NGOs) play a central role in ensuring protection, emergency aid and basic services for displaced populations. Guided by the Job Demands–Resources model, this study aims to generate knowledge about ho
content: Abstract Non-governmental organizations (NGOs) play a central role in ensuring protection, emergency aid and basic services for displaced populations. Guided by the Job Demands–Resources model, this study aims to generate knowledge about how NGO leaders in Greece interpret job demands affecting fieldworkers and organizational functioning, and how resources are mobilized to mitigate these demands and thereby support sustained humanitarian work. Seven semi-structured interviews were conducted and analyzed using template analysis. The analysis identified three key demands that constrained organizational functioning: (1) continuous exposure to extreme impressions, (2) navigating collaboration with government authorities, and (3) limited and unpredictable funding. Three core resources emerged as vital for sustaining operations: (1) ensuring staff suitability and ethical grounding, (2) supporting fieldworkers’ well-being and team resilience, and (3) coordination and collaboration between NGOs. The findings suggest that sustaining operations in this context involve exceptional adaptability, continuous recalibration of organizational practices, support for emotionally burdened staff, and the ability to steer organizations through persistent uncertainty.

title: Experiences of Whole Families Caring for Children with Medical Complexity: A Systematic Review
source: Journal of Child and Family Studies
summary: Abstract Family members provide crucial care for children with medical complexity (CMC). However, a detailed understanding of whole family experiences has not yet been synthesized. We aimed to synthesize current knowledge describing how car
content: Abstract Family members provide crucial care for children with medical complexity (CMC). However, a detailed understanding of whole family experiences has not yet been synthesized. We aimed to synthesize current knowledge describing how caring for CMC impacts shared family experiences and to inform how whole families caring for CMC could be better supported. This mixed methods systematic review adopted a convergent integrated synthesis approach. Databases were searched up to 8 July 2024, and records were reviewed using Rayyan, following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis’ (PRISMA) protocol. Included studies described experiences shared amongst two or more family members caring for CMC aged 0–18 years. Non-peer reviewed studies were excluded, alongside those published before January 1, 2013. Forty-nine studies were included, and five themes were identified. The overarching theme, Spectrum of normalization , described varied and dynamic experiences of reconstructing and maintaining a sense of normal family life while caring for CMC. The remaining themes were: (1) Family relationships (describing the positive and negative relational impacts of caring), (2) Intra-family roles, communication, and support (how family caring roles and responsibilities were organized and negotiated), (3) Healthcare and support service interactions (the impacts of hospitalizations and respite support services on families’ experiences), including two subthemes, and (4) Family context (e.g. the severity of conditions affecting CMC). This study demonstrates the need for greater commitment to family-centered healthcare that embeds support strategies and programs to support whole families caring for CMC, rather than targeting only primary carers.

title: Implementing the energy data space through the OneNet connector
summary: Abstract The energy sector is undergoing significant changes driven by the rise of distributed energy resources and the progression of digitalisation. This transformation generates vast amounts of data across heterogeneous stakeholders and
content: Abstract The energy sector is undergoing significant changes driven by the rise of distributed energy resources and the progression of digitalisation. This transformation generates vast amounts of data across heterogeneous stakeholders and platforms, creating the need for trusted data exchange while preserving data sovereignty. Data Spaces have emerged as a promising solution to address these challenges. This paper presents and analyses the OneNet Energy Data Space architecture and its implementation through the OneNet Connector and OneNet Middleware. The OneNet solution combines IDS and FIWARE technologies with harmonised Cross-Platform Services and semantic interoperability mechanisms to enable trusted and interoperable data exchange. Functional validation across multiple European demonstrators provided evidence of the feasibility of the OneNet approach for supporting interoperable energy services and flexibility markets, thereby supporting the energy transition.

title: Child deprivation and parental shielding: a European comparative analysis
summary: Abstract This paper investigates child material and social deprivation in six large European countries (Germany, Spain, France, Italy, Poland, and Romania) by using four waves of European Union Statistics on Income and Living Conditions sur
content: Abstract This paper investigates child material and social deprivation in six large European countries (Germany, Spain, France, Italy, Poland, and Romania) by using four waves of European Union Statistics on Income and Living Conditions survey (2009, 2014, 2021, and 2024). Relying on the 17 items included in the official child-specific material and social deprivation indicator used at the European level, we provide a systematic cross-country and over-time analysis. We jointly model both the risk of experiencing deprivation and the intensity of child-specific deprivation. Our results indicate that deprived households with children and at least one of the 17 items in deprivation actually encompass two distinct groups: one primarily lacking household items but largely successful in shielding children from the lack of child-specific items, and another experiencing more severe deprivation, characterized by the lack of both household and child-specific items. Deprivation affecting only child-specific items is relatively uncommon. We indirectly test the extent to which parents protect their children from deprivation by showing that households forgo the least severe household-level items before lacking the child-specific items and that individual-level deprivation is more likely in adults than children living with them. The econometric analysis identifies several factors that increase the risk of the more severe form of deprivation, and also documents cross-country heterogeneity, reflecting differences in welfare regimes and broader socio-economic conditions.

title: Assemblages of Survival: Migrant Food Security and Territorial Cooperation in Pandemic Quito
summary: Migration exposes families to multiple layers of vulnerability, particularly regarding food security and socio-economic stability. This chapter examines how migrant households in Quito, Ecuador, assembled diverse survival strategies to conf
content: Migration exposes families to multiple layers of vulnerability, particularly regarding food security and socio-economic stability. This chapter examines how migrant households in Quito, Ecuador, assembled diverse survival strategies to confront food insecurity during the COVID-19 pandemic. Drawing on a remote survey of 788 migrant families, we employed factor and cluster analyses to identify four distinct configurations of practice: the feminised absorption of scarcity, institutional and network activation, communal and trans-local reciprocity, and market integration. The findings reveal that food security cannot be understood solely through material deprivation; rather, it is dynamically shaped by the gendered distribution of care work, trans-local remittance obligations, and a family’s capacity for territorial cooperation. Furthermore, the analysis exposes a critical paradox where market-based integration often drives a detrimental dietary transition toward processed foods. Ultimately, we argue that addressing migrant precarity requires moving beyond monolithic humanitarian aid toward differentiated interventions tailored to the characteristics of families using each strategy and designed to alleviate the care crisis.

title: Structural, relational, and systemic conditions for hospice care: assessment of professional and institutional expectations in Switzerland
summary: Background Palliative care is a public health priority, yet access to it remains critically insufficient across Europe. In Switzerland, fewer than 10% of people requiring specialized palliative care in hospice settings receive it. Hospices
content: Background Palliative care is a public health priority, yet access to it remains critically insufficient across Europe. In Switzerland, fewer than 10% of people requiring specialized palliative care in hospice settings receive it. Hospices remain difficult to establish within a healthcare system whose financing pathways and insurance-based reimbursement are poorly adapted to hospice care. In Bern, the canton’s first neighborhood-based adult hospice is planned. Drawing on a public health social science framework, this study asks: what structural, relational, and systemic conditions do key actors consider necessary for an effective and equitable hospice? Methods We conducted a qualitative needs assessment through 16 semi-structured interviews across five actor groups: experts by experience; practitioners from palliative medicine, home care, hospital and hospice nursing; research experts; policymakers; and additional experts from social work, spiritual care, and umbrella organisations. We analysed transcripts using Mayring’s qualitative content analysis in MAXQDA24, combining inductive category formation with a multi-level micro–meso–macro framework as a sensitizing concept. Results Across actor groups, the hospice was understood as a holistic “last place of living”, offering dignity, family togetherness, and time to die for people underserved by existing care structures. At the micro level, participants emphasized communication safeguarding self-determination, patients and “loved ones” as one care unit, and a supportive team climate. Meso-level requirements included a homelike environment, integration into hospitals, nursing homes, and home care networks, multiprofessional staffing including trained volunteers, and recognized quality standards. Macro level constraints included donation-dependent financing and unequal financial, cantonal, and socio-cultural access, and limited societal visibility of dying. This situates hospices within the discourse on recognizing end-of-life and palliative care as integral to the health care continuum, highlighting interconnected of micro, meso, and macro conditions, reflecting palliative and end-of-life care complexity. Conclusion Based on participants’ accounts, findings support three public health actions: establishing neighborhood-based hospice infrastructure as an equity response to unmet need; developing financing and inter-cantonal care pathway policies that make access independent of age, means, and residence; and applying multi-actor assessment for needs-based intersectoral planning. Neighborhood-based approaches reposition the hospice as a community-embedded public health resource, improving access for underserved populations.

title: A Bayesian zero-augmented unit-Weibull quantile mixed model with application to COVID-19 mortality in Asia
source: Health Services and Outcomes Research Methodology
summary: Abstract Mixed-effects models are widely used to examine associations between correlated outcomes and set of covariates. However, in real-world outcome measurements are continuous and bounded within the interval of 0 and 1, exhibit correlat
content: Abstract Mixed-effects models are widely used to examine associations between correlated outcomes and set of covariates. However, in real-world outcome measurements are continuous and bounded within the interval of 0 and 1, exhibit correlation, skewness, and contain zeros; thus, existing conventional mixed-effects models are not suitable. Therefore, a Bayesian zero-augmented unit-Weibull quantile mixed-effects model that accommodates these complex data structures is proposed. Following the model development, Monte Carlo simulations were used to evaluate the model performance, and the results confirmed that the all true parameter values were recovered effectively. The model was applied to examine association between COVID-19 death rates and country-level factors, including vaccination rate, proportion of population aged $$\ge 65$$ years, hospital bed count, population density, income level, and interaction between GDP and income level in Asian countries, with temporal trends captured using a piecewise linear time specification. The Bayesian approach was used for parameter estimation, with the No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS), a variant of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC), implemented via the rstan package in R. The results from the continuous bounded component, which models the conditional median show that COVID-19 deaths increased until month 10, declined between months 10 and 14, rose again from months 14 to 20, and then declined thereafter. Furthermore, within-country vaccination, between-country vaccination, hospital bed count, and the GDP–income interaction were negatively associated with COVID-19 death rates, whereas population density and the proportion of the population aged $$\ge 65$$ years were positively associated with COVID-19 death rates. Likewise, the zero-augmented component show that between-country vaccination rate and hospital bed count increase the probability of observing zero COVID-19 death rates, whereas within-country vaccination rate and population density decrease the probability of observing zero deaths. The positive GDP–income interaction shows that the negative association between GDP and the probability of observing zero COVID-19 deaths is weaker in the upper-income group than in the lower-income group. Finally, the model comparison analysis highlighted that the proposed zero-augmented unit-Weibull quantile mixed model provided a better fit to the COVID-19 death rate data than the zero-augmented beta mixed model. The methodological development presented in this paper provides a statistical model for analyzing zero-augmented, bounded, and skewed response variables with a set of covariates. Its application to COVID-19 death rates in Asia highlights key factors associated with variations in death rates across countries, providing useful evidence for public health planning.

title: Tracking the Economy at High Frequency
summary: This paper develops a High-Frequency Economic Index (HFEI) for Ecuador using a Bayesian dynamic factor model estimated with weekly, monthly, and quarterly official indicators. A pseudo-week structure harmonizes the timing of observations an
content: This paper develops a High-Frequency Economic Index (HFEI) for Ecuador using a Bayesian dynamic factor model estimated with weekly, monthly, and quarterly official indicators. A pseudo-week structure harmonizes the timing of observations and their aggregation across frequencies. We compare twelve specifications that differ in their factor-loading dynamics and volatility assumptions, selecting the model with the lowest Deviance Information Criterion. We use the selected model to characterize historical economic conditions and estimate pseudo-weekly recession probabilities through a time-varying mean regime-switching model. In a pseudo-real-time evaluation over 2020–2024, the selected model reduces GDP forecast RMSE by 30–35% relative to an autoregressive benchmark. The framework integrates dispersed and asynchronous official statistics into a common measure of economic activity in a setting with limited timely information.

title: Understanding Society Innovation Panel Wave 18: Results from methodological experiments and new data
summary: Understanding Society includes an 'Innovation Panel' sample.This sample is used to test methods of conducting longitudinal surveys.Results from the Innovation Panel provide evidence about better ways of conducting these surveys, which is re
content: Understanding Society includes an 'Innovation Panel' sample.This sample is used to test methods of conducting longitudinal surveys.Results from the Innovation Panel provide evidence about better ways of conducting these surveys, which is relevant for people working on other studies, as well as informing decisions about how to run Understanding Society.This paper reports the experiments, methodological tests, and other new data collection carried out at Wave 18 of the Innovation Panel (IP18) from July to December 2025, with a small number of respondents completing in early January 2026.IP18 employed a mixed-mode design: some panel members were allocated to first be invited to a web version of the survey (with face-to-face as a follow-up mode), while others were invited to face-to-face first (with web as a follow-up mode); in both cases, telephone interviews were used as the third attempted mode.IP18 was a refreshment wave, adding new members to the panel.For households in the refreshment sample there were experiments around survey length and unconditional incentives.As with prior waves, several other methodological experiments were included in the survey.Survey methods experiments / evaluations were conducted on: whether anticipated life events are predictors of nonresponse in a longitudinal survey; gender differences in survey responses; how to increase informed consent to data linkage in web surveys; unpacking attitudes to ethnic and immigrant inequality; how to increase participation in stool sample collection; and how to increase participation in the youth survey using incentives.In addition, IP18 was used for new survey content.New content was carried related to: gradational gender identity; and unmet need for urgent dental care.

title: Every Agent Is a Code: Self-Models, Affect and the Limits of Self-Knowledge in Implicit-Coding Agents
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: A companion paper showed that every learner is a code: the cumulative log loss of a training pipeline is a code length, and Kraft's equality turns inductive bias into a conserved budget. Here the same accounting is extended from learners to
content: A companion paper showed that every learner is a code: the cumulative log loss of a training pipeline is a code length, and Kraft's equality turns inductive bias into a conserved budget. Here the same accounting is extended from learners to agents that have a body, act, and predict themselves. An agent is a triple of predictive maps: a world model, a policy and a self-model. We prove that the world model and the self-model together form one prefix code on the agent's whole interaction history (its life), which obeys Kraft's equality, and that the expected length of this code exceeds the entropy of the life by exactly the redundancy of the world model plus the self-opacity, the divergence of the self-model from the policy. Self-opacity has a floor, a conditional mutual information fixed by what the self-model can read; an agent whose policy reads its own self-prediction can be transparent to itself when the policy is continuous, and there is a policy for which every self-model pays at least $\ln|\mathcal{A}|$ nats per step. Affect is defined in the same units. A viability prior on body states is a code whose length is the homeostatic drive; valence is the decrease of drive and arousal the code length of the current observation. Valence is conserved: it telescopes, its long-run mean is zero for every agent in every environment, and mean drive equals the entropy of the body's occupancy plus its divergence from the viability prior. The error of anticipated valence is bounded by the square root of the interoceptive redundancy of the world model. A workspace of $M$ symbols bounds control by a rate–distortion function, and no statistic of behaviour identifies any of these internal quantities. The second part of the paper lets the agent rewrite itself. A self-modifying agent, one that replaces its world model, its self-model, its policy or its values by any rule, is still a code on its life, and the conservation laws become laws of self-modification. Under its own prior every agent expects to lose from every rewrite. The nats saved by a rewrite form a test martingale: if the current self is right, no strategy of self-modification saves $c$ nats with probability above $e^{-c}$, so savings are evidence against the former self. A rewrite gated by $\ln(1/\alpha)$ nats of evidence abandons a correct self with probability at most $\alpha$ and costs at most that many nats plus one step; any rule this safe needs a number of steps of life fixed by the evidence the world supplies; and the total gain of all rewrites is bounded by the initial ignorance of the agent. An agent that keeps its former self with prior weight $1-\alpha$ loses at most $\ln\frac{1}{1-\alpha}$ nats if it was right and $\ln\frac1\alpha$ nats more than the price of whatever it should have become, on every life, and by Kraft's inequality no agent does better on both counts. Becoming one of $N$ distinguishable selves costs $\ln N$ nats, and the prices obey Kraft's inequality. Values rewritten bef

title: Micronutrients in plant-based meat alternatives
summary: The expansion of the Australian meat analogue market has been motivated by consumer interest in health, sustainability and sensorial quality, although finding nutritional equivalence with animal meat remains a major challenge. Micronutrient
content: The expansion of the Australian meat analogue market has been motivated by consumer interest in health, sustainability and sensorial quality, although finding nutritional equivalence with animal meat remains a major challenge. Micronutrients in meat analogues are susceptible to degradation during processing, storage and often exhibit low bioaccessibility, which limits effective fortification. In response, we detail emerging micronutrient encapsulation technology as a promising strategy to improve micronutrient fortification in plant-based meat products. The review provides an overview of nutritional gaps and health implications in meat analogues, based on nutritional composition and short-intervention clinical trial evidence from small cohorts, as well as the current landscape of micronutrient fortification in Australia.

title: GRACE-AI: a governance-centric MLOps framework for risk-tiered control, continuous assurance, and explainability in high-stakes AI systems
summary: The recent successful adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in several important applications has made it imperative to integrate operational machine learning with governance frameworks to facilitate regulatory alignment, structured acco
content: The recent successful adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in several important applications has made it imperative to integrate operational machine learning with governance frameworks to facilitate regulatory alignment, structured accountability mechanisms, and risk-based decision-making. Current MLOps frameworks are good at controlling the technical lifecycle of AI models, but are less likely to support governance needs in regulated environments. This paper introduces a governance-oriented MLOps framework to support healthcare and financial AI systems, namely GRACE-AI (Governance, Risk, Assurance, Compliance, and Explainability for Artificial Intelligence). The proposed framework is composed of four interconnected layers, (i) Regulatory Alignment Layer: mapping regulatory requirements into pipeline constraints that incorporate information about governance; the Regulatory Alignment Layer is presented as a proposed architectural component for automated obligation extraction; its clause-level classification performance was not independently benchmarked in this study (ii) Dynamic Risk-Tiering Engine: assigning adaptive governance risk levels based on composite risk scores; (iii) Continuous Assurance Pipeline: drift detection, monitoring, automated recalibration, and anomaly tracking; and (iv) Explainability-by-Design Module: generation of stakeholder-oriented and interpretable explanations. The proposed framework was evaluated using three benchmark datasets supporting four prediction tasks across the healthcare and financial domains, achieving an average accuracy of 96.38% and an unweighted cross-task mean AUC of 0.973; this is 2.78 percentage points above the strongest evaluated standalone baseline (Transformer, 93.60%) and 6.06 percentage points above the mean of the five evaluated standalone baselines. In addition, GRACE-AI could cover 94.7% of the risk, reduce compliance overhead by 38.6%, and detect drift with an average latency of 1.8 s. The findings suggest that the proposed governance model is effective in a controlled experimental setting and could be used to enable trustworthy, governance-aware deployment of AI in regulated environments. In the future, the framework will be validated under operational, real-world conditions with human involvement and at production scale.

title: AI in Agricultural Pest Management: A Critical Review
summary: Artificial intelligence is widely promoted as a solution for automating pest monitoring and reducing crop losses, but many models fail when moved from laboratory conditions to real farms. This review critically examines AI application acros
content: Artificial intelligence is widely promoted as a solution for automating pest monitoring and reducing crop losses, but many models fail when moved from laboratory conditions to real farms. This review critically examines AI application across three sensing platforms i.e., retrofitted sticky traps with computer vision, drones and rovers for distinguishing mite damage from drought stress and acoustic sensors for detecting wood borers hidden inside trees. This review highlights that while deep learning reliably counts whiteflies and codling moths in controlled settings, performance collapses under variable lighting, dust, dew and occlusion. The core problems are rarely discussed in the literature; for instance, training datasets are often labeled by non-specialists, leading to systematic misclassification, models suffer from domain shift over a single growing season and the black box nature of neural networks erodes trust among farmers and regulators. False positives drive unnecessary pesticide use while false negatives cause crop loss. To the best of current knowledge, AI systems generally struggle to recognize a novel invasive pest in its first year of arrival. Through case studies from China, California and Brazil, it is demonstrated that trust depends on explainability and field validation, not on benchmark accuracy. This study proposes a tiered integration into existing IPM workflows. AI-only alerts, remote human checks and field visits. Unlike previous reviews that focus on model accuracy, this review critically examines why most AI fails in the field and proposes a tiered, human-centered integration pathway.

title: Securitization through inscription: National security documents and the making of a global threat lexicon (1987–2025)
summary: Securitization theory holds that actors construct threats by drawing on an existing “grammar” of security. We argue that they also draw on an existing threat lexicon, qualifying the authorial agency the theory attributes to securitizing act
content: Securitization theory holds that actors construct threats by drawing on an existing “grammar” of security. We argue that they also draw on an existing threat lexicon, qualifying the authorial agency the theory attributes to securitizing actors. Using computational text analysis, we examine how threat categories appear and are reused in 660 national security and defence documents published by 118 countries and territories between 1987 and 2025. Most countries overwhelmingly reuse categories already present in the documentary record, and the introduction of new categories is geopolitically concentrated and historically structured. We conceptualize strategy documents as inscription devices that stabilize threats as durable and portable objects, and states as selectors and adapters of an inherited lexicon more than as original authors. Securitizing agency lies in reproducing, modifying, or resisting categories made available by prior inscription, as well as in naming threats. Unequal early inscription may confer lasting agenda-setting power in strategic discourse.
