title: Assessing Ga9N9 and In9N9 nanorings as toxic gas adsorbents: a comprehensive DFT analysis
summary: Abstract Carbon monoxide (CO), nitrogen oxide (NO) and ammonia (NH 3 ) are harmful gases that can adversely affect the environmental quality and human health, so it is important to find effective materials to detect and remove them. Here, w
content: Abstract Carbon monoxide (CO), nitrogen oxide (NO) and ammonia (NH 3 ) are harmful gases that can adversely affect the environmental quality and human health, so it is important to find effective materials to detect and remove them. Here, we have investigated the interaction of gallium nitride (Ga 9 N 9 ) and indium nitride (In 9 N 9 ) nanorings with such toxic gases and their potential as gas sensing or capture materials using density functional theory (DFT). We find that the nature of the interaction is substantially affected by the type of gas. The NH 3 chemisorbs strongly to the two nanorings with adsorption energies of −1.46 eV on Ga 9 N 9 and − 1.13 eV on In 9 N 9 . This strong binding is manifested in pronounced structural changes, short adsorption distances, and a large charge transfer. In contrast, CO and NO interact only weakly through physisorption, with low adsorption energies and minimal effect on the nanoring structure. However, when we examined the electronic properties, three non-trivial insights emerged. First, although NO exhibits the weakest adsorption energy (− 0.19 to − 0.34 eV), it induces the largest electronic perturbation (HOMO-LUMO gap reduction from 3.74 to 2.63 eV) due to its unpaired electron and spin-polarization effects, demonstrating that strong binding is not required for high detectability. Second, water counterintuitively enhances NH 3 adsorption on Ga 9 N 9 (from − 1.46 to − 1.60 eV) due to differential solvation effects and electrostatic stabilization of the polar molecule. Third, the α and β spin channels of NO show dramatically different sensing responses (differing by ~ 10 4 ), suggesting potential for spin-selective gas detection. Thermodynamic calculations confirm that NH 3 adsorption is spontaneous and stable, while recovery time analysis shows that NH 3 desorbs very slowly at room temperature, making the nanorings more suitable for ammonia capture and storage than for reusable sensing. CO and NO, on the other hand, desorb quickly, which is ideal for reversible sensor applications. Overall, Ga 9 N 9 performs better than In 9 N 9 , showing stronger interactions and more pronounced electronic responses. These results position III-nitride nanorings as versatile materials that can be tailored either for capturing ammonia or for sensitively detecting NO, with the latter benefiting from NO’s strong electronic footprint despite weak binding, its anomalous solvation behavior, and its spin-selective response channels. Selectivity screening against common atmospheric gases (H 2 O, CO 2 , N 2 , O 2 ) confirms that NH 3 is preferentially adsorbed over all interferents on both nanorings and further reveals that singlet O 2 reacts destructively with In 9 N 9 , inserting into the ring via a new N–O bond, while leaving Ga 9 N 9 structurally intact, identifying Ga 9 N 9 as the more chemically robust and overall superior candidate material. Future computational studies should extend this framework by exploring larger nano

title: Marine Fuel Pathways under Uncertainty
summary: Abstract Maritime decarbonization assessments commonly rely on point estimates for fuel properties, lifecycle emissions, and costs, despite the substantial variability associated with production pathways, feedstocks, geographical regions, t
content: Abstract Maritime decarbonization assessments commonly rely on point estimates for fuel properties, lifecycle emissions, and costs, despite the substantial variability associated with production pathways, feedstocks, geographical regions, technologies, and future market conditions. This study develops a harmonized database of physical, environmental, and economic parameters for conventional and alternative marine fuels, focusing on well-to-wake (WTW) greenhouse gas intensities, fuel prices, lower heating values, and volumetric energy densities. Data are compiled from scientific literature, technical reports, institutional sources, and sector-specific cost tools, standardized into common units, and classified by fuel molecule and production pathway. Particular attention is given to the temporal evolution of fuel prices: the dataset spans 2020–2050, combining historical and contemporary estimates with long-term forecasts under different technological and market scenarios. For each parameter and fuel pathway, the first quartile, median, and third quartile are derived to characterize low, central, and high estimates and support uncertainty-aware maritime modelling. The results indicate that fossil fuels generally exhibit narrower parameter ranges, whereas biofuels, electrofuels, hydrogen, ammonia, and synthetic methane pathways display substantially greater dispersion. This variability primarily reflects differences in feedstocks, electricity sources, carbon origins, production technologies, geographical contexts, and underlying scenario assumptions. By quantifying how these ranges—and the projected evolution of fuel prices through 2050—affect estimated emissions and energy costs, this study demonstrates the limitations of deterministic fuel comparisons and provides transparent, harmonized inputs for lifecycle assessment, fuel-selection models, and maritime energy-transition scenarios.

title: Decision-Focused Learning for Optimal Control under Price and Carbon Emission Uncertainty: A Case Study in Sustainable Water Treatment
source: ERA: Education and Research Archive (University of Alberta)
summary: Water treatment plants (WTPs) are critical infrastructure but also significant energy consumers, accounting for approximately 2% of energy use in the United States and contributing significantly to greenhouse gas emissions. In this thesis,
content: Water treatment plants (WTPs) are critical infrastructure but also significant energy consumers, accounting for approximately 2% of energy use in the United States and contributing significantly to greenhouse gas emissions. In this thesis, we consider the problem of optimal control for the sustainable operation of a water treatment plant equipped with solar panels and batteries under uncertainty in electricity prices and carbon emissions. We formulate it as a receding-horizon control problem in which input parameters, such as future prices and carbon intensity, are provided by a time-series forecasting model. The traditional predict-then-optimize approach to solving a decision-making under uncertainty problem decouples training of the machine learning (ML) model from decision-making, which involves solving an optimization problem. As a result, the solver cannot provide feedback to the machine learning model during training, leading to a mismatch between the learning objective and the quality of the decisions. To address the mismatch, this thesis investigates the use of decision-focused learning (DFL) for receding horizon control of a grid-tied wastewater treatment plant. We optimize two separate goals: minimizing the plant's operating costs or carbon emissions. We first show that the structure of the underlying optimization problem depends on the chosen objective. Under some assumptions, we derive and prove a relaxation of our combinatorial optimization problem into a convex one. We then benchmark 7 state-of-the-art decision-focused learning methods designed for different types of optimization problems. We also benchmark 7 time-series forecasting models and select 2 for our experiments. Our results show that decision-focused learning can reduce operating costs by 3.8% and 2.5% with deterministic and stochastic decision-focused learning algorithms, respectively, compared to the traditional two-stage predict-then-optimize approach, underscoring the value of training forecasting models with task-specific loss functions rather than accuracy metrics such as mean squared error.

title: Pathways to carbon neutrality by 2040: Modeling a coastal-urban city nexus with blue carbon integration
summary: Abstract Acknowledging climate change is easy; designing and implementing effective, sustainable management strategies to mitigate it is far more challenging. To reduce carbon emissions, identifying actionable levers—particularly in complex
content: Abstract Acknowledging climate change is easy; designing and implementing effective, sustainable management strategies to mitigate it is far more challenging. To reduce carbon emissions, identifying actionable levers—particularly in complex socio-ecological systems (SESs) or city nexus—is critical for policymakers. The SES approach provides a robust lens for connecting anthropogenic and natural drivers of greenhouse gas increases. Using qualitative and possibilistic tools, like the Ecological Discrete-Event Network (EDEN) framework, we integrated various variables (e.g., transportation, maritime activities, land artificialization, and blue carbon ecosystem development) into a decision-support model. We developed the Socio-Economic Net (SEN) model to evaluate whether the costal-urban La Rochelle Metropolitan Area (France) could achieve carbon neutrality by 2040 through adaptive management, while addressing 16 of the 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Given prevailing social resistance to behavioral change, we hypothesized that this transition would be unattainable within the timeframe. However, our results demonstrated the opposite: carbon neutrality, alongside SDGs 13–17, was achievable under specific policy-driven scenarios. These included the implementation of green policies at national/EU levels, a shift from conventional to organic agriculture, and demographic stabilization. Critically, the SEN model revealed that top-down actions are essential to enable bottom-up changes, offering multiple, actionable pathways for local governments. For environmental managers and policymakers, this study demonstrates that systemic, multi-scale interventions can overcome apparent barriers to sustainability while also highlighting the trade-offs—economic, social, and ecological—that must be navigated. Finally, the EDEN framework offers a replicable approach for other coastal cities seeking to balance development and climate goals.

title: Renewable investment dynamics, green innovation markets, and transformation of the national carbon profiles in China
summary: Decarbonization of economic growth is a major policy concern of emerging economies, especially in China, where fast industrialization, growing energy demand, and massive clean-energy buildup are observed. Despite the common knowledge that r
content: Decarbonization of economic growth is a major policy concern of emerging economies, especially in China, where fast industrialization, growing energy demand, and massive clean-energy buildup are observed. Despite the common knowledge that renewable energy investment and green innovation are valuable avenues of carbon mitigation, the short-run adjustment and long-run equilibrium relationships between them and carbon emission are not well understood. This study examines the dynamic association between three variables of carbon emissions, renewable energy investment, green innovation, and economic growth in China by means of annual time-series data. The multidimensional nature of renewable energy investment and green innovation is reflected by the fact that they are constructed using principal component analysis to form composite indices. Upon finding evidence of cointegration between the core variables, the study uses a vector error correction model to estimate both the short-run dynamics and the long-run equilibrium relations. The results show that there is a stable long-run relationship between carbon emissions, renewable energy investment, green innovation, and economic growth. Renewable energy investment and green innovation are negatively but statistically insignificantly associated with carbon emission changes in the short-run, indicating that their effect of reducing emissions is not short-term and may need more time to adjust. The results of the error correction demonstrate that green innovation and economic growth are sensitive to disequilibrium in the long run, meaning they are significant adjustment channels during the process of low-carbon transition in China. The long-run outcomes also indicate that China is still at the stage of growth-with-transition when renewable implementation and innovativeness capacity is growing, yet complete decoupling of emissions has not been reached. The results suggest that renewable investments cannot yield instant carbon benefits absent green innovation, grid integration, industrial rejuvenation, and sustained policy co-ordination. This study emphasizes the importance of measures that would merge renewable energy investments, innovation-system building, and structural change to facilitate the long-term decarbonization pathway in China.

title: Mitigating climate change impacts in ruminants: Nutritional interventions to alleviate heat stress and enteric greenhouse gas emissions
summary: Abstract Anthropogenic emissions, such as CO 2 , CH 4 , and N 2 O, are linked to the Earth’s rising temperatures and have significantly altered the global climate; their impacts are evident in extreme climatic events. Rising human populatio
content: Abstract Anthropogenic emissions, such as CO 2 , CH 4 , and N 2 O, are linked to the Earth’s rising temperatures and have significantly altered the global climate; their impacts are evident in extreme climatic events. Rising human population, industrialisation, energy exploration, and transportation have sharply increased greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. Forestry, agriculture, and livestock contribute only a marginal share, yet ruminants are routinely singled out as major GHG emitters and blamed for global warming and climate variability. As the climate changes, livestock face increasing heat stress, which lowers gross production and typically raises GHG emissions per unit of output. Many national and international agencies track climate change and monitor GHG inventories, but more sophisticated and precise sector-level estimation methods are needed. Our analysis shows that the agri-livestock sector is not the leading contributor to anthropogenic emissions; instead, the largest share comes from energy exploration, construction, transport, and manufacturing. The agri-livestock sector can still meaningfully reduce its carbon load through nutritional interventions that mitigate both heat stress and GHG emissions in ruminants. Better management of dung, waste, and manure is another key area for improvement. A clear understanding of the total carbon credits generated and used across the value chain, from raw materials to final animal product, is also essential for sound sectoral policy. From this perspective, this review examines the impact of climate-related heat stress on ruminants, current continent-specific GHG inventories, and effective nutritional interventions to mitigate heat stress and GHG emissions in ruminants.

title: Dataset_BiLevel_Empty_Container_Casablanca_Corridor.xlsx
summary: This dataset supports the article “Bi-level optimization of empty-container balancing under blockchain-linked port-cost reduction scenarios and carbon pricing: A stylized Casablanca-centred corridor study”, submitted to the Journal of Econo
content: This dataset supports the article “Bi-level optimization of empty-container balancing under blockchain-linked port-cost reduction scenarios and carbon pricing: A stylized Casablanca-centred corridor study”, submitted to the Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control. The study uses a bi-level Stackelberg model in which a shipping company (leader) sets freight rates and internalizes an EU ETS carbon charge with leg-differentiated coverage, while a non-vessel-operating common carrier (follower) sets customer prices, repositions empty containers and manages inventories. The model is applied to a stylized quarterly Casablanca–Tanger Med–Algeciras–Valencia corridor. The Excel workbook is a data-source register for all 52 model inputs and contextual claims used in the article. Each value is classified as REAL (official, secondary or fully derived), MIXED (sourced component combined with an author assumption), SYNTHETIC (author-chosen modelling assumption) or DATA GAP. Sources include Marsa Maroc 2025 port tariffs, Bank Al-Maghrib exchange rates, Tanger Med, Algeciras and Valencia port authority traffic statistics, GLEC Framework v3.2 emission intensities, and EU ETS regulatory documents. The workbook contains: a READ ME; a master register with values, units, sources, URLs and notes; separate sheets for REAL, MIXED and SYNTHETIC inputs; a formula-based calculation check of the Casablanca cost anchors; a full bibliography; and a log of primary-source and route checks.

title: Asymmetric and dynamic effects of climate variability on crop and livestock production in Somalia
summary: Climate variability poses escalating risks to agricultural systems in fragile and climate-exposed regions, yet evidence on asymmetric and dynamic production responses remains limited. This study investigates the short-run and long-run effec
content: Climate variability poses escalating risks to agricultural systems in fragile and climate-exposed regions, yet evidence on asymmetric and dynamic production responses remains limited. This study investigates the short-run and long-run effects of climate variability on crop and livestock production in Somalia using annual data for 1989–2021. Crop and livestock production indices from the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) are combined with rainfall and temperature data from the Climatic Research Unit (CRU). A nonlinear autoregressive distributed lag (NARDL) framework is applied to examine asymmetric responses to positive and negative climate shocks, complemented by cumulative climate stress indicators and endogenous structural break controls. Structural instability is addressed using endogenous break tests. The results reveal statistically significant short-run asymmetries in the effects of temperature on both agricultural systems. Negative temperature shocks exert larger and more persistent adverse short-run effects than positive temperature changes, with coefficients significant at conventional levels for both crop and livestock production. In contrast, the long-run coefficients are generally statistically insignificant and imprecisely estimated, providing suggestive rather than conclusive evidence of persistent climate effects. Error-correction estimates provide strong evidence of convergence for livestock production, with approximately 45% of disequilibrium corrected annually ( p = 0.008), but only marginal evidence for crop production, for which approximately 30% is corrected annually ( p = 0.097). Baseline linear models overlook short-run nonlinear responses, emphasizing the need for asymmetric frameworks. The Climate Stress Index shows high-stress regimes have increased in both frequency and duration in recent decades. These findings show that short-run climate impacts on Somalia’s agriculture are asymmetric and system-specific: crop production is more sensitive and recovers more slowly than livestock. This underscores the need for climate-responsive policies, including investment in heat-tolerant crop varieties, improved water management, and adaptive support for pastoral systems in fragile environments.

title: Strategic Resilience in Rail Infrastructure: Lessons from International Resilience Initiatives
summary: Abstract Climate change is escalating extreme weather, profoundly challenging global railways. UIC’s RERA (Resilient Railways) initiative addresses these threats through two reports: “Resilient Railways facing High Temperatures” and “Resili
content: Abstract Climate change is escalating extreme weather, profoundly challenging global railways. UIC’s RERA (Resilient Railways) initiative addresses these threats through two reports: “Resilient Railways facing High Temperatures” and “Resilient Railways facing Heavy Rains”. While high temperatures can cause track buckling and heavy rainfall can lead to landslides, both disrupt services and compromise safety. RERA provides shareable lessons and a unified assessment methodology written by infrastructure managers. This paper examines the RERA frameworks, drawing insights from climate impact analysis and vulnerability assessments. It highlights adaptive solutions implemented by member organisations, demonstrating how harmonized approaches safeguard operations. The paper explores the role of multi-modal integration and knowledge sharing in building resilience. By embedding climate projections into planning, railways can transition from reactive to resilient systems, supporting sustainable mobility in a volatile climate.

title: Effect of Carbon Pricing on Global Environmental Sustainability and Economic Development: An Exploratory Approach
source: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MARKETING AND COMMUNICATION STUDIES
summary: This study critically examines the strategic implications of carbon pricing mechanisms on global environmental sustainability and economic development. Through a systematic literature review and content analysis, the research synthesizes fi
content: This study critically examines the strategic implications of carbon pricing mechanisms on global environmental sustainability and economic development. Through a systematic literature review and content analysis, the research synthesizes findings from peer-reviewed articles, reports, and policy documents published between 2010 and 2024. The study aims to analyze the effectiveness of carbon pricing in reducing greenhouse gas emissions, assess its economic impacts, explore environmental benefits, and understand the role of international cooperation in enhancing the efficacy of carbon pricing policies. The methodology involves a structured search strategy with rigorous inclusion and exclusion criteria to ensure the relevance and quality of the literature reviewed. The analysis reveals that carbon pricing, including carbon taxes and cap-and-trade systems, is a crucial tool for mitigating climate change while promoting economic growth and structural transformation. Key findings emphasize the potential of carbon pricing to drive innovation in green technologies, address social equity concerns, and highlight the importance of international policy coordination in mitigating cross-border carbon leakage and competitiveness issues. The study concludes that effectively designed and equitably implemented carbon pricing mechanisms can align environmental sustainability with economic development goals. Recommendations for policymakers stress the need for comprehensive strategies that integrate carbon pricing with broader economic and environmental policies, underscore the importance of international cooperation, and advocate for continued research to refine carbon pricing models and strategies. This research contributes to the ongoing discourse on carbon pricing, offering insights into its potential as a cornerstone of global climate governance and sustainable economic policy.

title: Derived data for meter-based assessment of carbon-aware building demand flexibility: Operational sensitivity and cross-domain reliability
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: This dataset contains derived scientific results supporting the assessment of carbon-aware building demand flexibility across 22 buildings, five sites and four assigned grid-emission areas. It includes measured-load assessment outputs, oper
content: This dataset contains derived scientific results supporting the assessment of carbon-aware building demand flexibility across 22 buildings, five sites and four assigned grid-emission areas. It includes measured-load assessment outputs, operational and temporal sensitivity, AER/LRMER carbon accounting, cross-domain prediction results, uncertainty summaries and figure source data. The complete research software and original third-party hourly datasets are not included. The results represent conditional assessments rather than physically validated demand-response interventions.

title: Residual Cap Albedo and Energy Balance: A Reflected-Sunlight and Thermal-Emission Budget for the Martian Polar Caps
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: Albedo decides how much sunlight a polar surface absorbs, and the two Martian ices absorb very differently. This paper budgets the residual caps from published albedos: at a solstice insolation of 500 watts per square metre, the north water
content: Albedo decides how much sunlight a polar surface absorbs, and the two Martian ices absorb very differently. This paper budgets the residual caps from published albedos: at a solstice insolation of 500 watts per square metre, the north water-ice cap absorbs 275 watts per square metre and the south carbon dioxide cap absorbs 175. Their net fluxes are 175 and 148 watts per square metre after thermal emission. The albedo difference is why the southern cap stays at the frost point while the northern cap warms.

title: Pore Scale Transport Aspects of Unconventional EOR Methods and H2/CO2 Storage
source: ERA: Education and Research Archive (University of Alberta)
summary: The increasing global energy demand and the urgent need to mitigate greenhouse gas emissions create a pressing challenge in our energy industry. Addressing this reality requires a diversified strategy that includes: (1) improving the effici
content: The increasing global energy demand and the urgent need to mitigate greenhouse gas emissions create a pressing challenge in our energy industry. Addressing this reality requires a diversified strategy that includes: (1) improving the efficiency of hydrocarbon extraction from existing, particularly unconventional, reservoirs to lower their carbon footprint; (2) directly reducing carbon dioxide (CO2) through carbon capture, utilization and sequestration (CCUS); and (3) developing scalable green energy alternatives like underground hydrogen storage (UHS). All these strategies, including enhanced oil recovery (EOR), CO2 sequestration, and UHS, rely fundamentally on complex fluid transport processes in porous media (i.e., subsurface formations). In particular, phase changes in nanopores, fluid transport at pore scale as well as effects of different parameters on the fluid flow have been of great interest recently. Consequently, mathematical, experimental, and more importantly visual analyses at the pore scale are needed. This PhD research uniquely employs a multiscale approach that integrates thermodynamic modeling, core-scale experimental evaluation, and pore-scale visualization. It began with the development of an empirical model to accurately predict the saturation pressure of pure hydrocarbons confined in nanopores. By accounting for confinement effects on phase behavior, the model more accurately predicted the energy requirements for solvent retrieval after solvent injection processes. This improved understanding of phase behavior under confinement is essential for optimizing solvent recovery in tight formations. Subsequently, the dynamics of matrix-fracture interactions were systematically investigated through spontaneous imbibition experiments conducted on three rock types: Berea sandstone, Indiana limestone, and tight sandstone cores. These experiments evaluated the efficacy of various chemical additives, including surfactants, high-pH solutions, and organic alkalis, in enhancing oil recovery. The study focused on their roles in altering wettability, modifying interfacial tension, and inducing emulsification, with a particular emphasis on the influence of rock type and boundary conditions on the recovery mechanisms. Anionic surfactant O342 and nonionic surfactant Tween 80 showed their efficacies in improving final oil recovery due to wettability alteration in sandstone rocks. Notable spontaneous emulsification was observed when chemicals were introduced, especially in countercurrent imbibition. The chemicals performed differently in carbonate cores than in sandstone cores. For example, while the cationic surfactant CTAB was ineffective in sandstone cores, it was highly effective and robust in carbonate formations. Building on these findings, visual aids were employed to explain the transport mechanisms during chemical EOR. Pore-scale visualization techniques were utilized to track fluid displacement, imbibition front, and residual oil developm

title: Carbon Footprint Reduction in Road Construction: Experimental Evaluation of Sustainable Materials for Rigid Pavement Concrete
source: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology
summary: Road construction consumes large quantities of cement, aggregates, bituminous materials and fossil fuel energy. The production and transportation of these materials, together with on-site construction operations, contribute to greenhouse ga
content: Road construction consumes large quantities of cement, aggregates, bituminous materials and fossil fuel energy. The production and transportation of these materials, together with on-site construction operations, contribute to greenhouse gas emissions. This paper examines the use of natural and waste-derived materials in rigid pavement concrete, based on the experimental programme reported in the supplied thesis. The materials considered are human hair, bamboo pieces/fibre, coconut (coir) fibre, ground granulated blast furnace slag (GGBS) and fly ash. The study compares compressive strength at different curing ages and material replacement or addition levels. The reported results indicate that human hair addition increased the 28-day M30 compressive strength from 33.60 MPa for the control mix to 37.25 MPa at 3% addition. Coconut fibre produced the highest reported 28-day strength of 40.50 MPa at 5% addition. For GGBS, the highest 28-day average strength was 34.22 MPa at 30% replacement, compared with 29.98 MPa for the control. In contrast, the bamboo series showed a progressive reduction in compressive strength as the reported replacement level increased, while fly ash replacement above 5% reduced 28- day strength in the reported series. These results demonstrate that sustainable materials must be proportioned individually rather than assumed to improve all concrete properties at every dosage. The thesis identifies potential environmental benefits through reduced use of conventional cement and aggregates and the productive use of waste resources. However, a project-specific lifecycle carbon inventory was not reported; therefore, this paper does not claim a quantified percentage reduction in CO₂ emissions. Further work should combine mechanical testing with a transparent life-cycle assessment and field validation.

title: Modulation of Structure and Methane Dry Reforming Behaviors for Hydrotalcite‑Derived Ni‑Based Catalysts via NiCu Bimetallic Ratios
summary: Dry reforming of methane (DRM) can simultaneously convert two typical greenhouse gases, CH4 and CO2, into syngas, which possesses dual values for greenhouse gas emission reduction and carbon resource utilization. However, this reaction suff
content: Dry reforming of methane (DRM) can simultaneously convert two typical greenhouse gases, CH4 and CO2, into syngas, which possesses dual values for greenhouse gas emission reduction and carbon resource utilization. However, this reaction suffers from high energy consumption and catalyst deactivation caused by surface carbon deposition and high-temperature metal sintering, which severely restricts its industrial application. In this work, a series of NiCuMgAl hydrotalcite precursors were synthesized by the urea hydrothermal method, and NiCu bimetallic catalysts were obtained after high-temperature calcination and H2 reduction. By adjusting the total NiCu metal content and Ni/Cu molar ratio, the effects of bimetallic component content and ratio on catalyst structure and DRM performance were systematically investigated. The results showed that all catalysts retained the hydrotalcite-derived sheet-like mesoporous structure, and Ni-Cu alloy was formed after reduction. Among them, the Ni4CuMgAl(8%) catalyst (8% total NiCu content, Ni/Cu = 4:1) exhibited the best comprehensive performance: at a reaction temperature of 600 °C and a mass space velocity of 36000 mL·g−1·h−1, the CH4 and CO2 conversions were stabilized at 34.8% and 48.5%, respectively, with an H2/CO ratio of 0.61. No obvious deactivation was observed within 12 h, and the carbon deposition amount after reaction was only 1.17%. The catalyst also showed good stability at 800 °C for 20 h, with CH4 and CO2 conversions maintained at 84.6% and 96.2%, respectively. XRD, XPS, and HRTEM confirmed the formation of Ni-Cu alloy, which modulated the electronic properties of active sites. The well-defined mesoporous structure and highly dispersed metal sites synergistically inhibited carbon deposition. This study provides experimental basis for the component optimization of hydrotalcite-derived NiCu bimetallic DRM catalysts.

title: Considering Felsic, Intermediate and Mafic Feedstocks for Biotic and Abiotic CO2 Removal
source: ERA: Education and Research Archive (University of Alberta)
summary: Carbon dioxide removal (CDR) is a necessary strategy to achieve net-negative emissions and stabilize Earth's climate. Storing CO2 as alkalinity through silicate weathering is one of the most efficient forms of inorganic carbon storage. In t
content: Carbon dioxide removal (CDR) is a necessary strategy to achieve net-negative emissions and stabilize Earth's climate. Storing CO2 as alkalinity through silicate weathering is one of the most efficient forms of inorganic carbon storage. In this study, the CO2 removal potential of six diverse mine tailings and ores, with felsic to ultramafic lithologies and diverse mineralogical compositions, were investigated (1) using HCl-leaching tests and (2) biotic and abiotic mineral dissolution experiments. HCl leaching experiments were performed at a nominal pH of 5.60, 4.41, and 3.89 — corresponding to aqueous CO2 concentrations of 0.04%, 10%, and 100%, respectively — and sampled at 1 week, 1 month and 3 months. Prior to leaching experiments, the feedstocks were characterized by quantitative X-ray diffraction (QXRD) to determine modal abundances of Mg- and Ca-bearing silicates. Modal mineralogy and dissolution rate constants were used to calculate the upper limits of H+ neutralization associated with mineral dissolution, as well as Mg and Ca release at pH 5.60, 4.41, and 3.89. Mafic and ultramafic feedstocks released more Mg and Ca and approached calculated values, which reflect far-from-equilibrium upper limits of silicate dissolution, more closely than what was observed for felsic feedstocks. Cation release occurred on the same order of magnitude as CO2-based experiments (Figure 1), indicating that simple HCl-dissolution experiments may be used as a proxy for more labour intensive H2CO3-leaching experiments. In a second set of experiments, cyanobacteria were added to selected feedstocks in a modified BG-11 growth medium. Cyanobacterial mats were incubated for 6 months with either phlogopite (a mica), forsterite (olivine), or tailings from two mines containing up to 32 wt.% phlogopite and 22 wt.% forsterite, respectively. Each substrate was tested under biotic and abiotic conditions. In the biological experiments, cyanobacterial growth increased pH and nutrient cycling, and in some cases reduced silicate dissolution rates.

title: ESGF-NG CMIP7.C4MIP.ACCESS-Consortium.ACCESS-ESM1-6.esm-flat10-cdr version 1
summary: Project: CMIP7 Coupled climate carbon cycle model intercomparison project: exploration of the response of the coupled carbon-climate system. Produced by: The ACCESS Consortium brings together Australian institutions contributing to the Aust
content: Project: CMIP7 Coupled climate carbon cycle model intercomparison project: exploration of the response of the coupled carbon-climate system. Produced by: The ACCESS Consortium brings together Australian institutions contributing to the Australian Community Climate and Earth System Simulator (ACCESS) and its submissions to the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP). Participating organisations contribute to different ACCESS models and scientific activities, supported through a combination of institutional investment and Australian Government research infrastructure and research programs, together with international collaborations. (Using Model/Source: ACCESS-ESM1-6 with Experiment esm-flat10-cdr) The model is an updated version of ACCESS-ESM1-5, as used for CMIP6 (Ziehn et al., 2020). Its dynamic components are the UK Met Office Unified Model atmosphere (v7.3) in a configuration similar to HadGEM2 including CLASSIC aerosols, with the CABLE land surface model (v3) including land biogeochemistry. The atmosphere is coupled to the MOM5 ocean with WOMBATlite biogeochemistry and CICE5 sea-ice using the OASIS-MCT coupler. Chemistry is prescribed including monthly mean, zonally-averaged ozone. Volcano forcing is prescribed as stratospheric optical depth as monthly means in four equal area latitude bands. Land-ice is represented by an ice tile in the land surface model. A grid-cell is either completely ice or ice-free and the ice tile distribution does not change in time. The main differences from ACCESS-ESM1.5 include corrections to how convective momentum transport had been applied in the atmosphere, a change to ocean albedo to better match observations, a correction to the passing of ocean carbon fluxes into the atmosphere, updates to improve energy and water conservation across the land and atmosphere, inclusion of 3 new plant functional types (c4 crops and two Australian tree types), improvements to the treatment of land-use change, updates to some of the land parameterisations or parameter values, the inclusion of a pseudo-iceberg scheme for distributing runoff from Antarctica and Greenland and a substantial update to ocean-biogeochemistry. Many aspects of the model infrastructure have also been improved to ensure greater provenance, better support for users and enhanced model throughput. A manuscript describing ACCESS-ESM1.6 is in preparation (Ziehn et al.). Experiment: Extension of `esm-flat10` where emissions decline linearly to -10 PgC / yr then stay constant until cumulative emissions (including the emissions in `esm-flat10`) reach zero. An extra 20 years is included at the end to allow for calculating averages over different time windows. CMIP7 is a project of the [World Climate Research Programme (WCRP)](https://www.wcrp-climate.org/), providing climate projections to understand past, present, and future climate changes. It is part of the [WCRP Earth System Modelling and Observations (ESMO) Core Project](https://wcrp-esmo.org/), which wa

title: Emergency medicine and sustainability: optimizing a knee trauma care pathway with life cycle assessment
summary: The carbon footprint of emergency care remains largely under-examined. This study quantified greenhouse gas emissions associated with the full clinical pathway of knee trauma patients treated at an outpatient emergency unit in University Ho
content: The carbon footprint of emergency care remains largely under-examined. This study quantified greenhouse gas emissions associated with the full clinical pathway of knee trauma patients treated at an outpatient emergency unit in University Hospitals of Geneva, Switzerland, to better understand the environmental impact of this care trajectory. Life Cycle Assessment methodology was applied to the functional unit of the management of one patient presenting with knee trauma, including diagnosis and initial treatment. Different clinical scenarios were modelled to reflect variations in care complexity and diagnostic imaging use. Results revealed that patient transportation, pharmaceuticals, medical consumables, and diagnostic imaging, particularly magnetic resonance imaging, are major contributors to the carbon footprint. These findings underscore the importance of optimizing care protocols and exploring sustainable alternatives in emergency healthcare to reduce associated greenhouse gas emissions.

title: Preparation of colorimetric test strips based on PtPdRu trimetallic nanozyme with enhanced peroxidase-like activity for shrimp freshness monitoring
summary: A colorimetric test strip was fabricated using PtPdRu trimetallic nanozymes for shrimp freshness monitoring. Specifically, PtPdRu trimetallic nanozymes were first synthesized via a reduction strategy and then anchored onto the strip surface
content: A colorimetric test strip was fabricated using PtPdRu trimetallic nanozymes for shrimp freshness monitoring. Specifically, PtPdRu trimetallic nanozymes were first synthesized via a reduction strategy and then anchored onto the strip surface by solvent evaporation. Benefiting from the intrinsic peroxidase-mimicking activity of PtPdRu trimetallic nanozymes, the strip changed from white to blue upon the addition of TMB and H₂O₂. Notably, the strip could interact with biogenic amine vapors, generating a colorimetric response during shrimp spoilage. When applied with shrimp samples, the strip color shifted from blue to pale blue or yellow, which strongly correlated with alkaline pH and ammonia surroundings. Finally, the strip realized shrimp freshness monitoring based on the inhibitory effect of alkaline pH/ammonia on the peroxidase-mimicking activity of PtPdRu trimetallic nanozymes. Therefore, this strip holds great promise as an advanced paper-based indicator for low-cost, in situ freshness detection of shrimp.

title: Comparative compositional characterization of New Zealand manuka honey and selected Chinese honeys using multiple chemical indicators
summary: Abstract New Zealand manuka honey is a high-value honey that has attracted increasing attention in the Chinese market. Comparing its chemical characteristics with those of selected Chinese honeys provides valuable information for understand
content: Abstract New Zealand manuka honey is a high-value honey that has attracted increasing attention in the Chinese market. Comparing its chemical characteristics with those of selected Chinese honeys provides valuable information for understanding compositional variability among honey samples. In this study, stable isotope ratios, carbon and nitrogen contents, saccharide composition, mineral element composition, and chemometric analyses were integrated to investigate compositional differences between New Zealand manuka honey and selected Chinese honeys of different botanical types. Clear compositional differences were observed among the predefined honey sample groups within the present dataset. Stable isotope ratios, carbon and nitrogen contents, saccharide composition, and mineral element composition each provided complementary information for characterizing honey samples, with mineral element composition making an important contribution to sample classification. Chemometric analyses, including principal component analysis (PCA), Fisher discriminant analysis (Fisher-DA), and artificial neural network (ANN) models, further showed that integrating multiple compositional indicators substantially improved classification performance, with the supervised models clearly distinguishing Chinese honey samples from New Zealand manuka honey. This study provides a comprehensive comparative compositional analysis of New Zealand manuka honey and selected Chinese honeys based on multiple complementary chemical indicators, providing comparative compositional data and an integrated analytical strategy for future studies on honey characterization, quality evaluation, and comparative analysis of commercial honey samples.

title: Bioprocessing of coconut husk to produce second-generation bioethanol using Zymomonas mobilis ZM4
summary: Abstract Coconut husk is an abundant lignocellulosic residue generated by the tropical coconut processing industry and remains largely underutilized despite its considerable carbohydrate content. This study developed an integrated strategy
content: Abstract Coconut husk is an abundant lignocellulosic residue generated by the tropical coconut processing industry and remains largely underutilized despite its considerable carbohydrate content. This study developed an integrated strategy involving sequential alkaline, dilute-acid, and bleaching pretreatment, enzymatic hydrolysis, and fermentation with Zymomonas mobilis for the valorization of coconut husk into bioethanol. The sequential pretreatment enhanced cellulose accessibility and resulted in substantial removal of lignin and extractive components while retaining a considerable proportion of the carbohydrate fraction. Enzymatic hydrolysis using a cellulase–hemicellulase cocktail released approximately 230 mg glucose g⁻¹ and 161.25 mg xylose g⁻¹ of raw coconut husk, corresponding to overall sugar recovery efficiencies of approximately 50–60% following pretreatment and hydrolysis. Fermentation of the hydrolysate by Z. mobilis resulted in an ethanol yield of 0.0975 g g⁻¹ raw biomass, corresponding to approximately 83% of the theoretical ethanol yield based on the available fermentable sugars. Overall, these findings demonstrate the potential of coconut husk as a feedstock for second-generation bioethanol production and highlight the integrated approach as a promising strategy for efficient lignocellulosic biomass conversion and agricultural waste valorization.

title: The Tongue of the Community: Code-Switching, Vernacular Authority and Postcolonial Identity in Ghanaian Theatre for Development Practice
source: International Journal for Early Childhood and Educational Research
summary: In Ghanaian Theatre for Development (TfD) practice, the use of indigenous languages, including Fante, Twi and Ewe, alongside or in place of English is commonly framed as a pragmatic measure for ensuring community accessibility and engagemen
content: In Ghanaian Theatre for Development (TfD) practice, the use of indigenous languages, including Fante, Twi and Ewe, alongside or in place of English is commonly framed as a pragmatic measure for ensuring community accessibility and engagement. This paper contests that framing. Drawing on fieldwork conducted in the Gomoa Mankoadze and Asebu communities respectively in the Central region of Ghana, it argues that code-switching in TfD performance is a postcolonial ideological act that works simultaneously as a dramaturgical strategy, a knowledge-legitimation device, and a decolonial refusal of linguistic coloniality. The paper introduces the concept of vernacular authority to describe the epistemological weight that indigenous-language performance carries in community contexts and develops a three-part typology of code-switching in TfD practice, namely functional, affective and authority switching grounded in observed performance work. Situating these practices within postcolonial literary and linguistic theory, the paper argues that the spoken, community-embedded TfD text constitutes a form of African literary production that postcolonial scholarship has not yet adequately theorised. The paper concludes by calling for a TfD poetics that takes the vernacular performance text seriously as literature, and for facilitator training that treats language choice as a theoretical and political rather than merely logistical matter.

title: From commodities to weapons: a political-economic critique of the "cost inversion" of FPV drones from the perspective of Marx's theory of machinery
source: Journal of Applied Economics and Policy Studies
summary: The systematic deployment of First-Person-View (FPV) drones in the Russia–Ukraine conflict has revealed a pronounced phenomenon of "cost inversion": FPV drones costing only a few hundred dollars each can repeatedly destroy high-value weapon
content: The systematic deployment of First-Person-View (FPV) drones in the Russia–Ukraine conflict has revealed a pronounced phenomenon of "cost inversion": FPV drones costing only a few hundred dollars each can repeatedly destroy high-value weapons platforms worth millions or even hundreds of millions of dollars. Tactical drones now account for 60% to 70% of total equipment losses. Taking Marx's theory of machinery as its analytical framework, this paper examines the theoretical implications of this phenomenon through the lens of the antagonistic relationship between "fixed capital" and "living labor". Although the concept of "cost asymmetry" in existing security studies describes the phenomenon, it fails to uncover the underlying logic of production relations. Drawing on the systematic deployment of FPV drones in the Russia–Ukraine conflict as an empirical case, this paper conducts an empirical analysis of their cost structures and exchange ratios based on publicly available data. It introduces the concept of "disembedding from the logic of fixed capital" and argues that FPV drones systematically dismantle high-value weapons platforms through three interconnected mechanisms: consumableization, commodity-based supply chains, and low operational barriers. These mechanisms enable FPV drones to escape the constraints imposed by the recovery of value invested in military fixed capital. This analysis extends Marx's theory of machinery from the sphere of production to the analysis of military technology, providing a new analytical framework for critique within the field of the political economy of war.

title: Classification algorithms for selecting crop types in Asian countries based on soil and climate parameters
summary: Classifying crops from environmental conditions can support agricultural data exploration, but an observed crop is not necessarily the most suitable crop for that land. We compare multinomial logistic regression, k-nearest neighbors (kNN),
content: Classifying crops from environmental conditions can support agricultural data exploration, but an observed crop is not necessarily the most suitable crop for that land. We compare multinomial logistic regression, k-nearest neighbors (kNN), and random forest on a transparent seven-country South Asian grid benchmark. Crop-area and surface-soil layers came from the open ACASA 50 km collection; annual mean temperature and precipitation were sampled from WorldClim 2.1 climate normals. For each grid cell, the largest of 12 crop-area layers defined the observed dominant-crop label. Cells without mapped crops, incomplete inputs, or less than 50% dominance were removed, and classes with fewer than 30 records were excluded, leaving 1,070 cells in seven crop classes. No crop-area layer was used as a predictor. Disjoint 2° spatial blocks supplied 642 training, 215 validation, and 213 test cells. On the held-out test blocks, kNN achieved 73.7% accuracy and 0.461 macro-F1, versus 70.9% and 0.441 for random forest and 70.0% and 0.398 for logistic regression. Its advantage over random forest in accuracy was 2.8 percentage points, but a paired block-bootstrap interval crossed zero. Leave-one-country-out tests were markedly less reliable, especially in Afghanistan and Pakistan. The results identify a modestly stronger within-region classifier for mapped crop dominance under this protocol; they do not validate agronomic suitability, yield benefit, or transfer to new countries.

title: CBAM's Impact on Thai Exporters' Low-Carbon Strategy: The Moderating Role of Green Transformational Leadership
summary: The European Union Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) introduces new compliance requirements for exporters in carbon-intensive sectors, including firms in emerging economies. This study examines the association between CBAM regulator
content: The European Union Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) introduces new compliance requirements for exporters in carbon-intensive sectors, including firms in emerging economies. This study examines the association between CBAM regulatory pressure (CRP) and low-carbon strategy (LCS) adoption among Thai listed exporting firms and tests whether green transformational leadership (GTL) moderates that association. The study uses a quantitative, cross-sectional documentary design. The auditable profile archive contained 100 numbered records; removal of five duplicate/replacement entries produced a final analytical sample of 95 unique firms. CRP, GTL, and LCS are arithmetic means of documentary items scored on a 1–5 scale. Models control for Firm Size, Export Intensity, and eight sector dummies, with Steel & Metals as the reference category. CRP was positively associated with LCS in Model 2 (standardized 𝛽 = .872, t = 13.31, p < .001; ΔR² = .421). In Model 4, GTL had a positive main effect (𝛽 = .766, p < .001), whereas the CRP × GTL interaction was not statistically significant (𝛽 = −.034, t = −0.82, p = .415; ΔR² < .001). Conditional CRP effects were positive at low, mean and high GTL, and the Johnson–Neyman transition points lay outside the observed GTL range. H1 was supported and H2 was not supported. The findings indicate that CBAM regulatory pressure and GTL are both positively associated with low-carbon strategy, but the proposed moderating role of GTL is not supported in this sample. title: European power and the structure of regulatory upgrading
summary: Abstract In light of the immense difficulty in achieving voluntary intergovernmental cooperation of all states, Nobel laureate William Nordhaus proposed to form a ‘Climate Club’ as a new architecture for international climate cooperation to
content: Abstract In light of the immense difficulty in achieving voluntary intergovernmental cooperation of all states, Nobel laureate William Nordhaus proposed to form a ‘Climate Club’ as a new architecture for international climate cooperation to counter free-riding behaviour of individual participating countries. To some extent, the European Union (EU) Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) is an embodiment of such a club, as it is designed to maintain market access for cooperative partners while imposing punitive measures on detractors. In this paper, we investigate how CBAM affects support for climate policies in EU trade partners, balancing Nordhaus’ focus on adaptation costs with a political economy approach that foregrounds political costs and bargaining power. We show that adaptation costs and ‘loyalty’ created by a lack of export alternatives have a strong influence on firm support. Bargaining power, meanwhile, affects the strength of the positions eventually taken by policymakers. When the EU relies upon trade partners for imports, they are more likely to try to leverage their position and gain concessions through negotiations or threats of retaliation. We test our argument by analyzing public debates through an automated text analysis of media in trade partner countries using large language models to identify affected actors and analyze their positions. Our study analyzes all newspaper articles in the Nexis Uni database mentioning CBAM since the European Commission released its official proposal in the ‘fit for 55’ package in July 2021. Our findings align with our expectations for both firm and policymakers, suggesting that success of CBAM and other policies which rely upon a club goods logic will depend on political factors as well as the cost-benefit factors identified by Nordhaus. While abatement costs are an important determinant of stakeholder positions, the political response from EU trade partners ultimately depend upon how costs are distributed, and the capacity of trade partners to bite back.

title: Common Ground: Aligning Forest Protection and the Transition Away from Fossil Fuels
summary: The transition away from fossil fuels and the protection of forests are both essential to achieving global climate goals. This UNEP policy brief examines how the two COP30 Roadmaps can be implemented together, focusing on the land-use impli
content: The transition away from fossil fuels and the protection of forests are both essential to achieving global climate goals. This UNEP policy brief examines how the two COP30 Roadmaps can be implemented together, focusing on the land-use implications of bioenergy, including biofuels, woody biomass and bioenergy with carbon capture and storage, as well as pressures from transition minerals. It explores how policy choices can prevent the energy transition from driving deforestation, forest degradation and competition for land, while recognizing the role of sustainable bioenergy in climate mitigation. The brief provides recommendations for aligning energy and land-use planning, strengthening carbon accounting and safeguards, and protecting forests, biodiversity and local livelihoods.

title: Does an improved financial eco-environment reduce marginal abatement costs? Evidence from CO₂ shadow prices across 26 Chinese provinces
summary: This study examines the nonlinear relationship between the financial eco-environment and CO₂ shadow prices and the associated transmission mechanisms from the perspective of marginal abatement costs. Using panel data from 26 Chinese provinc
content: This study examines the nonlinear relationship between the financial eco-environment and CO₂ shadow prices and the associated transmission mechanisms from the perspective of marginal abatement costs. Using panel data from 26 Chinese provinces over 2014–2024, a composite financial eco-environment index is constructed, and CO₂ shadow prices are estimated using a parametric directional distance function. The empirical analysis employs a two-way fixed-effects model, bootstrap methods, and a spatial Durbin model. The main findings are as follows. (Ⅰ) The financial eco-environment exhibits an inverted U-shaped relationship with CO₂ shadow prices. Marginal abatement costs initially increase and then decrease as the financial eco-environment improves. The estimated turning point is 0.4557, with the sample mean lying to its left. (Ⅱ) Tests of competing explanations indicate that the linear and squared terms of the financial eco-environment remain significantly positive and negative, respectively, after accounting for environmental policies, including central environmental protection inspections and national carbon market policy exposure, as well as nonlinear patterns in economic development and initial regional development conditions. The inverted U-shaped coefficient pattern remains stable. (Ⅲ) Fiscal investment in science and technology and public environmental attention represent two transmission channels associated with resource investment and public oversight, respectively. Both channels exhibit significantly positive conditional indirect effects at the sample mean of the financial eco-environment index, with the estimated effects decreasing as the index increases. (Ⅳ) The spatial marginal effects of the financial eco-environment exhibit distinct patterns. The estimated local direct and cross-regional indirect effects both decline as the financial eco-environment improves. The estimated indirect effects consistently exceed the direct effects and remain significantly positive across the representative levels examined.

title: Global overview on vehicular emission control: current strategies, effectiveness, challenges, and future research priorities
summary: Controlling vehicle emissions remains a critical challenge for improving urban air quality. Although multiple emission control strategies have been adopted worldwide, their main characteristics and outcomes remain scattered, hindering a sys
content: Controlling vehicle emissions remains a critical challenge for improving urban air quality. Although multiple emission control strategies have been adopted worldwide, their main characteristics and outcomes remain scattered, hindering a systemic understanding of what works, where, and under which conditions. This structured narrative review combines a structured literature search with an original regulatory maturity matrix, which scores programs to control vehicle emissions in 18 countries and regions and groups them by cluster analysis. The literature indicates a global convergence toward integrated regulatory frameworks that combine progressively more stringent emission standards, advanced after-treatment technologies, and improved compliance mechanisms for in-use vehicles. However, the regulatory maturity matrix shows that institutional and enforcement capacity has not kept pace with technical stringency in most programs outside the high-maturity group formed by Canada, China, the European Union, Japan, and the United States. In addition, management-based strategies, such as Low Emission Zones and fleet renewal and electrification incentives, are associated with improvements in air quality in urban centers, although observed effects are generally moderate and site-specific, and their effectiveness varies depending on enforcement capacity, infrastructure availability, and socioeconomic conditions. The evidence also suggests that coordinated, multi-instrumental approaches are more promising than isolated measures, although this conclusion relies mainly on modeling studies. By integrating scattered evidence into a unified framework, this review enhances the current understanding of emissions control policies and provides scientific support for policymakers, especially in developing regions experiencing rapid fleet growth and increasing pressures on air quality. Framework of regulatory and management approaches to vehicle emission control, combined as a complementary policy mix towards improved air quality

title: From single‑target conservation to comprehensive resource utilization: A case of VEP accounting for the eco-cultural heritage in Beijing
summary: Eco-cultural heritage faces the dilemma of transitioning from single-target conservation to comprehensive resource utilization. This study introduces the Value of Ecosystem Product in specific geographical units (VEP) theory to address this
content: Eco-cultural heritage faces the dilemma of transitioning from single-target conservation to comprehensive resource utilization. This study introduces the Value of Ecosystem Product in specific geographical units (VEP) theory to address this challenge, using Beijing’s Three Hills and Five Gardens as a case study. The research develops a three-dimensional analytical framework encompassing value identification, composite accounting, and layered transformation. Theoretically, it extends VEP from natural ecosystems to eco‑cultural composite systems by proposing a “three‑tier progressive” evaluation paradigm that distinguishes monetizable, quantifiable cultural services with partial monetization, and non‑quantifiable values, together with a “layered matching” transformation principle. This framework clarifies the identification criteria and transformation pathways for each value type while defining a normative “monetization boundary” that protects non‑tradable values from market forces. A simplified accounting of the Western Beijing rice fields is provided to illustrate the framework’s application in principle; this is a methodological demonstration rather than an empirical valuation, as it relies on secondary data and hypothetical assumptions rather than primary field surveys. The study also outlines a three-stage transformation model covering activation, appreciation, and realization, and identifies governance bottlenecks including fragmented property rights. The central argument is that value transformation should distinguish between tradable and non‑tradable values, and achieve a virtuous cycle of conservation and development through the synergy of market mechanisms and public safeguards. Policy implications are offered for the valuation and transformation of eco‑cultural heritage, though the proposed framework requires further empirical testing across diverse heritage contexts.

title: The socioeconomics of groundwater depletion and technology adoption: a mean field game and stochastic dynamics framework for rural agricultural systems
source: Journal of Applied and Advanced Research
summary: This article develops a comprehensive mathematical framework for the scenario analysis of coupled human-natural systems in rural agricultural contexts, integrating stochastic partial differential equations (SPDEs), mean field games (MFG), P
content: This article develops a comprehensive mathematical framework for the scenario analysis of coupled human-natural systems in rural agricultural contexts, integrating stochastic partial differential equations (SPDEs), mean field games (MFG), Pontryagin optimal control, dynamical systems bifurcation theory, and Bayesian nonlinear filtering into a unified analytical architecture. The system is formulated as a coupled stochastic dynamical system on a spatiotemporal domain, where a continuum of smallholder farmers strategically extract from a common-pool aquifer, adopt climate-resilient technologies through spatially nonlocal social learning, and optimize intertemporal profits under incomplete climate information. We derive the mean-field Nash equilibrium via the coupled Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman and Fokker-Planck equations, characterize the optimal switching boundary for binary technology adoption decisions, and prove existence and uniqueness of variational solutions for the groundwater and adoption SPDEs under uniform ellipticity and Lipschitz conditions. The deterministic skeleton of the coupled system is analyzed for Hopf, saddle-node, and cusp bifurcations, revealing critical thresholds for regime shifts and hysteresis in the groundwater-adoption state space. Bayesian learning is modeled through the Kushner-Stratonovich and Zakai equations, yielding adaptive expectations and a quantifiable learning premium. Scenario ensemble analysis employs quasi-Monte Carlo methods, Sobol variance decomposition, and polynomial chaos expansions to rank policy sensitivities and compute risk-adjusted outcomes. Six high-dimensional visualizations: surface plots, wireframe plots, mesh plots, and volume plots, illustrate the spatiotemporal groundwater depletion, crop yield response surfaces, Nash payoff manifolds, technology diffusion fronts, and climate-adaptation risk volumes. Policy implications include dynamically optimal groundwater pricing, adoption subsidies internalizing social learning externalities, climate information infrastructure investment, and robust decision-making under deep uncertainty.

title: Digital Solutions for Disruption Mitigation in MaaS and Automotive: A Mapping and Evaluation Framework
summary: Abstract This paper presents a dual-method approach for identifying and evaluating digital technologies that improve the resilience and sustainability of automotive and Mobility-as-a-Service (MaaS) ecosystems. The approach begins with techn
content: Abstract This paper presents a dual-method approach for identifying and evaluating digital technologies that improve the resilience and sustainability of automotive and Mobility-as-a-Service (MaaS) ecosystems. The approach begins with technology mapping, where ten digital technologies such as AI and IoT are examined for their potential to address ecosystem-specific disruptions. Technology suppliers are assessed based on resilience-improving capabilities such as adaptability, along with adoption barriers. The second part introduces an impact assessment methodology using simulation-based models to quantify the effects of disruptions and evaluate the benefits of digital technology adoption. A multi-criteria framework of KPIs is applied to measure improvements in resilience, operational efficiency, and sustainability under scenarios with and without technology implementation. These scenarios incorporate realistic supply chain risks, including energy shortages and cyberattacks. Quantitative models simulate operations, interactions, and timing within each ecosystem, enabling measurement of disruption impacts and the mitigating role of technologies. This methodology supports decision-making by linking technology capabilities to measurable performance gains.

title: A scenario-based assessment of methane mitigation technology pathways in the oil and gas sector
source: ERA: Education and Research Archive (University of Alberta)
summary: Methane is a highly potent greenhouse gas, making its mitigation one of the most effective strategies for achieving near-term climate benefits. The oil and gas sector is a dominant source of anthropogenic methane emissions, yet existing ass
content: Methane is a highly potent greenhouse gas, making its mitigation one of the most effective strategies for achieving near-term climate benefits. The oil and gas sector is a dominant source of anthropogenic methane emissions, yet existing assessments often rely on static marginal abatement cost representations or aggregated approaches that do not capture technology-specific adoption dynamics or policy-driven deployment pathways over time. This thesis develops and applies a scenario-based, bottom-up assessment framework to evaluate methane mitigation potential, technology adoption, and economic implications in the natural gas, conventional oil, and oil sands sectors through 2050. The framework integrates detailed methane emissions accounting, technology-level characterization, endogenous market-share modeling, and energy-system representation within the Low Emissions Analysis Platform (LEAP) through the LEAP-Canada model. Methane abatement measures are explicitly linked to emission sources across the oil and gas value chain and include pneumatic device upgrades, leak detection and repair (LDAR), compressor seal upgrades, vapor recovery units, green completions, and electrification measures. Technology adoption is simulated using a cost-based logit formulation that reflects relative annualized costs, carbon pricing environments, and market heterogeneity, enabling dynamic projection of technology penetration, methane emissions, cumulative mitigation, and marginal abatement costs under alternative policy scenarios. The framework is applied to Alberta, Canada’s largest oil and gas-producing jurisdiction. For the natural gas sector, methane emissions decline from 18.5 MtCO₂e in 2022 to 7.4 MtCO₂e in 2030 under zero carbon pricing (71% below 2012 levels), 6.5 MtCO₂e under a carbon price of 50 CAD/tCO₂e (74%), and 6.2 MtCO₂e under business-as-usual carbon pricing levels reaching 170 CAD/tCO₂e by 2030 (75%). By 2050, emissions decline further to 4.3 MtCO₂e (83% reduction), while maximum abatement scenarios achieve 3.0 MtCO₂e (88% reduction). Marginal abatement cost analysis shows that key measures, including pneumatic device upgrades and compressor seal upgrades, exhibit low or negative costs, while most remaining options fall below 60 CAD/tCO₂e. Methane mitigation increases natural gas supply costs by approximately 0.07 CAD/GJ, indicating limited impacts on energy affordability. For conventional oil and oil sands operations, methane emissions decline by 73% under zero carbon pricing and approximately 76% under carbon pricing scenarios by 2030, meeting Canada’s methane reduction target. By 2050, reductions reach up to 89% under maximum abatement scenarios. Across all sectors, LDAR, pneumatic device upgrades, compressor seal upgrades, and green completions account for the majority of modeled methane reductions. Sensitivity analysis indicates that results are most responsive to uncertainty in methane emission factors and technology costs. Overall, this resear

title: Plant bioluminescence for sustainable horticulture: Living biosensors, crop sentinels and precision crop monitoring
summary: Bioluminescence, although frequently framed as an ecological curiosity of fireflies, marine macrofauna and glow-in-the-dark fungi, has become a real-world tool for understanding plant biology. Over many decades, firefly luciferase-based rep
content: Bioluminescence, although frequently framed as an ecological curiosity of fireflies, marine macrofauna and glow-in-the-dark fungi, has become a real-world tool for understanding plant biology. Over many decades, firefly luciferase-based reporter systems have facilitated sensitive and quantitative measurements of gene expression, circadian rhythms and signalling in living plants. The ability to achieve bioluminescence within a single organism, where both luciferase and its substrate are produced on demand, has only recently been realised through the construction of bacterial, for example *Vibrio*, and fungal light-producing pathways. This transition is particularly relevant to agriculture and horticulture, where repeated, non-destructive monitoring can be achieved without external luciferin application. This article connects the molecular basis of different bioluminescence systems with their recent applications in crop and horticultural research. Particular focus is placed on autonomous reporters for defence hormones, pattern-triggered immunity and viral infection, sentinel plants for protected cultivation, high-throughput phenotyping and breeding, and lux-based microbial biosensors for agriculturally relevant contaminants. An ecological perspective is also important. Natural fungal bioluminescence may influence insect behaviour, while artificial light at night can disrupt plant–pollinator networks. Therefore, engineered luminous plants must be optically and ecologically characterised rather than presumed biologically neutral. Overall, bioluminescence currently holds its strongest value as an investigational and diagnostic platform rather than routine field-scale agronomic practice, where signal intensity, metabolic context, imaging conditions, genetic containment and regulatory acceptance remain major limitations.

title: Climate Change Is a Class Question: Against the Depoliticization of Green Transition
summary: The dominant paradigm of the ‘green transition’ often frames climate change mitigation as a technocratic, managerial, and market-oriented endeavor. By emphasizing carbon pricing, technological innovation, investment, and individual consumpt
content: The dominant paradigm of the ‘green transition’ often frames climate change mitigation as a technocratic, managerial, and market-oriented endeavor. By emphasizing carbon pricing, technological innovation, investment, and individual consumption, some forms of climate governance can obscure the structural distribution of responsibility, vulnerability, ownership, and political power. This review argues that climate change is fundamentally a class question—not because class provides an exhaustive explanation of ecological crisis or political responses but because class relations constitute a major dimension through which responsibility, vulnerability, ownership, labour, resources, and political influence are distributed and contested. Drawing on critical political economy, eco-Marxism, ecological economics, degrowth scholarship, and climate-justice research, we examine five interconnected dimensions: (1) asymmetric responsibilities and vulnerabilities; (2) the political economy and materiality of green capitalism; (3) the distribution of transition costs and benefits; (4) the institutional conditions of a democratic ecological transformation; and (5) the political mediation of climate conflict, including green backlash. We critically engage competing perspectives on green growth, decoupling, market instruments, technological innovation, and compensatory just-transition policies. We conclude that re-politicizing the green transition requires attention to class power, democratic control, redistribution, social protection, participation, and the institutional conditions under which different transition mechanisms operate.

title: Advancing hybrid renewable energy systems integrated with gas turbine and energy storage in Bangladesh: A multi-objective optimization approach
summary: The rapid expansion of solar photovoltaic (PV) and wind power is essential for reducing the carbon intensity of electricity supply; however, their weather-driven variability creates reliability challenges that require flexible generation an
content: The rapid expansion of solar photovoltaic (PV) and wind power is essential for reducing the carbon intensity of electricity supply; however, their weather-driven variability creates reliability challenges that require flexible generation and storage. This study develops and optimizes a utility-scale hybrid renewable energy system for Bangladesh integrating PV, wind, a hydrogen-fueled gas turbine, hydrogen storage through an electrolyzer-compressor-storage chain, and battery energy storage. Three cases are evaluated using hourly meteorological and load data: PV-wind-gas turbine; PV-wind-gas turbine with hydrogen storage; and PV-wind-gas turbine with combined hydrogen and battery storage. System sizing is formulated as a multi-objective optimization problem minimizing levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) and total CO₂ emissions and is solved using NSGA-II, CMOPSO, and MOEA/D, with performance assessed using standard metrics. Case 1 achieves a minimum LCOE of about 0.051 $/kWh but retains emissions above 6.5 × 10⁵ t CO₂/yr. Case 2 reduces emissions to about 4.6 × 10⁵ t CO₂/yr, although LCOE exceeds 0.13 $/kWh. Case 3 provides the best overall compromise, with a minimum LCOE of about 0.046 $/kWh and balanced solutions achieving 10–15% lower emissions than Case 1 at 0.057–0.063 $/kWh. Across the three scenarios, CMOPSO delivers the strongest overall search results. Sensitivity analysis shows that component costs, discount rate, and hardware efficiencies strongly influence the cost-emission trade-off, whereas moderate renewable-resource variations have comparatively limited effects on the Pareto front. In order to assess long-term reliability, future work should incorporate explicit component degradation, supply contingencies, additional renewable resources, and grid-market interactions.

title: Forest Carbon Benefit–Cost Analysis and Carbon Pricing Simulation Decision-Support Tool (Vietnamese)
summary: The Forest Carbon Benefit–Cost Analysis Tool is a Vietnamese-translated Excel-based decision-support model for Vietnam that compares a proposed forest carbon project with the current land-use activity and estimates the break-even carbon pri
content: The Forest Carbon Benefit–Cost Analysis Tool is a Vietnamese-translated Excel-based decision-support model for Vietnam that compares a proposed forest carbon project with the current land-use activity and estimates the break-even carbon price required for the project to become economically viable. It combines project costs, opportunity costs, carbon-credit generation, market participation costs and financial metrics to support transparent scenario and investment analysis.

title: A review on the efficiency of liquid complex fertilizers – comparative analysis with conventional fertilizers and assessment of their biological and agronomic effects
source: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology
summary: This study investigates the impact of complex liquid fertilizers on soil properties, nutrient absorption, and crop yield. The results demonstrate that liquid fertilizers significantly enhance soil fertility, increasing pH from 6.1 to 6.5, o
