summary: Abstract The safety of gob-side entry retaining (GER) in fully mechanized top coal caving (FMTC) panels involves the interacting evolution of surrounding rock deformation, roadside backfill body (RBB) damage, air leakage, oxygen migration,
content: Abstract The safety of gob-side entry retaining (GER) in fully mechanized top coal caving (FMTC) panels involves the interacting evolution of surrounding rock deformation, roadside backfill body (RBB) damage, air leakage, oxygen migration, and residual coal oxidation. However, the mechanical origin of leakage channel formation and its connection with spontaneous combustion risk remain insufficiently clarified. This study investigates the 090515 working face of Duanwang Coal Mine and develops a fracture-mediated framework linking top coal–RBB load transfer, RBB damage evolution, goaf air leakage, oxygen distribution, and carbon monoxide (CO) response. An analytical load-transfer model was established to clarify the role of top coal in the local bearing system, while three-dimensional discrete-element simulation was used to examine RBB fracture development and structural degradation. Sulfur hexafluoride (SF6) tracer tests were conducted to quantify the spatial attenuation of goaf air leakage, and laboratory oxidation tests and field gas monitoring were used to identify the site-specific oxidation-prone zone. The results indicate that insufficient top coal stiffness and progressive RBB damage are associated with deterioration of the local bearing and sealing system, while stronger leakage is observed in the near-face region. The measured SF6-derived apparent leakage velocity decreases with distance from the working face, allowing the leakage field to be divided into a high-variability zone, a transitional-attenuation zone, and a relatively stable low-velocity zone. Based on closed oxygen consumption tests and field gas monitoring, the 12–18% oxygen concentration range was adopted as a site-specific criterion for identifying the oxidation-prone zone in the 090515 goaf. Field application indicates that the integrated control strategy was associated with reduced roadway deformation and a short-term decrease in CO concentration during the available monitoring period. The findings provide a field-supported basis for coordinated control of surrounding rock stability and spontaneous combustion risk in FMTC conditions with GER.

title: Dual-task graph attention learning for stress-responsive gene regulatory network inference in Panax notoginseng
summary: Panax notoginseng is an important specialty crop and geo-authentic medicinal plant vulnerable to multiple stresses, with its stress responses regulated by complex gene regulatory networks. Limited species-specific regulatory evidence and sa
content: Panax notoginseng is an important specialty crop and geo-authentic medicinal plant vulnerable to multiple stresses, with its stress responses regulated by complex gene regulatory networks. Limited species-specific regulatory evidence and sample size make systematic analysis of transcription factor (TF)-target relationships difficult. We developed a dual-task graph attention network (DTGAT) with a shared graph attention encoder and joint optimization of link prediction and expression reconstruction for regulatory relationship prediction. DTGAT was first evaluated in Arabidopsis thaliana for methodological validation. On the independent test set, link prediction achieved an AUC of 0.9106 and an AUPR of 0.8933, while expression reconstruction achieved an R² of 0.8375 and a PCC of 0.9152; link prediction outperformed the evaluated baselines. DTGAT was then applied to transcriptomic data from stressed P. notoginseng together with a homology-mapped prior network, yielding 55,108 high-confidence candidate regulatory edges. Promoter motif analysis further provided sequence-level support for 22 newly predicted candidate regulatory relationships associated with stress responses. Published experimental evidence supported the biological plausibility of the candidate MYB–CCoAOMT relationship. These findings highlight the utility of DTGAT for prioritizing stress-responsive regulatory candidates in non-model medicinal plants.

title: Sustainable Paving Binder Alternatives Obtained via Thermochemical Processing of Biomass
summary: Abstract The transition to low-carbon transport infrastructure requires sustainable alternatives to petroleum-based bitumen that are technically viable and compatible with circular economy principles. This study investigates wholly bio-base
content: Abstract The transition to low-carbon transport infrastructure requires sustainable alternatives to petroleum-based bitumen that are technically viable and compatible with circular economy principles. This study investigates wholly bio-based paving binders produced via thermochemical conversion of biomass and industrial waste. Spirulina algae were processed by hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL), yielding a hydrophobic bio-crude with an average yield of 37.9 wt.% (dry basis), while industrial waste sludge was converted by pyrolysis followed by thermal evaporation, producing a bio-binder fraction corresponding to 2.2 wt.% of the original biomass. Rheological behavior was evaluated using Dynamic Shear Rheometer frequency sweep tests, and master curves of complex shear modulus (|G*|) and phase angle (δ) were constructed over temperatures of 20–70 °C and frequencies from 0.1 to 10 Hz. The sludge-derived binder exhibited |G*| values comparable to the conventional 50/70 bitumen, with δ values typically between 55° and 75°. The algae-derived binder showed higher stiffness and lower phase angles (≈50–60°) at low reduced frequencies, approaching the behavior of polymer-modified bitumen. These results demonstrate that thermochemically derived bio-binders can achieve bitumen-like rheological performance, supporting their use as partial extenders or functional components in circular asphalt systems. Further research is required to assess long-term aging and environmental compatibility.

title: Cracking, Chloride Transport, and Functional Recovery in Slag-Based Alkali-Activated Materials: A Review
source: International Journal of Concrete Structures and Materials
summary: Slag-based alkali-activated materials can develop favorable initial strength and chloride resistance; however, these properties do not establish their performance after cracking or healing. This critical review examines the activation chemi
content: Slag-based alkali-activated materials can develop favorable initial strength and chloride resistance; however, these properties do not establish their performance after cracking or healing. This critical review examines the activation chemistry, fracture, transport, and recovery across intact, damaged, and healed states. Published evidence is synthesized based on the material scale, exposure history, measured function, and reference conditions. Three within-study data visualizations illustrate why total porosity cannot replace pore size information, why electrical and diffusion measurements require separate interpretation, and why resonant frequency and tensile responses cannot be combined into a single healing percentage. Reinforced-beam studies have further shown that a comparable load capacity does not necessarily imply comparable crack widths or stiffnesses. Healing is evaluated separately based on the surface closure, internal sealing, water transport, chloride transport, and mechanical response. The analysis identifies a particular validation need in terms of the connection between healed cracks, chloride exposure at the reinforcement level, and independently corroborated steel conditions. An assessment framework and experimental priorities are proposed to test this connection under matched aging, realistic exposure, and reopening conditions. The resulting design perspective treats the initial matrix quality, resistance to damage, and recovery of a specified function as related objectives that require distinct evidence. Benefits for reinforcement protection or service life remain conditional where these links have not been established.

title: Understanding distribution patterns of secondary inorganic aerosols in two distinct environments through statistical learning
summary: Abstract. Sulfate and nitrate are major components of fine particulate matter, yet their concentration patterns and associated environmental factors remain insufficiently understood across contrasting environments. We analyzed observations
content: Abstract. Sulfate and nitrate are major components of fine particulate matter, yet their concentration patterns and associated environmental factors remain insufficiently understood across contrasting environments. We analyzed observations from urban Beijing, China (2018–2022), and the boreal forest in Hyytiälä, Finland (2018–2021). Gaussian mixture modeling and partial least squares discriminant analysis were combined to identify concentration regimes and assess the relative importance of environmental variables. Both compounds exhibited unimodal, lognormal-like concentration distributions in Hyytiälä and multimodal distributions in Beijing. In Beijing, concentrations of both compounds declined over the study period. From low to high concentration regimes, the relative importance of predictors shifted from gaseous precursors to air mass transport and relative humidity. This study provides a transferable statistical framework for characterizing aerosol pollution regimes and their associated environmental conditions.

title: Reinforcement Corrosion in Coral Aggregate Concrete: 20-Month In-Situ Comparison of Portland, Magnesium Phosphate, and Hybrid Fly Ash–Silica Fume Binders in the South China Sea
source: Journal of Marine Science and Engineering
summary: Reinforcement corrosion is a governing durability concern for coral aggregate concrete (CAC) structures in the South China Sea, yet long-term field evidence comparing alternative binder systems under natural marine exposure remains scarce.
content: Reinforcement corrosion is a governing durability concern for coral aggregate concrete (CAC) structures in the South China Sea, yet long-term field evidence comparing alternative binder systems under natural marine exposure remains scarce. This study reports a 20-month in-situ exposure campaign on a natural reef-flat platform in Zhanjiang Bay, in which HRB400 carbon steel and 316L stainless steel rebars were embedded in CAC prepared with Portland cement (PC), magnesium phosphate cement (MPC), and a hybrid fly ash–silica fume binder (HF) at a fixed water-to-binder ratio of 0.30. Open-circuit potential was monitored over early (0–5 months), middle (5–12 months), and late (12–20 months) exposure windows, and potentiodynamic polarization was measured at three snapshot ages (month 5; months 12–14; months 19–20), complemented by rapid chloride migration testing, XRD, and SEM–EDS. The corrosion behavior of carbon steel was strongly binder-dependent. In the MPC matrix, carbon steel underwent severe early-stage activation (icorr = 7.92 µA/cm2, equivalent to 91.9 µm/y), which is attributed to the near-neutral pore solution of the portlandite-free K-struvite matrix; the corrosion rate subsequently decreased by more than four orders of magnitude, a trend consistent with a transition toward transport-limited kinetics rather than a restoration of passivity. The HF binder yielded the lowest chloride migration coefficient (0.171 × 10−12 m2/s) and sustained low corrosion rates of carbon steel, plausibly reflecting pozzolanic pore refinement and chloride binding. 316L stainless steel remained below the RILEM TC 154-EMC passivity threshold (0.1 µA/cm2) in all three binders. These results suggest that binder–reinforcement compatibility, rather than matrix density alone, governs the long-term corrosion performance of CAC in reef-flat environments.

title: Proteomic profiles of uterine flushing fluid during the estrous cycle and early pregnancy in sheep
summary: Introduction The objective was to profile the uterine flushing fluid (UFF) proteome during the estrous cycle and early pregnancy and to identify potential candidate proteins associated with early pregnancy in Central Anatolian Merino ewes.
content: Introduction The objective was to profile the uterine flushing fluid (UFF) proteome during the estrous cycle and early pregnancy and to identify potential candidate proteins associated with early pregnancy in Central Anatolian Merino ewes. Methods UFF samples were collected from a total of 24 ewes on days 12 (pre-implantation period; P12, n = 4), 16 (implantation period; P16, n = 4) and 22 (post-implantation period; P22, n = 4) of pregnancy, and on their corresponding days (C12, C16, C22, n = 4 per group) of the estrous cycle and proteins were quantified by label-free LC–MS/MS. Results Of 2,020 quantified proteins, 1,616 were tested in each comparison (1,212 on day 22). Data were preprocessed using MetaboAnalyst 6.0, groups were compared with Student’s t -tests, and p -values were adjusted by the Benjamini–Hochberg method; because some proteins reached q < 0.05, proteins with unadjusted p < 0.05 and a fold change ≥1.5 or ≤0.67 were reported as nominally significant. Partial least squares discriminant analysis (PLS-DA) showed partial, overlapping separation between cyclic and pregnant groups along component 1 (44.2% of variance), driven mainly on days 16 and 22. In the pooled comparison, 368 proteins were nominally significant, and pairwise comparisons identified 46, 199, and 226 nominally significant proteins on days 12, 16, and 22, respectively. Most proteins were less abundant in pregnant UFF than in cyclic UFF, including ALAD (20.5-fold in cyclic ewes in the pooled comparison), whereas interleukin-1 receptor type 2 was approximately 17-fold more abundant in pregnant UFF on day 16. Enrichment analysis highlighted proteolysis and proteasome, nucleotide, amino acid, and fatty acid metabolism, and interleukin-1 signaling. Discussion Our exploratory findings suggest that uterine luminal fluid composition changes mainly from day 16 onward and identify candidate proteins associated with early pregnancy that require validation in larger studies.

title: A Critical Investigation of Hydrogen-Based Decarbonization Pathways for Africa’s Heavy Industries
source: International Journal of Energy Research Science and Engineering
summary: This paper examines the hydrogen potential as a means of decarbonization for heavy industries in Africa as a continent, focusing on its crucial role as an alternative to fossil fuels across several industries. It also evaluates hydrogen and
content: This paper examines the hydrogen potential as a means of decarbonization for heavy industries in Africa as a continent, focusing on its crucial role as an alternative to fossil fuels across several industries. It also evaluates hydrogen and its paramount role in the world decarbonization agenda with a focus on the economic and environmental effects. More specifically, hydrogen production pathways from renewable energy, for example, solar and wind energy, highlighting its gain in reducing carbon emissions and supporting a sustainable energy future. Furthermore, it evaluates the techno-economic assessment of the hydrogen production pathway in Africa. The review also highlights institutional, economic, and technical barriers and the essential infrastructure for the production and storage of hydrogen, specifically in the area of accomplishing the agenda for global energy transition. In addition, the study also emphasizes the importance of governmental policies and financial considerations as drivers of adoption of hydrogen technologies. The study concludes by outlining the future outlook and strategic recommendations for the transformative potential of hydrogen in decarbonizing key sectors, for example, the chemical industry, long-distance transportation, and heavy industry, such as the cement and steel industries. It depicts a remarkable contribution of hydrogen to a low-carbon global energy system and provides valuable insights into the role of hydrogen as a decarbonization pathway in Africa for heavy industries.

title: Accessibility and Sustainability in the Facial Paralysis and Facial Reanimation Journey: A Scoping Review
summary: Aims and Backgrounds Healthcare is a major global carbon emitter, driven by surgical waste, pharmaceutical inefficiencies, and long patient travel. Facial paralysis management requires complex, multidisciplinary care where delays degrade ou
content: Aims and Backgrounds Healthcare is a major global carbon emitter, driven by surgical waste, pharmaceutical inefficiencies, and long patient travel. Facial paralysis management requires complex, multidisciplinary care where delays degrade outcomes. This review synthesizes literature on sustainability and accessibility across the facial paralysis care continuum to formulate evidence-based clinical recommendations. Patient Selection Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, PubMed, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, and Scopus were searched through June 2026 using PICOS criteria to evaluate telemedicine, multidisciplinary care, ambulatory surgery, low-resource surgical alternatives, and vial protocols. Techniques Virtual visits reduced follow-up times by ~50% and costs up to 79.8% while maintaining high satisfaction. Multidisciplinary clinic models consolidated care, reducing provider visits (4.8 vs. 6.8; P < .01) and charges by 50%. Ambulatory surgical centers (ASCs) lowered costs by 26% and reduced readmissions relative to inpatient settings. Temporalis tendon transfer (TTT) and selective neurolysis offer single-stage, low-resource outpatient alternatives to complex microvascular procedures. Multi-patient botulinum toxin vial-sharing protocols successfully mitigated pharmaceutical waste with negligible complication rates. Conclusions and Clinical Relevance Transitioning toward digital health, multidisciplinary pathways, ambulatory routing, and optimized pharmaceutical protocols enhances sustainability and geographic access while preserving high-quality clinical outcomes.

title: Variational Physics-Informed Neural Networks on a Wheel-Rail Contact: A Sustainable and Intelligent Accelerated Computing Approach
summary: Abstract Railway transportation is a sustainable industrial sector in continuous evolution with integrated AI and digitalisation to increase passenger safety while facilitating railway personnel in maintenance decisions. This study introduc
content: Abstract Railway transportation is a sustainable industrial sector in continuous evolution with integrated AI and digitalisation to increase passenger safety while facilitating railway personnel in maintenance decisions. This study introduces a Variational Physics-Informed Neural Network (VPINN) technique implemented with the PhysicsNeMo framework, that combines physics knowledge with machine learning within the Scientific Machine Learning paradigm. The major cost of current AI is energy consumption for training large models and data, raising concerns about environmental impact. VPINN addresses key limitations of conventional Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) through integration by parts to reduce differential operator orders, requiring lower solution regularity and improving stability, which in turn lowers computational cost, energy use and associated carbon footprint. The work targets a research gap in the railway sector, where PINN applications remain limited compared to sectors, e.g. aerospace and automotive. We focus on learning the train wheel geometry and wheel–rail contact conditions by enforcing geometry constraints in the loss function. The proposed method enables more efficient, sustainable, accelerated physics-based ML computation on High-Performance Computing clusters and delivers more interpretable prognostic parameters, e.g. wheel stress and displacement fields under train loads, in line with EU transport policy priorities and ISO/EN standards.

title: Economic Implications of Low-Emission Technology Adoption in Brazil’s Power Sector
summary: The power sector is expected to play a key role in achieving Brazil’s 2050 climate neutrality goal, including through economy-wide electrification. This paper evaluates the economic and system-level impacts of deploying low-emission technol
content: The power sector is expected to play a key role in achieving Brazil’s 2050 climate neutrality goal, including through economy-wide electrification. This paper evaluates the economic and system-level impacts of deploying low-emission technologies in Brazil’s electricity sector under two net-zero pathways: a renewable-dominated transition and a thermal pathway based on carbon capture and storage (CCS). The analysis combines a high-resolution power system model (AURORA) with a macroeconometric, demand-led integrated assessment model (E3ME-FTT) that captures both hourly operational constraints and macroeconomic feedback. Both pathways achieve the complete decarbonization of the power sector by 2041, delivering cumulative emissions reductions of 936–985 MtCO2 relative to a reference scenario. Both pathways also generate positive absolute GDP growth. However, their performance relative to the Reference scenario diverges substantially. The Renewable-Dominated scenario consistently outperforms the Reference, with GDP up to 1.2% higher and employment up to 0.5% higher in 2050, and delivers a cumulative GDP gain of US$2015 1.8 trillion, measured as the sum of annual deviations from the Reference scenario over 2026–2050. The Thermal CCS scenario delivers a modest positive GDP deviation relative to the Reference in the near term (2026–2032), but turns GDP-negative relative to the Reference from approximately 2032 onwards, reaching a 1.4% shortfall by 2050, driven by persistent import dependence on CCS capital goods and higher operating costs. Its cumulative GDP deviation from the Reference is US$2015 1.7 trillion lower than the Renewable-Dominated scenario. Overall, these findings challenge the view that deep decarbonization entails economic costs, although outcomes depend strongly on the chosen technology mix and associated trade and investment structures.

title: Mechanotransduction in Liver Fibrosis: Sinusoidal Remodeling, Mechanometabolic Coupling, and Therapeutic Implications
summary: Liver fibrosis has traditionally been interpreted through biochemical pathways driven by chronic injury, inflammation, metabolic stress, and profibrotic cytokine signaling. However, fibrotic progression also involves mechanical remodeling o
content: Liver fibrosis has traditionally been interpreted through biochemical pathways driven by chronic injury, inflammation, metabolic stress, and profibrotic cytokine signaling. However, fibrotic progression also involves mechanical remodeling of the hepatic microenvironment. This review examines mechanotransduction in liver fibrosis, with particular emphasis on the sinusoidal niche as a mechanically responsive interface. During chronic liver injury, liver sinusoidal endothelial cell defenestration, altered shear stress, extracellular matrix deposition, and remodeling of the space of Disse modify the physical environment encountered by hepatocytes, hepatic stellate cells, macrophages, and endothelial cells. These changes are transmitted through integrins, focal adhesions, Rho-ROCK-dependent cytoskeletal tension, YAP/TAZ and MRTF-A/SRF signaling, mechanosensitive ion channels, and nuclear mechanotransduction, linking matrix mechanics to fibrogenic transcription, vascular dysfunction, and tissue stiffening. Specifically, in MASLD/MASH, lipid droplet expansion, hepatocyte nuclear deformation, perisinusoidal micro-stiffness, sinusoidal distortion, and increased intrahepatic resistance provide a disease-specific example of metabolic-mechanical coupling. MetALD/ALD add a membrane-level dimension, as alcohol exposure produces compartment-specific remodeling of plasma and organelle membranes and disrupts hepatocyte-extracellular matrix coupling. However, a direct membrane-fluidity-to-fibrosis pathway remains unproven. Clinically, vibration-controlled transient elastography and magnetic resonance elastography translate tissue-level mechanical changes into measurable information for fibrosis staging, monitoring, and risk stratification. This perspective also broadens antifibrotic strategies beyond collagen accumulation to include matrix cross-linking, cell-matrix mechanosensing, cytoskeletal contractility, nuclear mechanotransduction, and sinusoidal dysfunction. By integrating sinusoidal mechanics, cellular force transmission, clinical stiffness assessment, and therapeutic development, this review provides a mechanobiological framework to understand liver fibrosis and refine antifibrotic strategies.

title: Risk-aware digital twin maintenance of fiber-optic environmental monitoring infrastructure: a reproducible simulation study
summary: Introduction Digital twins can support maintenance of environmental monitoring infrastructure, but dependable decisions require consistent treatment of uncertain condition, usable sensing service, and intervention timing. Methods In this st
content: Introduction Digital twins can support maintenance of environmental monitoring infrastructure, but dependable decisions require consistent treatment of uncertain condition, usable sensing service, and intervention timing. Methods In this study, we develop a risk-aware maintenance framework for a synthetic fiber-optic monitoring network. An assumed-density state estimator keeps an unbounded Gaussian working state separate from bounded physical condition. Exact moments of a thresholded service map support a one-step, moment-based coverage screen, while paired counterfactual rollouts estimate the incremental value of preventive actions using the same service and cost model as physical evaluation. The implemented heuristic combines coverage restoration with positive-value action selection; it is not assigned a global optimality guarantee. A fully executable benchmark contains 120 logical maintenance units, four hypothetical hazard contexts, and a 180-month horizon. Results Across 80 paired evaluation seeds, the proposed policy maintains the nominal coverage floor at lower scenario cost than reactive maintenance and an independently calibrated condition threshold. This comparison is conditional on synthetic deterioration, maintenance-cost, and consequence assumptions; it is not an estimate of savings for an operating network. However, cheaper policies without a service-floor constraint provide less service, and the calibrated condition policy provides higher mean coverage. Uncertainty removal and unmodeled process dependence cause coverage shortfalls despite passing internal screens. Additional valuation and stronger-dependence checks examine the limits of the nominal comparison. Exhaustive small-network checks also identify two cases in which greedy selection misses an attainable screening condition. Discussion These results demonstrate a reproducible decision architecture and explicit cost–service trade offs, not field-validated early-warning performance or transferable economic savings.

title: Origin, biogeochemistry and carbon sequestration potential of earth mounds in floodplain wetlands of the Agulhas Plain, South Africa
summary: This paper documents the origin, biogeochemistry and carbon sequestration potential of a low-relief mound pattern on the Wiesdrift Floodplain, a critically endangered renosterveld wetland complex at the southernmost tip of Africa. Mound pat
content: This paper documents the origin, biogeochemistry and carbon sequestration potential of a low-relief mound pattern on the Wiesdrift Floodplain, a critically endangered renosterveld wetland complex at the southernmost tip of Africa. Mound pattern and morphology were investigated through geospatial analysis of a 0.5 m resolution LiDAR digital terrain model and orthophoto overlay and geostatistical analysis of mound spatial density and dispersal. Mound formation and chemical sedimentation dynamics were investigated through field sampling and laboratory analyses of physical and chemical characteristics of mound and interspace sediment, surface water and shallow (<1.5 m) groundwater samples, observations of floodplain inundation and flow patterns, description of a local hillslope-to-floodplain soil transition, and observations of floodplain biota. Mound formation on the floodplain is initiated by interactions between vegetation patches and physical (aeolian and fluvial) processes, which facilitate occupation by a harvester ant species and other biota requiring refuge from disturbance, and is subsequently enhanced and sustained by a combination of physical and chemical sedimentation processes. Calcite nodules started forming on the floodplain during the post-LGM marine transgression, coinciding with a transition to warmer and more climatically variable Holocene conditions, and along with biologically-processed buried organic matter, represent an important long-term store of relatively durable carbon in a setting where episodic drought and fire precludes widespread long-term surface organic matter accumulation. Further research is needed to understand processes and spatial patterns of carbon distribution in order to develop reliable estimates of long-term carbon storage for Wiesdrift and similar dryland wetlands. As soil inorganic carbon stocks are effectively irrecoverable over the lifetime of our current civilisation, there is a need for the South African wetland community to pay equal attention to renosterveld wetlands as has been paid to organic carbon-rich wetlands in other parts of the Cape Floristic Region.

title: Iron L-shell opacity measurements under solar convection zone conditions
summary: Abstract We report spectrally resolved measurements of iron $L$-shell opacity in a high-energy-density plasma produced by a Z-pinch dynamic hohlraum. An Fe/Al mixed sample is volumetrically heated by a $\sim6$~ns quasi-Planckian x-ray drive
content: Abstract We report spectrally resolved measurements of iron $L$-shell opacity in a high-energy-density plasma produced by a Z-pinch dynamic hohlraum. An Fe/Al mixed sample is volumetrically heated by a $\sim6$~ns quasi-Planckian x-ray drive and probed by a $\sim2$~ns backlighter pulse, both generated by the dynamic hohlraum, with the backlighter radiation at stagnation. Simultaneous single-shot measurements of Fe $L$-shell and Al $K$-shell absorption spectra provide self-consistent plasma diagnostics, yielding plasma conditions near $T_{\mathrm{e}}=115$~eV and $n_{\mathrm{e}}=1.4\times10^{22}$~cm$^{-3}$. The Fe $L$-shell opacity is determined from the measured transmission and compared with DCA--UTA and PrismSPECT calculations. These measurements open a new experimental window for opacity studies in the previously unexplored 100--150~eV hot-dense-matter regime relevant to stellar interiors.

title: Influence of Project Risk Management Practices on Performance of E-mobility Implementation Projects in Gasabo District, Rwanda
source: Journal of Research Innovation and Implications in Education
summary: This study examined the influence of Risk Management Practices on the performance of e-mobility implementation projects in Gasabo District, Rwanda. Specifically, the study assessed the influence of Risk Transfer practices on ProjectPerforma
content: This study examined the influence of Risk Management Practices on the performance of e-mobility implementation projects in Gasabo District, Rwanda. Specifically, the study assessed the influence of Risk Transfer practices on ProjectPerformance.The study adopted a descriptive and explanatory research design using a mixed-methods approach.The target population comprised 317 respondents, from which a sample size of 177 respondents was selected.Data were collected using structured questionnaires and semi-structured interviews and analyzed using SPSS.Descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation analysis, and simple linear regression analysis were used to examine the relationship and influence of Risk Transfer practices on Project Performance.The findings showed that insurance policies were used to minimize project risks, contractual agreements clearly defined risk responsibilities among stakeholders, outsourcing specialized services helped reduce operational risks, and risk-sharing mechanisms improved project stability.Correlation analysis indicated a strong positive relationship between Risk Transfer practices and Project Performance (r = .696,p < .001).Regression analysis further showed that Risk Transfer practices significantly influenced Project Performance, explaining 48.4% of its variation.The study concluded that Risk Transfer practices play an important role in improving the performance of e-mobility implementation projects.The study recommends strengthening insurance coverage, contractual risk allocation, outsourcing of specialized services, and risk-sharing mechanisms to enhance Project Performance in Gasabo District.

title: A 10-Year Carbon Lookback: A Framework to Quantify GWP Savings from Proactive Pavement Maintenance on Ireland’s National Road Network
summary: Abstract The transportation sector significantly contributes to greenhouse gas emissions, not only through vehicle use but also via the embodied carbon in infrastructure construction and maintenance. This paper presents the framework develo
content: Abstract The transportation sector significantly contributes to greenhouse gas emissions, not only through vehicle use but also via the embodied carbon in infrastructure construction and maintenance. This paper presents the framework developed for a 10-Year Carbon Lookback Analysis of Transport Infrastructure Ireland (TII) pavement improvement projects on the national road network (2014–2024), quantifying Global Warming Potential (GWP) savings from proactive maintenance. The developed methodology compares Actual GWP, derived from measured traffic and pavement condition data, with Notional GWP, representing emissions, had no interventions occurred. Key components of the methodology include User GWP, linked to vehicle emissions affected by surface quality, and Backlog GWP, capturing the latent carbon cost of deferred maintenance. Preliminary results show substantial GWP reductions are possible due to smoother surfaces lowering rolling resistance and optimizing the plan for carbon-intensive rehabilitation. The aim of application of the methodology is to project benefits to 2035, incorporating traffic growth, deterioration modelling, and future emission factors. A key innovation of the methodology is the integration of Backlog GWP to quantify emissions avoided through timely interventions. This framework presented in the paper will enable transport agencies to assess long-term carbon outcomes of maintenance strategies, supporting the integration of carbon accounting into asset management.

title: Climate impacts of transitioning shipping fuel
summary: Abstract Switching marine fuels reduces carbon emissions while altering the short-lived atmospheric species that influence climate change. Here we assess such effects by running Earth system model simulations with globally resolved well-to-
content: Abstract Switching marine fuels reduces carbon emissions while altering the short-lived atmospheric species that influence climate change. Here we assess such effects by running Earth system model simulations with globally resolved well-to-wake shipping emission as input. Comparing global shipping run on very-low-sulfur fuel oil, high-pressure liquefied natural gas, and blue ammonia with 2019 marine fuel mix, all alternatives reduce global sulfate burden most strongly along Northern Hemisphere shipping corridors and downwind continental regions; LNG and blue ammonia additionally reduce black carbon. Reduced aerosol availability leads to lower cloud droplet number concentration and consequently weaker shortwave cloud cooling. The resulting net top-of-atmosphere radiative response to fuel substitutions ranges from 0.19 to 0.34 W m − 2 , with the strongest responses over subtropical oceans. Despite similar sulfate reductions, LNG produces the weakest radiative response, whereas blue ammonia produces the strongest, highlighting the influence of co-emitted species and cloud sensitivity beyond sulfur alone.

title: Vegetation and water level-dependent emission factors for moist to wet bog peatlands in Germany
summary: Drained peatlands and other organic soils are important sources of greenhouse gases (GHGs) in many countries. They are included in national GHG inventories, which necessitates transparent and consistent upscaling methods. Focussing on moist
content: Drained peatlands and other organic soils are important sources of greenhouse gases (GHGs) in many countries. They are included in national GHG inventories, which necessitates transparent and consistent upscaling methods. Focussing on moist to wet sites on bog peat without or with low-intensity agricultural use in Germany, we developed an emission model based on published annual carbon dioxide and methane budgets. Vegetation influences GHG emissions directly, but also indicates site conditions. Vegetation data on a national scale in Germany, albeit mostly for areas of nature conservation interest, is available as biotope type data. Thus, eight aggregated biotope types are used as explanatory variables alongside water level (WL) and other site characteristics. Results are simplified to implied emission factors (IEF) for each vegetation type to be used when other information is unavailable. Annual GHG emissions differ between vegetation types and are modulated by WL and, for carbon dioxide only, temperature. However, Sphagnum paludiculture and sparsely vegetated bog sites show low methane emissions irrespective of WL. Overall, GHG emissions were highest for moist grasslands. IEF indicate net GHG emissions for all vegetation types, but semi-natural and Eriophorum -dominated sites were small carbon sinks. Developing moist grassland towards Sphagnum paludiculture or semi-natural vegetation will thus consistently be beneficial for climate change mitigation. Limited data availability increases uncertainties especially for sparsely vegetated bogs and treed areas, and prevents the calculation of separate IEF for transition mires and mountain bogs. Nevertheless, our results allow estimating bog GHG emissions over large areas and for different land-use scenarios.

title: Solvation-driven charge redistribution in high-voltage polyether electrolytes
summary: Polyether electrolytes (PPEs) are promising for high-voltage lithium-metal batteries (LMBs) because of their good electrode wettability, continuous Li+ transport pathways, and favorable compatibility with lithium metal. However, their appli
content: Polyether electrolytes (PPEs) are promising for high-voltage lithium-metal batteries (LMBs) because of their good electrode wettability, continuous Li+ transport pathways, and favorable compatibility with lithium metal. However, their application above 4.3 V is limited by electron-rich ether oxygen (EO) sites, oxidation-prone terminal groups, and unfavorable Li+-EO coordination. Increasing evidence indicates that high-voltage instability cannot be attributed solely to terminal-group oxidation, but is closely related to the coupling between Li+ solvation and the local electronic structure of EO. In this review, we introduce solvation-driven charge redistribution as a unifying framework for understanding and designing high-voltage PPEs. We discuss how regulation of Li+-EO-anion coordination can redistribute or homogenize electron density around EO sites, reduce excessive Li+-polyether interactions, lower the oxidative activity of the polyether backbone, and simultaneously influence Li+ transport and interphase chemistry. Recent molecular strategies, including solvation-regulating cross-linkers, weakly solvating cyclic-ether monomers, electron-withdrawing functional units, and optimization of the Li+/EO coordination environment, are systematically analyzed within this framework. Particular attention is given to the connection between bulk solvation/electronic structure and the formation of inorganic-rich electrode-electrolyte interphases. Finally, we discuss the mechanistic evidence, current limitations, and practical design requirements for translating these concepts into high-voltage LMBs.

title: Process-Informed Latent-State Discovery and Interpretable Ensemble Learning for Full-Scale Wastewater Treatment Monitoring
source: OIDA International Journal of Sustainable Development
summary: Abstract: Reliable wastewater treatment monitoring requires methods that convert multivariate sensor streams into operationally meaningful states. This study proposes a process-informed, cluster-guided framework integrating unsupervised reg
content: Abstract: Reliable wastewater treatment monitoring requires methods that convert multivariate sensor streams into operationally meaningful states. This study proposes a process-informed, cluster-guided framework integrating unsupervised regime discovery, semantic state labeling, and interpretable tree-based classification. Online hydraulic, aeration, thermal, dissolved-oxygen, nitrate, and ammonium data from the full-scale Tilburg wastewater treatment plant were analyzed. Clustering identified four recurrent conditions: low-load operation, stable nitrification, oxygen-limited operation, and shock-load/transition conditions. The derived labels were predicted from routinely available online inputs using Decision Tree, Random Forest, and XGBoost classifiers, which achieved accuracies of 0.960, 0.988, and 0.989, respectively. Misclassifications were concentrated near boundaries between neighboring states, indicating gradual process transitions rather than widespread model instability. Model interpretation linked predictions to physically meaningful drivers, particularly influent loading, staged aeration, and temperature. The framework therefore provides an accurate, interpretable basis for real-time monitoring, early warning, operational decision support, and future integration with plant control systems in practical applications. Keywords: latent operating regimes; semantic cluster labeling; full-scale WWTP analytics; nitrogen-conversion dynamics; aeration-control intelligence; explainable tree ensembles; weakly labeled process data

title: Contactless Interactions in the Cell by Exchange of Virtual Water Coherence Domains: A Hypothesis
summary: Although the molecular biology of the cell recorded impressive success, a complementarily novel perspective still may come out. Noncontact interactions, different to the hand-glove contact forces between spatially fitting molecules, were ev
content: Although the molecular biology of the cell recorded impressive success, a complementarily novel perspective still may come out. Noncontact interactions, different to the hand-glove contact forces between spatially fitting molecules, were evidenced between proteins in cytosol. By analogy to the atomic nucleus, where the exchange of virtual pions (pi mesons) explains the force between nucleons, we postulate an attractive force derived from a Yukawa potential; supposedly, the later is generated by exchange of virtual water coherence domains (CDs) between two proteins. The CDs are hypothetical spinless (S = 0) quasiparticles of ~13.6 eV effective mass (excitation energy), which can be roughly visualized as clusters of coherently oscillating water electric dipoles. With the CD exchange new features of the cell are explained. The CD effective mass defines an action range of 14.5 nm, which fits well to the mean distance of ~7 nm between proteins in cytosol (200 - 300 g/L density). Assuming a coupling constant of 3.5 eV∙nm, the Yukawa potential prevails on the thermal agitation up to ~10.1 nm. Accordingly, the CD exchange shows saturation, being limited to first neighbor proteins. In cytosol, this may explain the liquid state of macromolecular condensates, the small variation of protein density in different cells, and the independence of protein-protein attractions on amino acid sequence in condensates. The additional cohesion energy due to the CD exchange stabilizes the cell only a little more than the classical hand-glove interactions. A simple model based on the Yukawa potential was proposed, showing that at high enough protein concentration, the total mean energy (in modulus) in condensate suspension may exceed that of an equivalent homogenous protein solution. Thus, for sufficiently short interprotein distances (5.6 - 7 nm inside condensates and >7 nm outside) and with a few hundred condensates per cell, the condensates form spontaneously and are stable, according to potential energy minimization. Finally, the CD exchange frequency is consistent with intracellular communication channels of high speed and capacity. In brief, the postulated analogy of water CD exchange in cytosol to the atomic nucleus may open way to a better insight of certain cellular phenomena.

title: Tailoring mechanical response of AA8006 aluminum alloy through severe cold rolling: A process–structure–property study
source: Journal of Metals Materials and Minerals
summary: This study investigates the process–structure–property relationships of AA8006 aluminum alloy processed by twin-roll casting followed by cold rolling with thickness reductions ranging from 0% to 97%. Microstructural characterization reveals
content: This study investigates the process–structure–property relationships of AA8006 aluminum alloy processed by twin-roll casting followed by cold rolling with thickness reductions ranging from 0% to 97%. Microstructural characterization reveals progressive grain elongation and fragmentation of Al–Fe–Mn–Si intermetallic particles with increasing deformation. These microstructural changes are accompanied by a continuous increase in tensile strength from 156 MPa to 280 MPa and a significant increase in hardness, primarily attributed to work hardening and particle–dislocation interactions. Crystallographic characterization using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) demonstrates substantial texture evolution and grain subdivision during cold rolling, indicating the development of deformation-induced microstructures. The combined microstructural, mechanical, and crystallographic analyses provide a comprehensive understanding of the strengthening mechanisms and deformation behavior of severely cold-rolled AA8006 alloy, offering useful insights for optimizing thermomechanical processing routes in non-heat-treatable aluminum alloys.

title: Evolution of Near-Surface Structure, Oxidation State, and Electrochemistry of Li + /H + -Exchanged and Heat-Treated Li- and Mn-Rich NCM
summary: Anionic redox in Li- and Mn-rich (LMR) NCMs (Li 1+ δ [TM] 1− δ O 2 , 0.1 ⩽ δ ⩽ 0.2) enables high reversible specific capacities (≈250 mAh g −1 ), but voltage and capacity fading compromise cycle life. Acid washing can mitigate these effects
content: Anionic redox in Li- and Mn-rich (LMR) NCMs (Li 1+ δ [TM] 1− δ O 2 , 0.1 ⩽ δ ⩽ 0.2) enables high reversible specific capacities (≈250 mAh g −1 ), but voltage and capacity fading compromise cycle life. Acid washing can mitigate these effects, through partial Li + /H + exchange, subsequently released during heat treatment, leading to an O-depleted near-surface structure. Here, Li 1.14 [Ni 0.26 Co 0.14 Mn 0.60 ] 0.86 O 2 was washed in a phosphate buffer to avoid transition-metal (TM) dissolution and heat-treated at 120–650 °C. Thermogravimetric analysis coupled with mass spectrometry allows to quantify the H + content. Model materials (≈30 at% H + ) were used to track the near-surface structure and TM oxidation states. At 120 °C, X-ray diffraction detects a protonated phase, while X-ray absorption near edge structure reveals a partial shift to spinel coordination (near-surface ½ MO 2 + ½ M 3 O 4 ) at 180–240 °C. At 300 °C, O 2 is released, and further spinel M 3 O 4 is formed, converting to rock-salt MO from 450 °C. Electrochemical tests on 8.7 at% Li + /H + -exchanged samples after 120 °C show a first-charge overpotential due to H + . Only the 450 °C sample exhibits significantly higher impedance across the entire potential range. Despite lower initial capacities, samples heated to 120 °C and 450 °C exhibit superior long-term full-cell C/2 capacity.

title: A Low-Grade Heat Driven Thermo-Osmotic Energy Harvester
source: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology
summary: Across the globe, over 60% of primary energy produced by thermal power plants, industrial manufacturing, data centers, and solar thermal installations is lost as uncaptured low-grade waste heat below 100°C, while more than two billion peopl
content: Across the globe, over 60% of primary energy produced by thermal power plants, industrial manufacturing, data centers, and solar thermal installations is lost as uncaptured low-grade waste heat below 100°C, while more than two billion people simultaneously face acute freshwater scarcity and unreliable off-grid electricity access. To solve these critical global challenges, this indigenous, zero-emission benchtop prototype draws inspiration from natural transpiration in tall forest trees to convert low-grade warm water into a powerful trans-membrane vapour pressure differential across a hydrophobic nanoporous filter paper membrane. As pure water vapour diffuses toward a cold condensation chamber powered by a TEC1-12706 Peltier module and aluminum heat sink, the resulting high-velocity airflow spins a miniature micro DC impeller turbine. This turbine generates clean electrical energy, providing live visual confirmation by illuminating two series-connected Yellow and Green LEDs when thermal gradients exceed threshold levels. Simultaneously, the condensed permeate is collected as ultra-pure distilled drinking water with Total Dissolved Solids below 16 ppm, achieving over 99.4% salt rejection across diverse saline and industrial feed sources. Operational telemetry, including real-time chamber temperatures, is continuously monitored via a DHT11 sensor interfaced with an Arduino Uno microcontroller and displayed on a multiplexed 4-digit 7-segment LED display. This sustainable co-generation breakthrough offers a practical, scalable decentralized solution for industrial waste heat recovery and off-grid community empowerment.

title: KAYA identity-based modelling of carbon emissions in West Africa using interpretable quantum-optimised support vector regression
summary: Accurate forecasting of carbon emissions is vital for shaping sustainable environmental policies and advancing the Sustainable Development Goals, particularly those linked to climate action. Guided by the KAYA-identity, which links emission
content: Accurate forecasting of carbon emissions is vital for shaping sustainable environmental policies and advancing the Sustainable Development Goals, particularly those linked to climate action. Guided by the KAYA-identity, which links emissions to population, economic activity, energy use, and technology, this study examines seven forecasting approaches for West Africa. It applies univariate methods such as the Autoregressive model (AR) and the Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA), alongside multivariate techniques including Multiple Linear Regression (MLR), Extreme Learning Machine (ELM), Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), Support Vector Regression (SVR), and SVR combined with Quantum Particle Swarm Optimisation (SVR-QPSO). For interpretability, Shapley values are used to assess the contribution of each variable within the models. Among all approaches, SVR-QPSO delivers the strongest predictive performance. In the training sample, SVR-QPSO lowers the forecasting error of AR by 95.81% for Côte d’Ivoire, 93.34% for Ghana, 97.05% for Nigeria, and 92.55% for Senegal. In the testing sample, it improves on AR by 96.67% for Côte d’Ivoire, 95.15% for Ghana, 97.82% for Nigeria, and 93.37% for Senegal. SVR-QPSO is identified as the leading model for Ghana and Nigeria, SVR performs best for Côte d’Ivoire, and MLP is the strongest for Senegal. The findings show that SVR-QPSO and MLP offer valuable support for future climate policy design aimed at strengthening environmental resilience.

title: Dynamic Determination of Bulk Modulus and Speed of Sound from Real Injection Signals in Common-Rail Systems Using Conventional and Sustainable Aviation Fuels
summary: Abstract The deployment of sustainable aviation fuels (SAFs) and dual-use fuel strategies for aviation and ground transportation requires a detailed understanding of the hydraulic properties governing fuel injection-system behavior. This st
content: Abstract The deployment of sustainable aviation fuels (SAFs) and dual-use fuel strategies for aviation and ground transportation requires a detailed understanding of the hydraulic properties governing fuel injection-system behavior. This study presents a dynamic methodology for determining fuel density, bulk modulus, and speed of sound directly from rail-pressure, back-pressure, and injection-rate signals acquired during real common-rail injection events, eliminating the need for dedicated acoustic characterization equipment. Conventional diesel and Jet A1 were investigated alongside hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO), Fischer–Tropsch synthetic paraffinic kerosene (SPK-FT), and Jet A1/HVO and Jet A1/SPK-FT blends formulated at derived cetane numbers (DCN) of 46, 51, and 56. Experiments were conducted at injection pressures between 50 and 110 MPa and fuel temperatures from 293 to 313 K. The results show that fuel density is primarily governed by composition, whereas the dynamic bulk modulus is mainly controlled by rail pressure, increasing consistently with injection pressure for all fuels and blends. Temperature systematically reduces fuel stiffness, while fuels with similar density can exhibit significantly different bulk modulus and speed-of-sound values, highlighting the importance of compressibility in defining hydraulic behavior. Fuels with higher bulk modulus values exhibited faster pressure-wave propagation, reduced hydraulic injection delay, and earlier start of injection, confirming the dominant role of fuel compressibility in injection-system response. Jet A1 blends with HVO and SPK-FT displayed intermediate acoustic and hydraulic properties between those of the corresponding neat fuels, indicating a progressive and predictable transition with blend composition. Beyond the proposed methodology, this work provides a comprehensive database of density, dynamic bulk modulus, and speed-of-sound values for diesel, Jet A1, HVO, SPK-FT, and their blends under representative common-rail operating conditions. The results offer valuable input for injection-system calibration, combustion modeling, and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations while contributing to the assessment of SAFs and single-fuel-concept strategies for future low-carbon propulsion systems operating across transportation, power-generation, and aviation sectors.

title: Mechanical, saturation, and microstructural performance of coffee biochar-modified cement mortar incorporating basalt and limestone aggregates for semi-rigid pavement applications
summary: The utilization of agricultural waste-derived materials in pavement and cementitious systems has attracted increasing attention as a strategy for improving sustainability while reducing environmental burdens associated with conventional con
content: The utilization of agricultural waste-derived materials in pavement and cementitious systems has attracted increasing attention as a strategy for improving sustainability while reducing environmental burdens associated with conventional construction materials. This study investigated the performance of coffee biochar-modified cement mortar as a grouting material for semi-rigid pavement systems incorporating basalt and limestone aggregates. Coffee biochar produced from spent coffee grounds pyrolyzed at 350 °C was incorporated at a fixed replacement level of 15% of fine aggregate. The effects of aggregate type, water–cement ratio (0.50 and 0.55), and superplasticizer dosage (0%–2%) on flowability, compressive strength, mortar saturation, and microstructural characteristics were evaluated. Mechanical and physicochemical performance were assessed using compressive strength testing together with Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR), X-ray Diffraction (XRD), and Scanning Electron Microscopy coupled with Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (SEM–EDX). The results demonstrated that all mixtures achieved flowability values suitable for grouting applications, while mortar saturation exceeded 90% for both basalt and limestone porous asphalt systems, indicating effective infiltration into the interconnected void structure. The highest 28-day compressive strength of 56.99 MPa was obtained for the limestone mixture with a water–cement ratio of 0.50% and 0.8% superplasticizer dosage. Microstructural observations revealed differences in pore distribution, interfacial transition zone characteristics, and hydration product morphology among the investigated mixtures. FTIR, XRD, and SEM–EDX analyses suggested the development of hydration products and matrix densification, although direct quantification of hydration phases was beyond the scope of the study. The findings indicate that coffee biochar-modified cement mortar can provide satisfactory fresh, mechanical, saturation, and microstructural performance for semi-rigid pavement applications when mixture proportions are appropriately selected. However, the study was limited to a single coffee biochar replacement level (15%), one pyrolysis temperature (350 °C), and laboratory-scale short-term evaluation. Future studies should include biochar-free control mixtures, different biochar dosages, long-term durability assessments, and field-scale validation to confirm the applicability of coffee biochar-modified grouting mortars in semi-rigid pavements. The FTIR, XRD, and SEM results should be interpreted cautiously due to their inherent limitations, and further microstructural investigations are recommended to strengthen the findings.

title: Assessing Traditional Composting Monitoring Limitations to Inform Real-Time IoT-Based Monitoring: A Feasibility Study at the Kenya Institute of Organic Farming
source: Journal of Research Innovation and Implications in Education
summary: The rapid urbanization in developing countries has increased the volumes of municipal solid waste, wherein 40%-70% is organic waste.Whereas composting is one of the sustainable methods used to treat organic waste and for climate mitigation,
content: The rapid urbanization in developing countries has increased the volumes of municipal solid waste, wherein 40%-70% is organic waste.Whereas composting is one of the sustainable methods used to treat organic waste and for climate mitigation, its effectiveness can slow down due to poor monitoring practices.Traditional composting practices at the Kenya Institute of Organic Farming rely mainly on traditional monitoring, resulting in inconsistent compost quality, inefficient decomposition, and limited capacity to track or reduce greenhouse gas emissions (GHG).The purpose of this study is to assess the limitations of current composting practices at the Kenya Institute of Organic Farming in terms of monitoring accuracy, parameter consistency, and GHG estimation capability as a foundational step toward designing a real-time IoT monitoring system.A case study design was employed.Structured questionnaires were administered to a sample of 20 composting practitioners at the Kenya Institute of Organic Farming using purposive sampling.Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, and Spearman rank-order correlations, and qualitative data from each question's responses were subjected to inductive thematic coding.The findings revealed that moisture imbalance and temperature instability were the main operational challenges.Respondents strongly agreed that traditional monitoring is insufficient, and a chi-square test confirmed that these perceptions are universal across composting technologies.The study concludes that traditional monitoring constitutes a systemic limitation at the Kenya Institute of Organic Farming, regardless of the composting technology used.The study recommends accelerating the adoption and implementation of IoT-based real-time monitoring systems.

title: Struct-Stainability: a metric for Timber Use and Forest Restoration
summary: Abstract Purpose. This study introduces an interdisciplinary methodology for defining a sustainability metric supporting the joint engineering design of forestry operations and construction processes reliant on forest-based supply chains. F
content: Abstract Purpose. This study introduces an interdisciplinary methodology for defining a sustainability metric supporting the joint engineering design of forestry operations and construction processes reliant on forest-based supply chains. Focusing on forest restoration and sustainable management in ecologically fragile areas like Campania Felix in Southern Italy—where high-density conurbations have almost entirely replaced ancient lowland forests—the framework aims to harmoniously balance the quantification of environmental regeneration needs with the demand for structural construction materials. Methods. The methodology is tested through a case study assessing restoration opportunities for Campanian coastal psammophilous ecosystems and Pinus pinea habitats—and the related land resource requirements—to support the prospective solid-wood reconstruction of the columna - capreoli A-trusses in the Aula Magna of the Department of Architecture and Industrial Design at the University of Campania, hosted by the Monastery of San Lorenzo ad Septimum in Aversa. Proceeding from the metric determination of dimensional and volumetric requirements of structural timber and through growth and yield (alsometric) analyses, the computed bill-of-quantities figures are converted into an equivalent estimated land-time metric for reforestation and land-use planning. This conversion is achieved via the recently proposed struct-stainability axiom, which equitably pairs anthropic transformation demand with anthropogenic ecosystem restoration and preservation needs. Results and discussion. The main outcome of this study is the definition of the San Lorenzo space-time Unit (SLU), ultimately quantified to be 8,200 m² over a time range of 70 years, representing a twofold contextual reforestation plan that implements, on the obverse, land allocation and forest operations exclusively destined to ecosystem restoration and, on the reverse, land allocation and sustainable forest engineering for the timber supply chain (short-wood supply chain). The resolution of an SLU-based optimality model design problem is also illustrated. Although this quantitative outcome depends on several specific assumptions adopted in the present case study, the knowledge gained provides an encouraging proof of concept of the convergence of the proposed algorithmic schemes and experienced geographically informed design-individuation processes into well-defined actions of built environment regeneration. Conclusion. Overall, the illustrated general methodology of Struct-stainability design , in its Construction-driven and Biodiversity-driven variants, offers a multidisciplinary approach scalable to other regional case studies with a promising potential of contributing to the harmonization of structural needs, forest planning, and long-term sustainability goals.

title: Salinity delays rhizoid formation and blocks tuberization in the threatened terrestrial orchid Anacamptis coriophora, and chitosan with yeast extract alleviates the damage in vitro
summary: Abstract Background Tuberous terrestrial orchids of western Asia are dug from the wild to make salep, and asymbiotic seed culture can supply plants for reintroduction. Many candidate sites are degraded or slightly saline, yet nothing is kno
content: Abstract Background Tuberous terrestrial orchids of western Asia are dug from the wild to make salep, and asymbiotic seed culture can supply plants for reintroduction. Many candidate sites are degraded or slightly saline, yet nothing is known about how salinity affects early development of these orchids or whether elicitors can soften the damage. Seeds of Anacamptis coriophora were sown on P723 medium containing every combination of three NaCl levels (0, 50, 100 mM), three chitosan doses (0, 20, 40 mg L⁻¹) and three yeast extract doses (0, 2, 3 g L⁻¹). Results Salinity delayed every germination stage, and rhizoid formation was the most sensitive step (10.5, 24.6 and 52.4 days at 0, 50 and 100 mM). Germination fell from 72% to 60% and 44%, plantlet fresh weight fell by 72% at 50 mM and by 98% at 100 mM, and no tubers formed at 100 mM. NaCl explained 94 to 96% of the variance in plantlet biomass, whereas yeast extract was the main source of variance in chlorophyll content. At 50 mM, malondialdehyde, catalase and superoxide dismutase rose by 63%, 49% and 29%. Without salt, neither elicitor improved germination or growth. Under 50 mM NaCl, 20 mg L⁻¹ chitosan shortened the time to protocorm formation from 46 to 32 days, and 40 mg L⁻¹ chitosan with 3 g L⁻¹ yeast extract tripled plantlet fresh weight and raised tuber fresh weight 4.7-fold. Of 300 trait pairs, 131 were significantly correlated, but only 55 remained so once the NaCl effect was removed; after this correction catalase activity was negatively related to malondialdehyde (partial r = − 0.70). Principal component analysis, two-way clustering and a salt tolerance index (53 ± 1.2%) all set the chitosan plus yeast extract combination apart from the other salt treatments. Conclusions A. coriophora is salt-sensitive from germination onwards, and tuber formation is the most vulnerable trait. Elicitors are not needed for routine propagation, but a combination of 40 mg L⁻¹ chitosan and 3 g L⁻¹ yeast extract restored much of the growth lost at moderate salinity and is a candidate pre-conditioning treatment for plants destined for reintroduction.

title: Tropical stem efflux decreases under elevated canopy CO2 independent of dark leaf respiration
summary: Elevated CO 2 may alter plant respiration and gas exchange in tropical forests, contributing uncertainty to carbon budget projections under climate change. We present results from the Enhanced Levels of Emissions in Volcanically Active Trop
content: Elevated CO 2 may alter plant respiration and gas exchange in tropical forests, contributing uncertainty to carbon budget projections under climate change. We present results from the Enhanced Levels of Emissions in Volcanically Active Tropical Ecosystems (ELEVATE) project, a naturally elevated CO 2 investigation in a tropical forest. We examined stem CO 2 and CH 4 efflux, and leaf dark respiration ( R d ) responses to elevated CO 2 and compared observations to the Community Land Model version 5 (CLM5). Stem efflux significantly declined with elevated CO 2 (CO 2 : R² = 0.27, p = 0.01; CH 4 : R² = 0.15, p = 0.06), whereas CLM5 predicted increases (CO 2 : R² = 0.72, p = 0.02). Observed stem efflux also declined with higher air temperature (CO 2 : R² = 0.60, p = 0.07; CH 4 : R² = 0.82, p = 0.01); while CLM5 predicted a positive (CO 2 : R 2 = 0.75; p = 0.03) or no relationship (CH 4 : R 2 = 0.24; p = 0.32). Neither in-situ nor CLM5 R d were correlated with elevated CO 2 . CLM5 underestimated stem CO 2 and CH 4 efflux by 141% and 200%, respectively, whereas it underestimated R d by 14–34%. Contrasting stem efflux responses likely reflect soil moisture- and transport-mediated constraints not represented in CLM5, and contribute to significant model uncertainty.

title: Deterministic modeling of nanofluid stability in high-viscosity biodiesels: a Tri-Coupled Fluid–Acoustic–Particle Framework
summary: Background The synthesis of stable nanofluids within high-viscosity biofuel matrices is often limited by the complex coupling between fluid rheology and acoustic physics. This study proposes a predictive “Tri-Coupled Fluid–Acoustic–Particle
content: Background The synthesis of stable nanofluids within high-viscosity biofuel matrices is often limited by the complex coupling between fluid rheology and acoustic physics. This study proposes a predictive “Tri-Coupled Fluid–Acoustic–Particle Framework” that numerically integrates fuel physicochemical properties, acoustic impedance matching, and deagglomeration kinetics. Methods Methyl Oleate was utilized as a physicochemical surrogate to model the dispersion behavior of Multi-Walled Carbon Nanotube (MWCNT) and specific metal oxide agglomerates (Cerium Oxide (CeO 2 ), Aluminum Oxide (Al 2 O 3 ), and Titanium Dioxide (TiO 2 )) within n-butanol blends across 16,800 scenarios. Results n-Butanol functions as an acoustic transfer agent, reducing viscous damping and potentially enhancing the cavitation efficiency index by approximately 8.6% at a 30% blending ratio. A distinct regime separation was identified: metal oxide dispersion is mixing-limited, whereas MWCNT dispersion is energy-limited. Implications The model reveals a “cross-particle consistency” defined as the uniform enhancement of processing efficiency across varying nanoparticle types suggesting that fluid-side rheological modifications dominate the dispersion outcome. This framework provides a deterministic methodology for optimizing nanofluid production in viscous media.

title: Formulating Cannabidiol (CBD) by Oiling Out and Spray Drying
summary: Abstract Purpose Cannabidiol (CBD) exhibits promising pharmacological effects for the treatment of various medical conditions. However, its poor aqueous solubility and pronounced lipophilicity lead to low oral bioavailability, limiting its
content: Abstract Purpose Cannabidiol (CBD) exhibits promising pharmacological effects for the treatment of various medical conditions. However, its poor aqueous solubility and pronounced lipophilicity lead to low oral bioavailability, limiting its therapeutic potential. This study aims to develop and evaluate a new Oiling-Out production strategy based on spray drying. The obtained CBD containing powders are characterized by their particle properties and dissolution behavior. Methods This approach focuses on particle size reduction by generating submicron CBD droplets via a continuous Oiling-Out process, followed by immediate embedding in a polymeric carrier during spray drying. Since mixing conditions strongly influence droplet size, Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations were employed to analyze mixing performance and residence time in two mixer configurations: a T-mixer and a swirl mixer. Pure CBD, a physical mixture as well as an amorphous solid dispersion served for comparison. Results The process led to solid systems containing CBD with enhanced dissolution behavior compared to crystalline drug substance. The drug release was even faster than the release from the amorphous solid dispersion formulation with comparable particle properties. Conclusion The study demonstrates the potential of spray drying as a versatile and scalable process for the development of solid formulations of poorly water-soluble drugs such as CBD. The investigated formulation strategy provides process-relevant insights for the design of spray-drying-based manufacturing routes to enhance dissolution performance and support the development of oral CBD products.

title: FeOCl catalyst activation of peroxymonosulfate for degradation of lomefloxacin in water: Preparation, activation, and degradation mechanism
summary: FeOCl catalysts were prepared using a partial pyrolysis method. Lomefloxacin hydrochloride (LMF) served as a representative antibiotic to evaluate the catalytic performance of FeOCl through activation of permonosulfates (PMS). Under conditi
content: FeOCl catalysts were prepared using a partial pyrolysis method. Lomefloxacin hydrochloride (LMF) served as a representative antibiotic to evaluate the catalytic performance of FeOCl through activation of permonosulfates (PMS). Under conditions of a 10 mg/L FeOCl dosage, a 2 mM PMS concentration, a 20 mg/L LMF concentration, and an initial pH of 5.6, the LMF removal rate and reaction rate constant reached 54.39% and 0.0067 min −1 , respectively, within 60 min. Quenching experiments and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) analysis revealed that reactive oxygen species (ROS) involved in LMF degradation included SO 4 • − , •OH, O 2 • − , and 1 O 2 , with both •OH and SO 4 • − playing important roles. Redox reaction between Fe(II) and Fe(III) enhanced the activation properties of this system. Based on liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) analysis of intermediates, 13 potential intermediate products were identified, and three potential degradation pathways were proposed. Toxicity assessment software analysis indicated that while degradation lowered the toxicity of most intermediates, certain intermediates retained high toxicity.

title: Confinement property in the JT-60SA first operation phase
summary: Abstract In JT-60SA, the global energy confinement time τ E has been evaluated to be 0.1-0.2 s for 1 MA hydrogen discharges and compared with the ITERL-96P(th) scaling. Because local measurements of ion temperature T i , electron density an
content: Abstract In JT-60SA, the global energy confinement time τ E has been evaluated to be 0.1-0.2 s for 1 MA hydrogen discharges and compared with the ITERL-96P(th) scaling. Because local measurements of ion temperature T i , electron density and effective charge are not available in the first operation phase and the number of discharges and their parameter range are limited, the present results should not be considered definitive. As heating power increased, τ E tends to shorten in the same trend as the scaling. τ E is shorter than the scaling but approaches the scaling with increasing density. For 0.4-0.6 MW ohmic heating plasmas, τ E increases with increasing collisionality and saturates. For 0.6-0.8 MW ohmic heating and electron cyclotron resonance heating (ECH) plasmas, τ E continues to increase up to higher collisionality and reaches the scaling. The turbulence simulations with the trapped gyroLandau-fluid model assuming a linear T i profile show that the dominant turbulence mode is trapped electron modes. The linear growth rate decreases with increasing collisionality and saturates at a low level in the 0.4-0.6 MW ohmic heating plasma, suggesting the transition from the linear ohmic confinement regime to the saturated ohmic confinement regime. For 0.6-0.8 MW ohmic heating and ECH plasmas, the saturation occurs at higher collisionality, indicating that the linear confinement regime extends to higher collisionality. The global particle confinement time excluding recycling contributions, τ p , has also been evaluated to be 0.301±0.015 s, approximately twice τ E , from the frequency responses in a density feedback control experiment. From τ p and the effective particle confinement time including recycling τ p * , a recycling coefficient is obtained as 0.865±0.013. The sub-unity recycling coefficient indicates that wall recycling is insufficient to maintain plasma density, consistent with hydrogen retention due to the first hydrogen discharge with continuous gas injection.

title: Synthetic Pathway Modulation of Metal Organization in Multivariate Metal–Organic Frameworks
summary: Multivariate metal-organic frameworks (MTV MOFs) incorporate various metals and/or linkers within a periodic backbone, offering structural diversity and emergent functionalities. Typically, conventional one-pot synthesis does not allow for
content: Multivariate metal-organic frameworks (MTV MOFs) incorporate various metals and/or linkers within a periodic backbone, offering structural diversity and emergent functionalities. Typically, conventional one-pot synthesis does not allow for any control over the spatial arrangement or sequencing of metals within the framework. Here, we present a synthetic strategy to alter metal arrangement in multimetallic MTV MOFs, yielding materials with nearly identical composition yet distinct properties. Using isostructural mCB-Co and mCB-Ni MOFs, we generate two MTV MOFs with different one-dimensional Ni/Co arrangements, resulting in distinct semiconducting and magnetic properties. High-resolution electrospray ionization mass spectrometry (ESI-HRMS) reveals the formation of distinct precursor species in solution, suggesting that prenucleation chemistry influences the final metal arrangement. This work establishes a new approach for modulating metal arrangement in MTV MOFs, enabling tunable functional properties in multimetallic frameworks for applications in catalysis, electronics, and quantum materials.

title: Fresh and degraded maize shoot and root residues temporarily change hydraulic properties of a loamy soil
summary: Mulching and incorporation of crop residues (CR) into soils are common strategies to sustain soil carbon stocks, return nutrients, and regulate water losses through bare soil evaporation. To date, implementing the effects of mulching strate
content: Mulching and incorporation of crop residues (CR) into soils are common strategies to sustain soil carbon stocks, return nutrients, and regulate water losses through bare soil evaporation. To date, implementing the effects of mulching strategies into soil-plant-atmosphere models remains a challenge as there is limited information on how this layer of CR changes with time and how it thereby influences processes such as evaporation, water infiltration or the transport of pollutants. An important, hitherto unknown key property of a mulch layer and the incorporation of plant residues is their influence on soil hydraulic properties (SHP) as well as on the persistence of these effects over time. We hypothesized that increasing amounts of incorporated maize CR increases water retention and reduces unsaturated hydraulic conductivity, and that the quality of the CR would determine the persistence of the effects, i.e., that mulching with relatively fast decaying shoot residues would be less persistent than incorporating root residues. In a laboratory study, we quantified the effect of maize CR in various concentrations (0 wt %, 2 wt %, and 5 wt %) on the SHP of a loam soil and additionally measured the SHP of a mulch layer (100 wt % CR) from saturation to oven dryness. We differentiated between shoot and root CR to quantify the effect of biomass quality and adapted the simplified evaporation method to measure the hydraulic properties of 100 % CR layer. The experiments were run in triplicate in a climate constant room (20 °C, 65 % RH) and repeated after three weeks of incubation under optimal conditions for biological activity (30 °C, 90 % RH) to simulate organic matter degradation after harvest. CR decay was monitored by carbon and nitrogen composition of fresh material, after the first measurement of SHP (pre-incubation) and at the end of the experiment (post-incubation, incubation plus second measurement of SHP).
