title: Optimizing Asphalt Performance Through Affordable Fiber Reinforcement
summary: Abstract Incorporating fibers including basalt, ceramic, and glass into SBS-modified asphalt mixtures enhances their performance, enabling a reduction of SBS content from 7% to 3% alongside the addition of 0.3% fibers. This study evaluates
content: Abstract Incorporating fibers including basalt, ceramic, and glass into SBS-modified asphalt mixtures enhances their performance, enabling a reduction of SBS content from 7% to 3% alongside the addition of 0.3% fibers. This study evaluates the performance efficiency and life cycle costs of fiber-reinforced mixtures compared to the conventional SBS-7% mixture. Maintenance strategies were developed for each mixture scenario within the life cycle cost analysis framework. Furthermore, 3D finite element simulations using the Burgers-Logit model were employed to assess fatigue and rutting damage. Performance efficiency indicators were subsequently calculated. Results reveal that basalt fiber (BF) and ceramic fiber (CF) mixtures deliver similar, superior performance compared to the SBS-7% mixture, with reduced maintenance requirements. Due to higher procurement costs of CF, BF mixtures offer a balance of cost and performance thereby achieving a 19% improvement in performance efficiency.

title: Enhancing the efficiency and sustainability of geothermal energy piles in cold regions using innovative backfill materials and layout optimization
source: ERA: Education and Research Archive (University of Alberta)
summary: Geothermal energy piles (GEPs), which integrate heat exchanger pipes into foundation piles, provide an efficient and space-saving approach for using shallow geothermal energy for building heating and cooling. GEPs are of particular interest
content: Geothermal energy piles (GEPs), which integrate heat exchanger pipes into foundation piles, provide an efficient and space-saving approach for using shallow geothermal energy for building heating and cooling. GEPs are of particular interest for cold regions, where heating demand is high, and replacing fossil-fuel-based systems is important for reducing energy consumption and carbon emissions. However, the wider application of GEPs in cold regions still faces many challenges. Conventional cementitious backfill materials used for GEPs often have limited heat-storage capacity and have high environmental impacts. In addition, heating-dominant operation can cause significant changes in ground temperature, potentially reducing system efficiency. In response to these issues, this thesis aims to develop heat-storage backfill materials and optimize GEP layouts for cold-region applications to reduce ground temperature changes. Experiments investigated the thermal, mechanical, and environmental performance of MPCM-enhanced cementitious backfill materials with flake graphite and LC3. Numerical models and an optimization framework were developed to evaluate GEP system performance and minimize ground temperature changes under heating-dominant operation. The results show that incorporating low-melting-point MPCMs and flake graphite improved the heat-storage and heat-transfer performance of cementitious backfill materials. For example, the P5G12-6°C backfill material increased the total extracted heat during a 30-minute heating operation by approximately 7% compared with the control mixture. MPCM incorporation also improved freeze–thaw durability. After 28 freeze–thaw cycles, the oven-dry thermal conductivity reduction decreased from 33.3% for the MPCM-free sample to 14.1% for the sample containing 5% MPCM, while the unconfined compressive strength reduction decreased from 35.8% to 21.3%. In addition, the LC3-based mixture containing 5 wt.% MPCM and 12 wt.% flake graphite achieved thermal conductivity values of 2.12 W/(m·K) under oven-dry conditions and 2.83 W/(m·K) under saturated conditions, while reducing global warming potential by about 33% compared with OPC-based backfill materials. The numerical results show that the developed L-P5G12 backfill material improved GEP system performance compared with conventional backfill material. Over the first decade of operation, the average coefficient of performance increased from 4.348 to 4.381, and the average seasonal energy efficiency ratio increased from 28.593 to 29.169. Compared with conventional heating and cooling methods, the GEP system using L-P5G12 achieved average energy savings of 77.2% for heating and 28.0% for cooling, with a total CO2-equivalent emission reduction of 180.82 tonnes over 10 years. The optimized layouts reduced ground temperature change by up to approximately 1.6 °C for selected cases and reduced computational time by more than 95% compared with the full simulation approach. title: The Delayed Escape: Quantifying the Role of Nanobubbles in Methane Retention Following Hydrate Dissociation
summary: Abstract Methane hydrate destabilization is a fundamental process in marine carbon cycling, where the micro-scale gas partitioning dictates its ultimate fate. While the macroscopic release of methane to the atmosphere is well-documented, th
content: Abstract Methane hydrate destabilization is a fundamental process in marine carbon cycling, where the micro-scale gas partitioning dictates its ultimate fate. While the macroscopic release of methane to the atmosphere is well-documented, the kinetic pathways of methane retained in the aqueous phase remain insufficiently understood. In this study, we investigated the evolution and stability of methane nanobubbles (NBs) generated during hydrate dissociation in a controlled laboratory setting. The post-dissociation aqueous phase was characterized over a 10-day period to determine NB size, concentration, and zeta potential. Complementary physicochemical analysis—including pH, oxidation-reduction potential (ORP), temperature, oxygen level, and electrical conductivity—elucidated the water chemistry governing NB longevity. Our quantitative model evaluates NBs under both high-pressure (scenario A) and near-ambient (scenario B) core states. Under either paradigm, these NBs function as concentrated methane reservoirs. Despite a marginal macroscopic supersaturation, the localized methane density within the NBs is over 850 times (scenario A) or 30 times (scenario B) higher than that of the dissolved phase. Interfacial adsorption analysis indicated that a specific amount (0.29% for scenario A and 8.2% for scenario B) of the NB-bound methane is partitioned at the gas–liquid interface. This surface accumulation, combined with a measured zeta potential of –7 to –18 mV, provides a robust kinetic barrier against immediate gas dissolution. These results demonstrate a “delayed escape” mechanism, where NBs act as persistent reservoirs that temporarily sequester methane in a high-fugacity state. Although the macroscopic contribution of the NB phase to the total bulk dissolved inventory is minor (<0.01%), the intense local enrichment creates micro-heterogeneous hotspots. This work shifts the focus from bulk solubility limits to micro-kinetic pathways, offering critical insights for refining gas transport models and improving the temporal accuracy of methane emission predictions in hydrate-bearing systems while avoiding over-extrapolation to regional or global carbon budgets.

title: DEVELOPMENT OF DEAMINATIVE CARBON-CARBON BOND FORMING REACTIONS AND THEIR APPLICATIONS
summary: This dissertation is focused on developing methods that form new carbon-carbon bonds through the activation of C–N bonds in primary aliphatic amines. In addition, the application of deaminative methods to both radiolabeling and total synthe
content: This dissertation is focused on developing methods that form new carbon-carbon bonds through the activation of C–N bonds in primary aliphatic amines. In addition, the application of deaminative methods to both radiolabeling and total synthesis are explored. Chapter 1 is an overview of C-N bond activation in the literature, and the advantages of utilizing alkyl amines as non-traditional electrophiles. C-N bond activation has been demonstrated on many different substrates but alkyl amines are one of the most abundant precursors available to chemists, making them of particular interest. Their use as an electrophile would provide advantages over traditional electrophiles as they are easily purified and can be protected and deprotected easily allowing for late-stage functionalization. The use of unactivated alkyl amines in deaminative cross-couplings was limited until recently when our group published on the use of 2,4,6-triphenyl alkylpyridinium salts (Katritzky salts) in nickel-catalyzed Suzuki-Miyaura cross-coupling. After our seminal publication the development of many different methods for the activation of alkylpyridinium salts have been developed, allowing chemists to now think of amines as alkyl radical precursors rather than just nucleophiles. Chapter 2 describes an electroreductive cross-coupling of alkylpyridinium salts with aryl halides. C(sp2)-C(sp3) bonds are one of the most common moieties in pharmaceuticals and natural products. As such new methods for making C(sp2)-C(sp3) bonds are continuing to be explored. Ourselves and others have demonstrated methods for the reductive arylation of alkylpyridinium salts, but these methods lack generality for α-primary and α-secondary alkylpyridinium salts. We explored the use of electrochemical reduction to achieve more general conditions for these two substrate classes. In collaboration with chemists at Merck, we utilized the HTe-Chem reactor and the IKA Electrasyn to rapidly optimize conditions for α-primary alkylpyridinium salts. Furthering this collaboration to include Dr. Christo Sevov at The Ohio State University allowed us to expand our work to α-secondary salts. Our method showed excellent functional group tolerance on both the aryl bromide and alkylpyridinium salt, showing good results on Merck’s informer halide library. This method was also extended to the library synthesis of 24 different molecules at once utilizing the HTe-Chem reactor. We envision that this method will be extremely powerful for medicinal chemists, allowing for late-stage functionalization of complex molecules under mild conditions. The NMR spectra associated with this chapter can be found in Appendix A. Chapter 3 describes the application of our deaminative reductive methylation in the synthesis of radiotracers via the use of carbon-11 methyl iodide. title: Advancement in Hydrogen Production Technologies
source: International Journal of Energy Research Science and Engineering
summary: With the possibility of carbon dioxide emission-free burn when used as an energy carrier, hydrogen is gaining increasing interest as an energy carrier for transport and industry. But production, storage and supporting infrastructure problem
content: With the possibility of carbon dioxide emission-free burn when used as an energy carrier, hydrogen is gaining increasing interest as an energy carrier for transport and industry. But production, storage and supporting infrastructure problems remain to be overcome to achieve wider deployment. The aim of this review is to briefly summarize the existing and new hydrogen production technologies, their current uses and the required storage technologies for a hydrogen economy. As well as being used in the production of ammonia and methanol, hydrogen could also be used in mobility and in other areas that are looking for alternative energy systems with lower emissions. The pathways studied are coal and biomass gasification, pyrolysis and other thermochemical methods, photo-chemical (photolytic) conversion, biological (bio-chemical) conversion, steam, plasma and aqueous-phase reforming. Technical advancement is suggested in the literature to be able to boost the amount of hydrogen available for these industrial and transport applications by 2023 to 2050. The value of the potential will rely on the technology efficiency, the cost and environmental impact of production technologies. The increased use of low-carbon hydrogen thus has the potential to decrease reliance on fossil fuels and help to lower carbon dioxide emissions, depending on the hydrogen production method.

title: ESGF-NG CMIP7.ScenarioMIP.ACCESS-Consortium.ACCESS-ESM1-6.scen7-h version 1
summary: Project: CMIP7 Future scenario experiments. Exploration of the future climate under a (selected) range of possible boundary conditions. In CMIP7, the priority tier for experiments is conditional on whether you are doing emissions- or concen
content: Project: CMIP7 Future scenario experiments. Exploration of the future climate under a (selected) range of possible boundary conditions. In CMIP7, the priority tier for experiments is conditional on whether you are doing emissions- or concentration-driven simulations. There is no way to express this in the CVs (nor time to implement something to handle this conditionality). This means that, for your particular situation, some experiments may be at a lower tier than is listed in the CVs. For example, the `vl` scenario is tier 1 for concentration-driven models and tier 2 for emissions-driven models. However, in the CVs, we have used the highest priority tier (across all the possible conditionalities). Hence `vl` is listed as tier 1 in the CVs (even though it is actually tier 2 for emissions-driven models). For details, please see the full description in the ScenarioMIP description papers. Produced by: The ACCESS Consortium brings together Australian institutions contributing to the Australian Community Climate and Earth System Simulator (ACCESS) and its submissions to the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP). Participating organisations contribute to different ACCESS models and scientific activities, supported through a combination of institutional investment and Australian Government research infrastructure and research programs, together with international collaborations. (Using Model/Source: ACCESS-ESM1-6 with Experiment scen7-h) The model is an updated version of ACCESS-ESM1-5, as used for CMIP6 (Ziehn et al., 2020). Its dynamic components are the UK Met Office Unified Model atmosphere (v7.3) in a configuration similar to HadGEM2 including CLASSIC aerosols, with the CABLE land surface model (v3) including land biogeochemistry. The atmosphere is coupled to the MOM5 ocean with WOMBATlite biogeochemistry and CICE5 sea-ice using the OASIS-MCT coupler. Chemistry is prescribed including monthly mean, zonally-averaged ozone. Volcano forcing is prescribed as stratospheric optical depth as monthly means in four equal area latitude bands. Land-ice is represented by an ice tile in the land surface model. A grid-cell is either completely ice or ice-free and the ice tile distribution does not change in time. The main differences from ACCESS-ESM1.5 include corrections to how convective momentum transport had been applied in the atmosphere, a change to ocean albedo to better match observations, a correction to the passing of ocean carbon fluxes into the atmosphere, updates to improve energy and water conservation across the land and atmosphere, inclusion of 3 new plant functional types (c4 crops and two Australian tree types), improvements to the treatment of land-use change, updates to some of the land parameterisations or parameter values, the inclusion of a pseudo-iceberg scheme for distributing runoff from Antarctica and Greenland and a substantial update to ocean-biogeochemistry. title: AfriERW: Enhanced rock weathering readiness atlas for Africa, assessment data
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: AfriERW assesses whether conditions in 54 African countries favour starting and verifying enhanced rock weathering (ERW) for carbon dioxide removal. It is published by the Net-Zero Carbon Emission Lab (NCEL), Kwame Nkrumah University of Sci
content: AfriERW assesses whether conditions in 54 African countries favour starting and verifying enhanced rock weathering (ERW) for carbon dioxide removal. It is published by the Net-Zero Carbon Emission Lab (NCEL), Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST). This deposit (release 3.0.1, 14 November 2026) contains country readiness results from 16 indicators in 7 dimensions with evidence grades and rank uncertainty, a seven-link chain of conditions with threshold variants, a feedstock register of 95 deposits with analysed samples and a contaminant screen, an accredited laboratory register, Article 6 and social-licence coding, a unified register of African ERW evidence, and a tropical evidence map of 440 studies with a research-gap register. Every field is described in CODEBOOK.csv. Imputed values are flagged. Web application: https://afrierw.ncelknust.org Provisional status: Provisional research output. The underlying studies are being prepared for peer review and values may change. Not for investment or crediting decisions. Contact: ncel@knust.edu.gh

title: Hydroxyl Megamasers
summary: Hydroxyl megamasers (OHMs) are 18 cm maser sources with luminosities exceeding those of Galactic OH masers by factors of a million or more. These extreme phenomena are powerful tools for probing the role of gas-rich mergers and starbursts i
content: Hydroxyl megamasers (OHMs) are 18 cm maser sources with luminosities exceeding those of Galactic OH masers by factors of a million or more. These extreme phenomena are powerful tools for probing the role of gas-rich mergers and starbursts in the evolution of galaxies, particularly at high redshifts.a) This paper begins with an overview of the discovery of astrophysical masers and the subsequent identification of OHMs as a distinct class, emphasizing their empirical association with ultra-luminous infrared galaxies (ULIRGs). Observed features commonly linked to OHMs — including active galactic nuclei (AGN) and molecular outflows — are then introduced as potential indicators of the energetic environments in which OHMs reside. The physical origins of OHM emission are explored through the energy level structure of the hydroxyl (OH) molecule and the mechanisms that allow for 18 cm line amplification. Key amplification mechanisms are examined alongside the role of dense molecular gas, traced by species such as hydrogen cyanide (HCN) and carbon monoxide (CO). The paper then presents physical conditions thought to drive OHM activity, including the drivers necessary for masing to occur. Together, these topics establish a foundation for interpreting OHMs as markers of extreme star formation and merger-driven evolution in the universe.

title: Cross-Departmental Simulation Training for EEOI and CII Compliance: A Collaborative Model for Deck and Engine Officers
summary: The Energy Efficiency Operational Indicator and the Carbon Intensity Indicator are ship-level metrics, but the decisions that move them are split between two departments trained largely apart from each other: routing, speed, and cargo-plann
content: The Energy Efficiency Operational Indicator and the Carbon Intensity Indicator are ship-level metrics, but the decisions that move them are split between two departments trained largely apart from each other: routing, speed, and cargo-planning decisions belong to the deck department, while fuel consumption and engine-load management belong to engine officers, and current simulator training at STIP Jakarta reflects that departmental split rather than the operational reality that EEOI and CII outcomes depend on deck and engine decisions made in coordination. This paper describes the design and pilot testing of a cross-departmental simulation training exercise bringing nautical and engineering cadets together into shared voyage scenarios where EEOI and CII outcomes depend explicitly on cross-departmental coordination, drawing on team-training research establishing that coordinated task performance requires practicing coordination directly rather than assuming it emerges from separately trained individual competencies. Mixed nautical-engineering cadet teams completing the cross-departmental exercise achieved better simulated voyage emissions-efficiency outcomes than teams of cadets from a single department working the same scenario without a coordinating counterpart, with the advantage concentrated in scenarios requiring a real-time trade-off between a routing decision and an engine-load decision. These findings support cross-departmental simulation training as a structural complement to single-department curriculum reform for closing the applied-readiness gap this research program has identified in decarbonization-relevant operational competency.

title: A Simulator-Based Green Curriculum Module Bridging IMO’s GHG Strategy and Engine Cadet Training
summary: The IMO’s 2023 revised greenhouse gas strategy sets binding intermediate emissions-reduction targets and, through associated instruments such as the Carbon Intensity Indicator, translates those targets into operational metrics that engine c
content: The IMO’s 2023 revised greenhouse gas strategy sets binding intermediate emissions-reduction targets and, through associated instruments such as the Carbon Intensity Indicator, translates those targets into operational metrics that engine cadets will need to manage directly once they hold watchkeeping responsibility. This paper describes the design and pilot testing of a simulator-based curriculum module built specifically to connect that regulatory framework to hands-on engine-room decision-making, addressing a gap this research program’s baseline studies identify repeatedly: cadets know the regulation exists but are not trained to operate under it. The module was developed through iterative design cycles informed by instructor and cadet feedback, following an action-research approach, and structures simulator scenarios around fuel-efficiency and emissions-management decisions tied directly to CII-relevant operational parameters rather than treating regulation and engine operation as separate curriculum units. Pilot cohorts completing the module showed improved performance on a post-module assessment measuring cadets’ ability to translate regulatory targets into specific operational decisions, with the largest gains in scenarios requiring cadets to weigh a fuel-efficiency decision against a competing operational constraint, the kind of applied trade-off reasoning the module was specifically designed to develop. These findings support integrating regulatory content directly into simulator-based operational training, rather than teaching regulation and operational skill as parallel but disconnected curriculum strands.

title: Broad-scale feasibility of enhanced rock weathering for carbon dioxide removal
source: ERA: Education and Research Archive (University of Alberta)
summary: Enhanced rock weathering (ERW) has the potential to be one of the easiest, most-cost effective ways to achieve gigatonne-scale carbon dioxide removal (CDR) from the atmosphere to help mitigate climate change. Because of this, vast amounts o
content: Enhanced rock weathering (ERW) has the potential to be one of the easiest, most-cost effective ways to achieve gigatonne-scale carbon dioxide removal (CDR) from the atmosphere to help mitigate climate change. Because of this, vast amounts of funding are being funneled into ERW research and ERW companies, but despite ERW’s promise, many questions remain namely: 1. What will the true costs and input emissions be for large-scale ERW deployment? 2. How can we improve the costs, time-commitments, and efficacy of ERW measurement, monitoring, reporting, and verification (MMRV)? 3. Can mine tailings be used to improve the costs and net removal of ERW without causing unwanted side-effects? This thesis presents a preliminary answer to all of the above questions, helping to demonstrate that ERW can be feasible at scale if done correctly. The first part of this thesis is a life cycle assessment (LCA), techno-economic analysis (TEA), and geographic information systems (GIS) based assessment of ERW for North America. It looks at the cradle-to-grave costs and input emissions for deploying ERW anywhere across the continent. It assesses the extraction and comminution of rock powders from 140 mines, comprising four different relevant lithologies (basalt, kimberlite, serpentinite, wollastonite), their transportation across more than 600,000 road, rail, and shipping pathways, and their spreading at more than 200,000,000 hectares of farmland. This approach is the most extensive LCA/TEA assessment ever completed for ERW, and highlights the fact more than half of North American farmland is accessible for less than 100 USD per tonne of CDR. The second part of this thesis proposes a new means of MMRV for ERW involving remote sensing. It assesses the spectral variability of different spreading densities of six different rock types (basalt, calcite, kimberlite, metabasalt, serpentinite, wollastonite) to see if handheld remote sensing may be a feasible way to track ERW. While this work has not demonstrated the ability to directly quantify CDR, it demonstrates that varying spreading densities of ERW amendment can be resolved with high accuracy using spectral band ratios, suggesting that remote sensing may be useful to monitor the spreading of ERW amendments, and their subsequent weathering over time. The third and final part of this thesis is a growth chamber trial in which five different rock types (basalt, kimberlite, metabasalt, serpentinite, wollastonite), including two mine tailings, are assessed for carbon dioxide removal potential, and contamination concerns. This trial ran for three months and demonstrated that each of the five rock types has the potential to generate CDR through both alkalinity and secondary pedogenic carbonate formation. Further, it helped to dispel some contamination concerns, as very few regulatory contaminant limits were surpassed, and only at high spreading densities. title: Green, Blue, and Grey Hydrogen: Energy Pathways and Sustainability Implications
source: International Journal of Energy Research Science and Engineering
summary: Hydrogen is the most abundant element in the universe. It is also the simplest consisting of one proton and one electron. However, since it is not found on Earth in is elemental form there are many different methods of producing it from hyd
content: Hydrogen is the most abundant element in the universe. It is also the simplest consisting of one proton and one electron. However, since it is not found on Earth in is elemental form there are many different methods of producing it from hydrogen-containing molecules. The route chosen to produce hydrogen will determine whether it is described by one of the colours, grey, blue, green.turquoise,black, brown or pink.Global hydrogen use was about 120 Mt/a and is expected to rise to 530 Mt/a in 2050. More than 70 Mt/a of hydrogen are used for oil refining (39 Mt/a) and ammonia production (32 Mt/a). In addition, around 50 Mt/a of hydrogen are used in carbon-containing gas mixtures, syngas, for methanol production (14 Mt/a) and steel manufacturing (5 Mt/a) as well as for electricity and heat generation (30 Mt/a) .Hydrogen economy contributes to the vision of bridging technologies and the role in the transition to a sustainable hydrogen in a circular economy by providing pathway to decarbonization across multiple sectors while also integrating with existing waste streams to create new value. In industries such as steel, chemicals, and transportation ,hydrogen acts as a cleaner substitute for carbon-intensive feed-stocks,The cost of producing hydrogen using renewable sources in 2023 was still higher than fossil fuels. The cost of producing electricity from solar panels was between $20 and $120 per Megawatt-hour (depending on the region and type of renewable electricity produced), which is expected to decrease to $14 to $90 by 2030.Grey cannot be the endgame. Blue and turquoise are strategic bridges using our gas advantage. Green is the long term goal for climate, jobs, and energy security.Nigeria should set a National Hydrogen Roadmap. This map shall define clear 2030/2050 targets for blue, turquoise, and green hydrogen with emissions standards for each pathway. Gas shall be used as a bridge, not a crutch: The deployment of CCS for blue hydrogen and pilot methane pyrolysis for turquoise shall be embraced. Mandate methane leak monitoring and link to flare gas reduction programs.

title: Beyond Financials: Carbon Emissions and Distance to Default in Indian Firms
summary: Abstract This paper investigates the relationship between greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, environmental performance, and corporate default risk among Indian listed firms. Default risk is proxied by a Merton-based Distance to Default (DD) me
content: Abstract This paper investigates the relationship between greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, environmental performance, and corporate default risk among Indian listed firms. Default risk is proxied by a Merton-based Distance to Default (DD) measure. The sample covers 301 firms listed on the National Stock Exchange of India during 2016–2023, representing 2,408 potential firm-year observations before variable-specific missingness. We use two-step system generalized method of moments (system GMM), supplemented by pooled ordinary least squares (OLS) and fixed- and random-effects estimates. In the principal system-GMM specifications, Scope 1 emissions are negatively associated with DD (reported coefficients of − 0.844 and − 1.170; p < 0.001), whereas Scope 2 emissions are not statistically significant. The Scope 1 estimate is not statistically significant in the fixed-effects specification. Environmental-score coverage is sparse, and dynamic specifications including the score retain only 16 observations, preventing reliable inference for that measure. We interpret these findings as associations in the estimation samples, rather than as evidence of causation. Uneven reporting coverage, differences across estimators, and sensitivity to controls limit the generalisability of the results.

title: Carbon flow calculation model and emission reduction effect evaluation of power grid with distributed energy
source: International Conference on Advanced Optics and Photonics Research in Engineering (AOPR)
summary: To address the challenge of carbon emission assessment brought by large-scale integration of distributed energy into power grids, this paper proposes a carbon flow calculation model for power grids containing distributed energy. The model i
content: To address the challenge of carbon emission assessment brought by large-scale integration of distributed energy into power grids, this paper proposes a carbon flow calculation model for power grids containing distributed energy. The model introduces carbon emission intensity into traditional power flow calculation, and realizes quantitative analysis of carbon flow at each node and branch of the power grid by defining node carbon flow balance equation and branch carbon flow calculation method. Taking the IEEE 33-node distribution network as the simulation object, different distributed energy access schemes are set up, and the carbon flow distribution and carbon emission reduction effect under each scheme are compared and analyzed. The simulation results show that the proposed model can accurately quantify the carbon flow characteristics of the power grid, and a reasonable distributed energy access scheme can effectively reduce the total carbon emission of the power grid, providing theoretical support for low-carbon planning and operation of the power grid.

title: Production–Logistics Recovery Under Temporal Carbon and Reliability Constraints: A Bound-Aware Optimization Framework
summary: We develop a mixed-integer optimization framework that restores a common service requirement after a production or transport disruption under separate temporal carbon and operating-hazard constraints. Carbon debt is measured against a froze
content: We develop a mixed-integer optimization framework that restores a common service requirement after a production or transport disruption under separate temporal carbon and operating-hazard constraints. Carbon debt is measured against a frozen no-disruption plan, as under a supply contract that commits each delivery window to the plan’s emissions and requires any excess to be made good later; early savings cannot finance later emissions. In a proof-of-concept study on synthetic networks, solver bounds establish a positive repayment premium over a cumulative cap in all 12 Small comparisons, with a median optimal premium of 1.33–1.53% over six periods (1.25–1.44% in a matched re-solve) and 0.35–0.54% over ten. Debt-time exposure falls by a median 91.2%, yet total emissions rise in five cases, and carbon prices up to 150 MCU/kg CO2e match it in only seven of twelve networks. Two documented disruptions on composite networks show what the model captures: after the 2021 power-rationing halt in Zhejiang, no carbon commitment against the frozen plan can be met without a recovery allowance; during the 2026 Strait of Gibraltar ferry closures, cumulative-cap plans left up to 190 t CO2e of unrepaid debt, removed by terminal repayment at an optimal premium of at most 0.38%. The results demonstrate the framework rather than estimate industry-wide effects.

title: REVISION SOBRE RUTEO DINÁMICO DE VEHÍCULOS Y EMISIONES DE CO₂
summary: Evidencias, metadatos bibliográficos y matriz de extracción del artículo "ANÁLISIS BIBLIOMÉTRICO SOBRE RUTEO DINÁMICO DE VEHÍCULOS Y EMISIONES DE CO₂ UTILIZANDO VOSVIEWER " (Diego Saúl Cueva Ramos, 2026 — Ingeniería de Sistemas, Universidad
content: Evidencias, metadatos bibliográficos y matriz de extracción del artículo "ANÁLISIS BIBLIOMÉTRICO SOBRE RUTEO DINÁMICO DE VEHÍCULOS Y EMISIONES DE CO₂ UTILIZANDO VOSVIEWER " (Diego Saúl Cueva Ramos, 2026 — Ingeniería de Sistemas, Universidad Nacional de Ucayali). El estudio caracteriza la producción científica sobre DVRP y sostenibilidad ambiental indexada en Scopus (evolución temporal, tipos de documento, fuentes, idiomas y estructura temática) mediante mapas de coocurrencia de términos, superposición temporal y densidad construidos con VOSviewer, complementados con una matriz de cribado y extracción algorítmica para el periodo 2022–2026. Búsqueda: Base de datos Scopus, consultada en noviembre de 2026 sin filtros iniciales de periodo o tipo documental mediante dos cadenas: Búsqueda General (Macro): TITLE-ABS-KEY("dynamic vehicle routing" OR "DVRP") (852 registros). Búsqueda Específica (Micro): TITLE-ABS-KEY(("dynamic vehicle routing" OR "DVRP") AND ("CO2" OR "carbon" OR "emission*")) (27 registros). Contenido del dataset: (1) exportaciones originales en formato CSV de Scopus con resúmenes (abstracts) y palabras clave (1_export_scopus_DVRP.csv y 2_export_scopus_DVRP_CO2.csv); (2) matriz de filtrado y extracción sistemática en Excel (Matriz_DVRP_CO2_Extraccion_Filtrado.xlsx) con el resumen PRISMA, el cribado de los registros únicos y la extracción técnica de los 18 estudios centrales (2022–2026); y (3) capturas en alta resolución de los seis mapas bibliométricos (vistas de red, superposición temporal y densidad para ambos conjuntos). Parámetros de VOSviewer: Mapa general (n = 852): coocurrencia de términos con umbral mínimo de 15 ocurrencias (81 términos distribuidos en 5 clústeres). Mapa específico (n = 27): coocurrencia de términos con umbral mínimo de 3 ocurrencias (23 términos en 3 clústeres)

title: Microwave Pre-treatment and Microstructural Evidence of Ore
summary: Abstract This study seeks to investigate the effect of microwave pretreatment on the grindability of ore using single-mode and multimode configurations. Particle size distribution analysis and SEM microstructural characterization were emplo
content: Abstract This study seeks to investigate the effect of microwave pretreatment on the grindability of ore using single-mode and multimode configurations. Particle size distribution analysis and SEM microstructural characterization were employed to evaluate comminution efficiency. Results show that microwave pretreatment significantly enhanced size reduction, with pretreated samples achieving a P80 of approximately 80 μm after 60 minutes of grinding, compared to 400 μm for untreated ore. Multimode pretreatment produced more extensive microcrack networks and interconnected fractures than single-mode treatment, correlating with improved grinding performance. These findings demonstrate that microwave pretreatment is an effective method for weakening ore microstructure and reducing grinding energy consumption.

title: Design, Techno-Economic Analysis, and Experimental Characterization of Molten Salt Electric Thermal Energy Storage Systems for Industrial Heat Decarbonization
source: ERA: Education and Research Archive (University of Alberta)
summary: The decarbonization of medium- and high-temperature industrial process heat above 100°C is constrained in cold-climate regions by a limitation of conventional molten salt thermal energy storage, namely its dependence on circulating salt thr
content: The decarbonization of medium- and high-temperature industrial process heat above 100°C is constrained in cold-climate regions by a limitation of conventional molten salt thermal energy storage, namely its dependence on circulating salt through external pumps and piping in which the salt freezes and damages equipment as ambient temperatures fall toward -40°C. This thesis develops and validates a single-tank electric thermal energy storage system that removes this limitation by storing the salt within one insulated tank and extracting heat internally through an embedded air-to-salt heat exchanger, so that no salt leaves the tank and the freeze-prone external loop is eliminated. The work proceeds as a single connected study, beginning with a cold-climate-specific conceptual design, establishing its economic case, demonstrating that its central components function as intended, and projecting the validated result toward industrial deployment. The economic case was established through a techno-economic and comparative assessment of the design for Alberta, Canada, configured at high temperature using binary chloride salts contained in engineered concrete tanks to deliver heat at approximately 700°C. Across nine charging scenarios and four carbon-pricing trajectories over a thirty-year lifetime, a grid-connected hybrid configuration combining concentrated solar thermal input with electric charging achieved a round-trip efficiency of up to 90%, the lowest levelized cost of heat among the renewable options at 19 dollars per megawatt-hour of heat, and use-phase emissions 83% below those of a natural gas baseline. These results identified the configuration as economically competitive but rested on the assumption that its central and previously undemonstrated components, the embedded heat exchanger and the thermocline on which single-tank operation depends, would perform as the models assumed. That assumption was tested by constructing a lab-scale thermal energy storage prototype based on the conceptual design, in which medium-temperature binary nitrate salts were used in place of the highly corrosive high-temperature chloride salts to limit corrosion effects on the thermal measurements. The prototype was charged to approximately 530°C and discharged with air across two laminar flow rates, while seven vertically distributed thermocouples measured the thermocline progression. The embedded heat exchanger achieved near-unity effectiveness at both flow rates, delivering hot air at a peak temperature of 520°C, close to the hottest salt temperature at the topmost region of the tank, where the exit of the coil is located. The thermocline strengthened during discharge rather than degrading, increasing the vertical temperature difference six-fold and preserving the thermal quality of the stored heat throughout extraction, in contrast to the mixing-driven degradation of the thermocline, typical of conventional single-tank systems. The measured experimental round-trip

title: Mobile signaling data reveal spatial synchrony between mega event population hotspots and commercial zones across transit isochrones
summary: Abstract Mega events cause late-night transit bottlenecks, yet point-based transit data cannot show where attendees are before entering stations. We quantified the spatial synchrony between mega-event population hotspots and nighttime comme
content: Abstract Mega events cause late-night transit bottlenecks, yet point-based transit data cannot show where attendees are before entering stations. We quantified the spatial synchrony between mega-event population hotspots and nighttime commercial zones with mobile signaling data from the Busan Fireworks Festival. Hourly net population (event minus baseline night) on the H3 grid was converted into Gi*-weighted kernel density surfaces and compared with commercial-facility surfaces within transit isochrones using a Fuzzy IoU. Among the three primary zones, the 0–60 min zone showed the highest concordance, peaking at 47.07% at 23:00, whereas the 0–15 and 60–120 min zones remained at 9–16%. Overlap in the 0–60 min zone exceeded two spatial null models; the zone ranking held under alternative baseline nights, most implementation settings and most alternative metrics, whereas the level of the index depends on the smoothing radius and on the set of input cells. The event night had 22–24% more stays per cell than the baseline night, with spatially clustered net population. These aggregate patterns are consistent with a staging role of districts within about one hour of transit travel, although the mechanism itself cannot be confirmed with aggregate data; 60 min is proposed as an operational reference range, not an optimum.

title: When does a model's estimate count as assurance evidence? Traceability, attributability and contestability, with a satellite worked example
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: An estimate that a model produces outside the reporting entity, such as a satellite methane rate, a machine-learning plume detection or a figure a language model extracts from a report, is not audit evidence just because it is accurate. Thi
content: An estimate that a model produces outside the reporting entity, such as a satellite methane rate, a machine-learning plume detection or a figure a language model extracts from a report, is not audit evidence just because it is accurate. This working paper proposes three conditions under which such an estimate becomes evidence: traceability (the chain from observation to figure can be re-walked), attributability (the figure can be tied to an identifiable facility, entity and accountable actor) and contestability (the reporting entity can rebut it on stated grounds). It sets out where such an estimate sits under ISSA 5000: as information from a source external to the entity (para 90), through a practitioner's expert (paras 56–58) or a management's expert (para 92), or not at all. A worked example traces published Tanager-1 and EMIT methane plumes near an underground coal mine in Queensland's Bowen Basin to the mine's Safeguard Mechanism figures. The provider documents and versions the quantification. Attribution, annualisation and the link to the reported figure are left to the user. The reported figure sets a unit-surrender obligation, so the gap reaches the financial statements. The example illustrates a method; it is not an estimate of any mine's emissions and does not suggest misreporting. The deposit includes a standard-library Python script that regenerates every figure in the worked example from public sources. Data sources: Carbon Mapper plume catalogue (used under Carbon Mapper's Terms of Use and cited, not redistributed); Climate TRACE (release 5.12.0); Clean Energy Regulator, 2024–25 baselines and emissions data. Retrieved 17 November 2026.

title: Smart Automated Menstrual Pads Incinerating Disposer Hybrid Assembly
source: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology
summary: This paper presents the development of an automated system for the hygienic disposal of used menstrual pads through controlled electrical incineration. The system uses an ESP32-S3 microcontroller to manage user detection, door locking, and
content: This paper presents the development of an automated system for the hygienic disposal of used menstrual pads through controlled electrical incineration. The system uses an ESP32-S3 microcontroller to manage user detection, door locking, and the overall operating process. A VL53LDK Time-of-Flight sensor detects the presence of a user and triggers the electromagnetic door lock to open, allowing 15 seconds for pad insertion. The system is designed to collect two pads per batch before automatically starting the incineration process. A ceramic heater operates for a preset duration of 14 minutes, reaching a maximum reported temperature of approximately 420 °C. The smoke generated during incineration is directed through a filtration unit containing activated carbon and HEPA filters, while the resulting ash is collected in a separate ash tray. The developed prototype integrates automated pad loading, batch-based incineration, smoke filtration, and ash collection into a single disposal system

title: Evaluating distributed construction with life cycle assessment: a scenario-based comparative study of construction-stage environmental impacts
source: The International Journal of Life Cycle Assessment
summary: Abstract Purpose Distributed construction (DC) decentralizes fabrication and assembly across multiple locations while planning and coordination remain centralized. Empirical data on its construction-stage greenhouse gas impacts relative to
content: Abstract Purpose Distributed construction (DC) decentralizes fabrication and assembly across multiple locations while planning and coordination remain centralized. Empirical data on its construction-stage greenhouse gas impacts relative to conventional construction and traditional modular construction are limited. This study addresses this gap by providing a scenario-based comparative life cycle assessment of DC’s construction-stage environmental performance using a U.S. hospitality project. Methods The study develops an attributional, comparative evaluation of life cycle greenhouse gas emissions (GHG) for a newly built hotel in Alpharetta, Georgia. The study evaluates three construction and production configurations: conventional construction (CC), traditional modular construction (TM), and a modeled distributed construction (DC) scenario that differs from TM mainly in its production and logistics network. The functional unit is the complete hotel project, with results also normalized per guestroom and per unit floor area. The system boundary follows EN 15978 production and construction stages A1–A5 and includes material production, transportation, construction energy and water use, and material impacts associated with construction waste. Scenario development draws on project documentation, published literature, industry presentations, professional meetings, and explicitly documented scenario assumptions. Sensitivity analysis examines key assumptions, including transport distance, facility proximity, payload and backhaul treatment, material-loss factors, construction duration, and energy intensity. Results and discussion Under the modeled assumptions, the DC scenario has the lowest modeled construction-stage A1–A5 GHG emissions among the three scenarios. Total A1–A5 emissions are approximately 1,168 t CO₂e for CC, 1,055 t CO₂e for TM, and 1,004 t CO₂e for DC, representing estimated reductions of 14% relative to CC and 5% relative to TM. DC’s incremental advantage over TM mainly comes from lower transportation and construction energy- and water-related impacts. Modeled material impacts are identical for TM and DC and about 8% higher than for CC because of the double-layer module walls, and DC waste-associated impacts are slightly higher than TM because of the additional kitting-stage loss. The advantage relative to CC depends strongly on the assumed CC site material-loss factor; TM no longer has lower emissions than CC when the CC site loss falls below approximately 15%. Sensitivity analysis indicates that transportation performance depends heavily on facility proximity; under the current route, payload, and return-trip assumptions, DC transportation emissions reach parity with TM at a Rapid Plant-to-site distance of approximately 178 miles (287 km). These results are scenario-dependent: DC remains below TM across the other tested parameter ranges, but the advantage disappears when the Rapid Plant is more than approximately 245 mi (395 km) from t

title: Loss of vegetation cover, surface warming, and depletion of carbon stocks in Surakarta City, Indonesia: A multitemporal Landsat analysis 2015–2025
summary: The expansion of built-up areas in medium-sized Javanese cities can reduce vegetation cover, increase land surface temperature (LST), and alter urban carbon stocks. This study assessed changes in vegetation cover, LST, and estimated carbon
content: The expansion of built-up areas in medium-sized Javanese cities can reduce vegetation cover, increase land surface temperature (LST), and alter urban carbon stocks. This study assessed changes in vegetation cover, LST, and estimated carbon stocks in Surakarta, Indonesia, in 2015, 2020, and 2025 using Landsat 8 OLI/TIRS imagery processed in ArcGIS Pro. Vegetation density was assessed using the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), while LST was derived from thermal band 10 with brightness temperature and emissivity corrections. Above-ground biomass was estimated from NDVI and converted to carbon stocks using a carbon fraction of 0.47; stocks were subsequently expressed as CO2 equivalents using a factor of 44/12. Between 2015 and 2025, the non-vegetated class expanded from 165.30 ha (3.54%) to 1,303.44 ha (27.92%), while the high-greenness class declined by 38%, from 584.74 to 362.66 ha. Minimum LST increased by 1.74 °C, and the mapped high-temperature zone expanded. Estimated carbon stocks decreased by 16.7%, from 22,776.04 to 18,971.93 t C, equivalent to approximately 13,948.40 t CO 2 e. About 80.95% of the estimated net carbon-stock loss occurred during 2015-2020. These findings highlight the importance of conserving urban vegetation and mature trees, while recognizing uncertainties associated with year-specific classification thresholds and the lack of local field calibration for the biomass model.

title: The Polar Energy Balance: A Carbon Dioxide Condensation Temperature and Latent-Heat Flux Budget
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: The polar energy balance is governed by a single temperature: the carbon dioxide frost point of 148 kelvin. This paper budgets it from first principles: thermal emission at the frost point is 27.2 watts per square metre, summer sunlight abs
content: The polar energy balance is governed by a single temperature: the carbon dioxide frost point of 148 kelvin. This paper budgets it from first principles: thermal emission at the frost point is 27.2 watts per square metre, summer sunlight absorbed by carbon dioxide frost is 175 watts per square metre, and subliming a metre of frost over a hundred and fifty days of spring demands 72.8 watts per square metre. The balance between absorbed sunlight, emitted heat and latent heat sets the timing of the seasonal cycle.

title: Climate narratives and media coverage in different regimes
summary: Different forms of government may exhibit different levels of environmental commitment. Previous studies indicate that democracies are often more likely than autocracies to adopt environmental protection policies. In this paper, we examine
content: Different forms of government may exhibit different levels of environmental commitment. Previous studies indicate that democracies are often more likely than autocracies to adopt environmental protection policies. In this paper, we examine whether regime type is also associated with differences in media coverage of climate change. As political institutions can be associated with press freedom and the media environment, we aim to investigate whether democratic and non-democratic countries differ in the volume of climate change reporting. Through a quantitative econometric analysis, we explore the relationship between political institutions and climate-related newspaper articles published by a selection of monitored media outlets. The analysis, based on media and institutional data for 16 countries over the period 2004–2023, examines whether democracies exhibit higher levels of climate change media coverage compared to their autocratic counterparts, while accounting for selected economic and environmental factors. In particular, we also consider whether autocracies display substantial climate-related coverage, potentially consistent with more centralized communication strategies, or whether climate change receives comparatively limited media attention. The results indicate a positive association between democratic status and the normalized volume of climate change media coverage across the specifications considered. However, the limited variation in political regime type over time and the relatively small number of countries prevent causal conclusions. Furthermore, the available data capture the volume of climate-related coverage but do not allow us to identify the content or political orientation of individual articles, or whether communication strategies are coordinated by political authorities.

title: Reforming tropical forest finance to unlock large-scale cooperation
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: This is a pre-print of an article submitted to peer-review. Abstract We combine a calibrated model of jurisdictional forest-conservation rewards with a voluntary-contribution game to study reforms to the Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TF
content: This is a pre-print of an article submitted to peer-review. Abstract We combine a calibrated model of jurisdictional forest-conservation rewards with a voluntary-contribution game to study reforms to the Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TFFF). At a donor cost of US\$1 billion yr⁻¹, direct funding, a uniform marginal reward and a budget-dependent reference level raise avoided emissions from about 9 to 40 MtCO₂ yr⁻¹. Using a global social cost of carbon of US$210 tCO₂⁻¹, the optimized mechanism implies an EU contribution of US\$0.8 billion yr⁻¹ and an EU–China coalition contribution of US\$6.7 billion yr⁻¹ purely based on self-interest. A binding 25% third-party match raises total funding to US\$13.1 billion yr⁻¹ and avoided emissions from 141 to 220 MtCO₂ yr⁻¹. Our results show how efficient reward design and conditional commitments can reinforce each other to mobilize international climate finance and deliver additional mitigation.

title: Train-Based Detection of Railway Insulated Joints Using Differential Eddy Current Sensors
summary: Abstract Ensuring rail infrastructure integrity is crucial for passenger safety and freight transport efficiency. Continuous monitoring of railway track components, therefore, plays a vital role in ensuring safe and reliable railway operati
content: Abstract Ensuring rail infrastructure integrity is crucial for passenger safety and freight transport efficiency. Continuous monitoring of railway track components, therefore, plays a vital role in ensuring safe and reliable railway operations. Traditional inspection methods, such as manual and visual inspections, often miss subtle defects, especially when track components are obscured due to harsh environmental conditions, leading to increased risks and costly maintenance. To address these challenges, a differential eddy current sensor was developed that can be mounted on in-service trains for regular inspections. As an electromagnetic-based non-destructive testing (NDT) method, the proposed sensor can inspect components without direct contact, making it ideal for detecting flaws under challenging conditions. This non-contact capability enables accurate, high-speed monitoring and detection of track components with minimal operational disruption. The current study focuses on detecting railway insulated joints using the proposed sensor system. The investigation includes results from laboratory tests and field measurements to evaluate sensor performance under realistic conditions. In addition, initial multi-physics simulation results are presented to illustrate the magnetic interaction between the sensor and track components. These simulations are particularly valuable for addressing data imbalance in future defect detection, by enabling the generation of representative data for rare or hard-to-observe fault.

title: Exploring Spatial Spillovers and Nonlinear Effects of New-Type Urbanization on Carbon Emissions: Evidence from Chinese Cities
source: Journal of Urban Planning and Development
summary: Abstract The harmonization of human development and ecological sustainability constitutes a fundamental objective within China’s modernization framework. This paper examines how new-type urbanization (NU) supports this balance through carbo
content: Abstract The harmonization of human development and ecological sustainability constitutes a fundamental objective within China’s modernization framework. This paper examines how new-type urbanization (NU) supports this balance through carbon intensity (CI) reduction. This paper utilizes data from 287 Chinese cities spanning 2013–2021 to comprehensively measure the indicators of NU based on the entropy weight method from five subsystems, including population urbanization (Pnu), economic urbanization (Ecnu), spatial urbanization (Spnu), social urbanization (Snu), and ecological urbanization (Econu). The threshold regression and spatial effects model are deployed to delve into the nonlinear link between NU and CI. The primary findings are threefold: (1) Ecnu and Pnu exhibit double-threshold effects on the link between NU and CI, while government technical support ( lngov ), Snu, Spnu, and Econu show single-threshold effects. The reduction effects of NU vary across different thresholds. (2) CI demonstrates strong spatial autocorrelation, with NU’s spillover effects transitioning from negative to positive. (3) Dynamic spatial panel analysis confirms an inverted U-shaped NU-CI relationship, with spillover effects transitioning from initially increasing to subsequently reducing carbon emissions in adjacent regions. These findings provide robust theoretical and empirical evidence for NU as a catalyst for achieving negative emissions in urban sustainability transitions.

title: Sustainable Tramway Superstructure Solutions: Design, Construction, and Life-Cycle CO2 Analysis for Livable Urban Environments
summary: Abstract The paper presents an attempt to estimate the ecological footprint over the entire lifetime of embedded rail track structures in tramways, using data from Hungary’s urban environment. Despite the numerous advantages of tramways, su
content: Abstract The paper presents an attempt to estimate the ecological footprint over the entire lifetime of embedded rail track structures in tramways, using data from Hungary’s urban environment. Despite the numerous advantages of tramways, such as reduced noise and vibration, continuous elastic rail support, and low maintenance requirements, there has yet to be an investigation of their environmental performance. Therefore, in the present study, the Life Cycle Assessment method was applied to examine an example embedded tram track structure composed of a 59Ri2 grooved rail, the relevant polyurethane and PVC materials used as embedding materials and void formers, and a reinforced concrete slab. Based on the applied database (ICE 3.0), the embodied CO 2 of the chosen track structure was calculated using 1-track-meter material quantities and transportation data, and expressed as components, each normalized by its service life. The results show that the sum of the components of the rail, the embedding material, and the PVC void formers account for 66.8% of the annualized embodied CO 2 . These components are replaced simultaneously with the rails. In the case of the concrete slab, despite its high initial embodied CO 2 due to the longer lifetime in the calculation, the total annualized embodied CO 2 is much lower. Based on the examination carried out for a period of 60 years, the total amount of embodied CO 2 for a 1-track meter-long rail track structure was 2353.416 kgCO 2 . With the method proposed in this study, a design-phase comparison of the applied solutions for the embedded rails can be conducted, and, through the optimization of the tramway infrastructure, it can be ensured that the rails have a long life, effective maintenance, and the use of resource-efficient materials.

title: Grade Separation Versus Reversible Median Lanes at a Saturated Urban Ring Road Junction in a Hot-Arid Gulf City: A Calibrated Microsimulation and Life-Cycle Appraisal for Kuwait’s Fourth Ring Road
summary: Ring roads carry most peak-hour traffic in Gulf cities, where buses serve under 6% of trips. The eastern end of Kuwait’s Fourth Ring Road is among the country’s most congested junctions, yet upgrade plans rest on default parameters. We buil
content: Ring roads carry most peak-hour traffic in Gulf cities, where buses serve under 6% of trips. The eastern end of Kuwait’s Fourth Ring Road is among the country’s most congested junctions, yet upgrade plans rest on default parameters. We built a Simulation of Urban MObility (SUMO) model from turning counts and a field-measured saturation flow of 2056 passenger car units per hour per lane, reproduced within 0.4%. Nine options, covering signal control, approach widening, grade separation of through traffic, a 222 m reversible median lane in two configurations and three combinations, were run at current, +25% and +50% demand in both peaks, with emission modelling and a 30-year appraisal. The grade separation package (overpass, slip roads, residual signal) cut mean delay from 60.0 s to 12.3 s, moved the signal user delay proxy from level-of-service (LOS) band E to C, held LOS C at +50% demand and reduced carbon dioxide emissions by 19%; its benefit–cost ratio is 1.6, above unity only if demand grows. Actuation and widening together cut delay by 25% and postponed breakdown by about a decade (benefit–cost ratio 6). The reversible lane had no effect at any demand level because the signal, not the mainline, limits capacity.

title: Characterizing ENSO Teleconnections Impact on Gross Primary Productivity across CMIP6 Earth System Models
summary: Abstract The El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) is the dominant mode of interannual variability in the climate system, altering global circulation patterns and causing changes in temperature and precipitation in remote regions through tele
content: Abstract The El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) is the dominant mode of interannual variability in the climate system, altering global circulation patterns and causing changes in temperature and precipitation in remote regions through teleconnections. Because ecosystems are sensitive to climate variations, ENSO teleconnections have large implications for the magnitude of carbon uptake by terrestrial vegetation at interannual timescales. Using ten CMIP6 Earth System Models during 1950–2014, we find global carbon uptake is reduced 0.68± 0.18 PgC per °C increase in the Nino3.4 sea surface temperature, primarily due to reduced gross primary productivity (GPP), with a secondary contribution from increased heterotrophic respiration. We quantify the ENSO impact on GPP and identify several key regions in the tropics (Amazon, Southeast Asia) and extratropics (Australia, Northwest North America) where the ensemble shows regionally coherent, statistically significant changes to GPP. In the Amazon, most models suppress GPP due to increased temperature, but three models exhibit a weaker reduction or slight enhancement in GPP. Inter-model differences in background soil moisture state mediate the relative importance of temperature compared to radiation in controlling total and ENSO-driven GPP variability in the Amazon, with drier models exhibiting a stronger temperature-driven response and tending to exhibit greater reductions in GPP associated with ENSO. Our results suggest that, across the ensemble, land model sensitivities to simulated physical climate anomalies play a large role in the GPP response to ENSO conditions and that these responses differ regionally even within the same latitude range.

title: Hydrophilic–hydrophobic flow-field engineering for passive water management in high-power-density PEMFCs
summary: Effective water management remains a major limitation to high-power-density proton exchange membrane fuel cells (PEMFCs), where excessive liquid-water accumulation restricts oxygen transport and intensifies concentration losses. This study
content: Effective water management remains a major limitation to high-power-density proton exchange membrane fuel cells (PEMFCs), where excessive liquid-water accumulation restricts oxygen transport and intensifies concentration losses. This study investigates a spatially engineered hydrophilic–hydrophobic flow-field strategy for passive water management, with particular emphasis on the orientation of surface wettability relative to reactant flow. Four configurations are evaluated using a three-dimensional, non-isothermal, two-phase electrochemical model: uniform wettability, hydrophilic-to-hydrophobic (Phil → Phob), hydrophobic-to-hydrophilic (Phob → Phil), and alternating wettability. The Phob → Phil configuration exhibits the best overall performance, increasing peak power density from 1.78 to 2.21 W cm -2 , corresponding to a 24.2% improvement over the reference case. Under high-load conditions, it reduces flooded cathode area from 31% to 15%, oxygen depletion from 34% to 18%, and mass-transport losses from 205 to 108 mV. Temperature non-uniformity and total exergy destruction are further reduced by approximately 42.9% and 28.4%, respectively. Moreover, 89.8% of the active area operates within ±10% of the mean current density, demonstrating substantially improved electrochemical uniformity. Capillary-pressure analysis reveals that performance is governed not simply by wettability contrast, but critically by its spatial direction along the flow path. These findings establish directional hydrophilic–hydrophobic engineering as an effective passive approach for coordinating water removal, oxygen accessibility, and membrane hydration while extending stable high-power-density PEMFC operation.

title: Geogenic Fluoride in Groundwater - Sources and Remediation
source: International Journal of Scientific Research in Science and Technology
summary: Fluoride-rich groundwater is a major health concern in arid and semi-arid regions, where long-term consumption of water containing fluoride above 1.5 mg/L can cause dental and skeletal fluorosis.In these aquifers, fluoride mainly originates
content: Fluoride-rich groundwater is a major health concern in arid and semi-arid regions, where long-term consumption of water containing fluoride above 1.5 mg/L can cause dental and skeletal fluorosis.In these aquifers, fluoride mainly originates from natural minerals such as fluorite, apatite, micas, and clays through water-rock interactions.This review connects the geological sources of fluoride with the chemical processes responsible for its release and accumulation in groundwater.It discusses the mineral sources and hydrogeological conditions that favour fluoride enrichment, along with the major factors controlling its mobilization, including mineral dissolution, alkaline pH, high bicarbonate levels, cation exchange, evaporation, groundwater residence time, and interactions with oxide and clay surfaces.The review also compares different fluoride removal methods, including adsorption, coagulation, ion exchange, and membrane processes, considering their removal efficiency, cost, waste generation, and suitability for rural communities.Finally, it identifies key research gaps, particularly the limited integration of mineral-scale processes with regional groundwater models and the lack of testing of remediation materials under real groundwater conditions.A framework is proposed to help select suitable fluoride mitigation methods based on local groundwater chemistry and environmental conditions.

title: Пројекат хотелско-пословног објекта са интегрисаним зеленим фасадама
source: Zbornik radova Fakulteta tehničkih nauka u Novom Sadu
summary: The paper deals with the design of a hotel-business building, with a particular emphasis on the integration of green spaces into the architectural solution. Through the application of green facades, terraces, and internal gardens, their imp
content: The paper deals with the design of a hotel-business building, with a particular emphasis on the integration of green spaces into the architectural solution. Through the application of green facades, terraces, and internal gardens, their impact on spatial quality, user comfort, and overall experience is analyzed. Special attention is given to the functional organization of the building and the integration of various facilities into a unified whole.

title: ОРГАНІЗАЦІЙНО-ФІНАНСОВІ ЗАСАДИ ПІДВИЩЕННЯ КАПІТАЛІЗАЦІЇ СУБ’ЄКТІВ ПРИРОДНО-ЗАПОВІДНОЇ СПРАВИ НА ОСНОВІ ЗАСТОСУВАННЯ ІНСТРУМЕНТІВ ВУГЛЕЦЕВОГО КРЕДИТУВАННЯ
summary: У статті розглянуто теоретико-методологічні та інституційні основи застосування карбонових сертифікатів як інноваційного фінансового інструменту розвитку територій природно-заповідного фонду України. Проаналізовано міжнародний досвід регуль
content: У статті розглянуто теоретико-методологічні та інституційні основи застосування карбонових сертифікатів як інноваційного фінансового інструменту розвитку територій природно-заповідного фонду України. Проаналізовано міжнародний досвід регульованих та добровільних ринків вуглецевих кредитів, зокрема специфіку систем EU ETS, California Cap-and-Trade та UK ETS, а також визначено можливості перенесення деяких їхніх елементів у вітчизняну практику. Обґрунтовано перспективність залучення установ природно-заповідного фонду до ринку вуглецевих кредитів з огляду на потенціал природних екосистем щодо поглинання та депонування вуглецю. Визначено послідовність підготовки, валідації, моніторингу, верифікації, випуску, обліку та реалізації карбонових сертифікатів. Доведено, що впровадження карбонових сертифікатів може бути перспективним напрямком диверсифікації джерел фінансування територій природно-заповідного фонду, сприяти капіталізації природних активів, відновленню екосистем, збереженню біорізноманіття та інтеграції України у європейські й глобальні ринки вуглецевих кредитів.

title: NOAA Global Systems Laboratory experimental pollen forecasting using the Pollen Emissions for Climate Models (PECM) with the Rapid-Refresh coupled to Chemistry (RAP-Chem) model
summary: Abstract. Pollen impacts millions of Americans, yet US-based operational models lack its representation. We evaluate real-time, tree, grass, and weed pollen forecasts from the Rapid-Refresh coupled to Chemistry (RAP-Chem) model and the Poll
content: Abstract. Pollen impacts millions of Americans, yet US-based operational models lack its representation. We evaluate real-time, tree, grass, and weed pollen forecasts from the Rapid-Refresh coupled to Chemistry (RAP-Chem) model and the Pollen Emissions for Climate Models version 2 (PECM v2.0) across North America for 2025. We evaluate RAP-Chem using counts from National Allergy Bureau (NAB) stations and a novel observational product from Pollen Sense. Pollen Sense correlated moderately with NAB (Spearman r = 0.50–0.70) and demonstrated moderate skill in reproducing phenology (start, peak, and end-of-season; SOS/POS/EOS), with mean absolute errors (MAE) for tree, grass, and weed pollen of 21.0/13.9/22.4 d; 5.2/18.4/6.6 d, and 19.2/44.2/21.4 d, respectively validating its spatial evaluation utility. At NAB stations, RAP-Chem best simulates weed pollen (r(NAB) = 0.74, r(Pollen Sense) = 0.75), followed by grass (0.53, 0.36) and tree (0.40, 0.29) pollen, with similar skill to Pollen Sense in reproducing NAB phenology (MAE = 19.9/20.7/13.8 d, 24.0/17.6/12.2 d, and 32.8/65.2/12.2 d). Total pollen has correlations r(NAB) = 0.44 and r(Pollen Sense) = 0.42. US-wide, RAP-Chem and Pollen Sense phenology agree best for weed pollen. RAP-Chem underestimates tree and grass pollen at most NAB sites and overestimates Pollen Sense tree pollen in forested areas. RAP-Chem grass and weed pollen magnitudes strongly depend on a post-processing correction for model-omitted gravitational settling, while correlation and phenology are unaffected. This experimental framework marks a critical advancement toward pollen forecasting and public health exposure management in the US.

title: Expanded ME-model analysis capabilities enable genetic recoding, proteostasis, RNA decay, and cofactor essentiality in bacterial models
summary: Genome-scale metabolic models (M-models) are widely used to understand and manipulate microbial metabolism in silico, and are characterized by an extensive availability of automated reconstruction, analysis tools, and simulation software. T
content: Genome-scale metabolic models (M-models) are widely used to understand and manipulate microbial metabolism in silico, and are characterized by an extensive availability of automated reconstruction, analysis tools, and simulation software. The scope and accuracy of M-models was greatly improved by the development of metabolic and gene expression models (ME-models) aimed to infer the optimal allocation of individual macromolecules such as proteins, RNA, and enzymatic complexes which constrain metabolic fluxes to their availability and abundance. Although ME-models reconstruction and simulation is currently aided by open-source software such as coralME, COBRAme, ECOLIme, and solveME, they lag behind their M-model counterparts and lack formal analysis tools such as gene essentiality analysis, that would facilitate a broader adoption of ME-models in research. Moreover, the rigid and incomplete formulation of ME-models limit advanced analyses they are theoretically capable of, including the simulation of genomically recoded organisms, protein homeostasis, enzyme cofactor essentiality, and RNA decay. Here, we present coralME v1.3, a vastly improved software version aimed to expand the applicability of ME-models by adding support for translation of non-canonical amino acids, protein and RNA degradation reactions, use of arbitrary coupling coefficients and parameter values, and formalized gene and cofactor essentiality analyses. This work expands, formalizes, and streamlines ME-model reconstruction and analyses for applied research.

title: The Interaction between Microplastics and Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons: Mechanisms and Ecosystem Consequences
summary: This review systematically examines the interactions between microplastics (MPs) and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) in environmental systems, with a focus on the factors governing their co-behavior and combined ecological effects.
content: This review systematically examines the interactions between microplastics (MPs) and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) in environmental systems, with a focus on the factors governing their co-behavior and combined ecological effects. The influence of MP properties, including polymer type, particle size, and aging characteristics, on the adsorption, transport, and bioavailability of PAHs across soil, aquatic, and atmospheric media is analyzed. Key mechanisms such as hydrophobic partitioning, π–π interactions, and surface adsorption are discussed in relation to environmental conditions such as salinity, pH, and organic matter content. Evidence on the combined toxicological effects of MP-PAH complexes on organisms is further synthesized. These interactions can lead to either synergistic or antagonistic outcomes across different species and exposure pathways. Based on identified research gaps, several critical directions for future studies are proposed, including the need for more realistic long-term exposures, advanced degradation techniques, and a better understanding of mixed pollutant dynamics. This review aims to provide a theoretical foundation for ecological risk assessment of coexisting MPs and PAHs and support the development of integrated strategies for environmental pollution prevention and control.

title: Valorization of pistachio shell waste into a biochar/Zeolite-13X composite for CO2 adsorption: Role of porous structure and surface chemistry
summary: Abstract In the present investigation, a biochar-based adsorbent was prepared from pistachio shell waste-derived biochar (BPS). The obtained biochar was modified with Zeolite-13X particles to prepare a BPS/Zeolite-13X composite. The adsorbe
content: Abstract In the present investigation, a biochar-based adsorbent was prepared from pistachio shell waste-derived biochar (BPS). The obtained biochar was modified with Zeolite-13X particles to prepare a BPS/Zeolite-13X composite. The adsorbents were used to capture carbon dioxide from a gas stream. SEM-EDX, FTIR, BET, and XRD analyses were performed to characterize the obtained adsorbents. According to the results, the surface area of BPS and BPS/Zeolite- 13X was 184.74 and 357.05 m 2 /g, respectively. The increase in surface area after the modification suggested that the surface properties of BPS were improved by adding Zeolite- 13X particles. Under the selected experimental conditions (80% CO₂ and 60 min), the experimental equilibrium CO2 adsorption capacities (qe) of BPS and the BPS/Zeolite-13X composite were 0.869 and 1.237 mmol g⁻¹, respectively. The highest adsorption capacity of the BPS/Zeolite-13X composite was obtained at a BPS/Zeolite-13X mass ratio of 70:30. The Sips isotherm predicted maximum adsorption capacities (qm) of 1.04 and 1.54 mmol g⁻¹ for BPS and BPS/Zeolite-13X, respectively. The isotherm and kinetic models demonstrated that the adsorption of CO2 was best described by the Sips and pseudo-second-order models for BPS and BPS/Zeolite-13X adsorbents. The mechanism of CO2 adsorption was clarified on the example of the BPS/Zeolite-13X composite, which revealed the presence of van der Waals forces, electrostatic attraction, and possible hydrogen bonding. Therefore, the fabricated adsorbent showed promising performance for CO₂ capture, demonstrating the potential of pistachio shell waste-derived materials.

title: Quantifying the Global Warming Potential of Trifluoromethyl Hypofluorite (CF 3 OF): Infrared Absorption Cross-Sections and Decay Measurements
summary: Abstract. Trifluoromethyl hypofluorite (CF3OF) is being investigated as an alternative gas for plasma processing, but assessment of its global warming potential (GWP) requires compound-specific measurements of infrared absorption and persis
content: Abstract. Trifluoromethyl hypofluorite (CF3OF) is being investigated as an alternative gas for plasma processing, but assessment of its global warming potential (GWP) requires compound-specific measurements of infrared absorption and persistence.
